modules.title: Two Pointers
modules.summary: Two indices move through a sequence under a rule, so each element is examined once instead of once per pair.

blocks.text: Two indices move through a sequence under a rule, so each element is examined once instead of once per pair.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Two people walking toward each other along a bookshelf, each stepping only when their side cannot be part of the answer.
Clues in the problem

items: The input is sorted, or can be sorted
You need a pair or triple that meets a condition
You compare elements from both ends, or merge two sequences

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Using it on unsorted data where order matters
Moving both pointers when only one should move
Off-by-one on l < r versus l <= r

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why is it safe to discard an element when you move a pointer?
blocks.text: With sorted input, the element at the pointer fails even with the most favourable partner still available, so it cannot be part of any answer.

blocks.title: How do you skip duplicates in a three-sum?
blocks.text: Sort first. Skip the fixed element when it equals the previous one, and after each hit move both inner pointers past equal values.
The problem in plain words
Two linked lists are each in ascending order. Splice their nodes into one ascending list and return its head.

rows: the non-empty list is the answer

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Equal values (taking from the first list keeps the merge stable)
One list much longer than the other

blocks.text: Brute force
Collect all values, sort, rebuild: O((n + m) log(n + m)).
Optimal approach
Use a dummy head and a tail reference. Repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes and advance that list. Attach whatever remains.

items: Create a dummy node; tail = dummy.
While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller and advance it.
Attach the leftover list and return dummy.next.

blocks.caption: mergeTwoLists

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Every node is attached once. The dummy node removes the special case for the first element.
Why it is correct
The list after dummy is always sorted and contains exactly the nodes consumed so far; the next node attached is the minimum of everything remaining.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Merge k sorted lists.
blocks.text: Put the head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its successor. O(N log k). Merging the lists pairwise in rounds gives the same bound.

blocks.title: Write it recursively.
blocks.text: If either list is empty return the other. Otherwise take the smaller head and set its next to the merge of the remainder. It uses O(n + m) call stack.

blocks.title: Why does <= keep the merge stable?
blocks.text: On a tie it takes the node from the first list, so equal elements keep their original relative order.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Merging two already sorted feeds, such as two time-ordered event logs. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 21: Merge Two Sorted Lists

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Merge Two Sorted Lists?
quiz.why: Every node is attached once. The dummy node removes the special case for the first element.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Ignoring case and everything except letters and digits, check whether the text reads the same forwards and backwards.

rows: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Only punctuation or spaces counts as a palindrome
Digits count as characters ("0P" is false)

blocks.text: Brute force
Build the cleaned string, reverse it, and compare: O(n) time and two extra copies.
Optimal approach
Clean once into an array, then walk inward from both ends comparing pairs. Stop at the first mismatch.

items: Lowercase and keep only letters and digits.
Set l at the start and r at the end.
While l < r, compare; on a mismatch return false.
Move both inward. If they meet, return true.

blocks.caption: isPalindrome

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Each kept character is compared at most once. This version uses O(n) space for the cleaned array because Swift String has no O(1) integer indexing; skipping unwanted characters with String.Index would bring space to O(1) at the cost of readability.
Why it is correct
A sequence is a palindrome exactly when position i equals position count − 1 − i for every i, which is what the two pointers check.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it without building a second array.
blocks.text: Use two String.Index values. Advance or retreat past characters that are not letters or digits, then compare the lowercased characters. O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: Allow deleting at most one character.
blocks.text: On the first mismatch, check whether the remainder is a palindrome after skipping the left character or after skipping the right one.

blocks.title: How do Unicode characters affect this?
blocks.text: A Character is a whole grapheme cluster, isLetter and isNumber accept non-ASCII characters, and case mapping can change the number of characters in some scripts. For ASCII input none of this matters; say which you assume.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Normalising and comparing user-entered codes while ignoring spacing and punctuation. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Valid Palindrome?
quiz.why: Each kept character is compared at most once. This version uses O(n) space for the cleaned array because Swift String has no O(1) integer indexing; skipping unwanted characters with String.Index would bring space to O(1) at the cost of readability.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Vertical lines of given heights stand at positions 0, 1, 2 and so on. Choose two lines so that the container they form with the ground holds the most water. The water level is set by the shorter line.
Edge cases

items: The tallest line is not necessarily used

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every pair of lines: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Start with the widest container, one pointer at each end. The shorter line limits the area, and moving the taller one inward can only make things worse, so move the shorter one.

items: Move the pointer at the shorter line inward; repeat while l < r.

blocks.caption: maxArea

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each step moves one pointer and they meet after n − 1 steps. Every line must be looked at, so O(n) is the floor.
Why it is correct
Suppose the left line is shorter. Any container using it with a line further in is narrower and no taller than this line, so it cannot beat the current area. That line can be discarded safely.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why move the shorter line and not the taller one?
blocks.text: The shorter line caps the water level. Keeping it and moving the taller line makes the container narrower without raising that cap, so the area can only shrink.

blocks.title: What if both lines have the same height?
blocks.text: Either pointer may move. Neither line can form a larger container with a line further in unless that line is taller, and moving one of them will find it.

blocks.title: How does Trapping Rain Water differ?
blocks.text: Here you choose two lines and ignore the ones between. In Trapping Rain Water every bar holds water above itself, limited by the tallest bars on both sides, and the amounts are summed.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Choosing two supports that maximise the usable span under a height limit. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 11: Container With Most Water

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Container With Most Water?
quiz.why: Each step moves one pointer and they meet after n − 1 steps. Every line must be looked at, so O(n) is the floor.

rows: O(1) besides the output and the sort

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find every distinct group of three values that adds up to zero. The same group of values must not be reported twice.
Edge cases
Brute force
Try every triple and de-duplicate with a set: O(n³).
Optimal approach
Sort the array. Fix the first value, then find pairs in the rest that sum to its negative using two pointers. Skip equal neighbours for the fixed value and after each hit so no triple repeats.

items: For each index i, skip it if it equals the previous value.
Set l = i + 1 and r = last; move l right when the sum is too small and r left when it is too large.
On a sum of zero record the triple, move both pointers, and skip values equal to the one just used.

blocks.caption: threeSum

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting is O(n log n) and each fixed value runs one linear two-pointer scan. No general algorithm substantially faster than quadratic is known for this problem.
Why it is correct
For a fixed first value the two-pointer scan finds every pair with the required sum, as in Two Sum II. Skipping duplicates only removes triples with identical values.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How do you extend this to four numbers?
blocks.text: Add an outer loop that fixes one more value and run the three-number method on the rest, skipping duplicates at each level. That is O(n³).

blocks.title: Find the triple whose sum is closest to a target.
blocks.text: Use the same sorted two-pointer scan, but instead of testing for zero keep the sum with the smallest distance to the target, and move the pointers by comparing the sum with the target.

blocks.title: Why is skipping duplicates on the left pointer alone enough?
blocks.text: After a hit both pointers move. Once the left value differs from the previous one, the required right value differs too, so the same triple cannot be formed again.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding three ledger entries that cancel out exactly. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for 3Sum?
quiz.why: Sorting is O(n log n) and each fixed value runs one linear two-pointer scan. No general algorithm substantially faster than quadratic is known for this problem.

lessons.title: 19. Remove Nth Node From End of List

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Delete the node that is n places from the end of a singly linked list and return the head, ideally in one pass.
Edge cases

items: Removing the head (n equals the length)

blocks.text: Brute force
Count the nodes, then walk to position length − n and unlink: two passes.
Optimal approach

Put a dummy node before the head. Advance a lead pointer n steps, then move lead and a trailing pointer together until lead is on the last node. The trailing pointer is then just before the node to remove.

items: dummy.next = head; lead and trail start at dummy.
Move both forward until lead has no next node.
Set trail.next = trail.next.next and return dummy.next.

blocks.caption: removeNthFromEnd

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass over the list with two references. The dummy node removes the special case of deleting the head.
Why it is correct
The gap between lead and trail stays n. When lead is the last node, trail is n nodes before it, which is the node just ahead of the one to delete.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is the dummy node needed?
blocks.text: When the head itself is removed there is no real node before it. The dummy node gives every node, including the head, a predecessor, so one piece of code handles all cases.

blocks.title: What if n can be larger than the length?
blocks.text: Stop while advancing the lead pointer if it reaches nil, and return the list unchanged or report an error, depending on what is agreed.

blocks.title: Do it recursively.
blocks.text: Recurse to the end and count on the way back. Each call returns its distance from the end; the call whose next node has distance n unlinks it. It uses O(n) call stack.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Dropping the nth most recent entry from a singly linked history. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 19: Remove Nth Node From End of List

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Remove Nth Node From End of List?
quiz.why: One pass over the list with two references. The dummy node removes the special case of deleting the head.

lessons.title: 167. Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
The numbers are already in ascending order. Find the two positions whose values add up to the target and report them counting from 1.
Edge cases

items: No valid pair (this solution returns an empty array)

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every pair, or binary-search the partner for each element: O(n²) or O(n log n).
Optimal approach
Put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, only moving the left pointer right can increase it; if too large, only moving the right pointer left can decrease it.

items: Compute the sum of the two ends.
Equal: return both positions plus one.
Too small: l += 1. Too large: r −= 1.

blocks.caption: twoSumSorted

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each step discards one position for good, so at most n − 1 steps happen. Sorted order is what makes discarding safe; no dictionary is needed.
Why it is correct
If the sum is too small, numbers[l] is too small even with the largest remaining partner, so it cannot be in any answer. The mirror argument applies to r.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Extend it to three numbers.
blocks.text: Fix one index and run the two-pointer search on the part to its right. O(n²) overall; skip equal neighbours to avoid repeated triples.

blocks.title: What if the array were not sorted?
blocks.text: Use the dictionary method in O(n) time and O(n) space, or sort first in O(n log n), keeping the original indices if they are needed.

blocks.title: Why is this better than the dictionary approach here?
blocks.text: It needs no extra memory and no hashing, and it uses the sorted order that the input already guarantees.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Pairing the lightest and heaviest parcels to hit a weight target from a sorted list. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 167: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted?
quiz.why: Each step discards one position for good, so at most n − 1 steps happen. Sorted order is what makes discarding safe; no dictionary is needed.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Bars of different heights stand side by side, each one unit wide. After rain, water collects in the dips between taller bars. Compute the total amount of water held.

rows: six unit cells of water in the dips
the gap of depth 3 between two walls

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Fewer than three bars hold nothing
Strictly rising or falling bars hold nothing

blocks.text: Brute force
For each bar, scan left and right for the tallest bars and add min(leftMax, rightMax) − height: O(n²).
Optimal approach

Water above a bar is limited by the shorter of the tallest bars on each side. Use two pointers. Always process the side whose current bar is lower: the other side is guaranteed to have a bar at least as tall, so the running maximum on this side alone decides the water level.

items: l and r start at the ends; leftMax, rightMax and water start at 0.
If height[l] < height[r], update leftMax, add leftMax − height[l], and move l right.
Otherwise update rightMax, add rightMax − height[r], and move r left.

blocks.caption: trap

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each bar is processed once. Precomputing prefix and suffix maximum arrays is also O(n) time but O(n) space; a monotonic stack is a third O(n) method.
Why it is correct
When height[l] < height[r], some bar at or right of r is taller than everything processed on the left so far, so the level over bar l is exactly leftMax. The mirrored argument holds on the right.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with prefix and suffix maximum arrays.
blocks.text: Build leftMax[i], the tallest bar from the start to i, and rightMax[i], the tallest from i to the end. The water over bar i is min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) − height[i]. O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.title: Solve it with a monotonic stack.
blocks.text: Keep a stack of indices with decreasing heights. When a taller bar arrives, pop the top as the floor of a basin; the water added is the distance between the new bar and the new top, times the height difference above the floor.

blocks.title: How does it change in two dimensions?
blocks.text: Use a min-heap seeded with all border cells. Repeatedly pop the lowest boundary cell and visit its neighbours: a lower neighbour holds water up to the boundary height and is then pushed with that height.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Estimating how much a terrain profile retains, such as pooling on an uneven surface. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Trapping Rain Water?
quiz.why: Each bar is processed once. Precomputing prefix and suffix maximum arrays is also O(n) time but O(n) space; a monotonic stack is a third O(n) method.

modules.title: Sliding Window
modules.summary: Maintain a contiguous range and its summary. Grow on the right; shrink on the left when the range breaks a rule.

blocks.text: Maintain a contiguous range and its summary. Grow on the right; shrink on the left when the range breaks a rule.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A train window passing scenery: new things enter on one side and old ones leave on the other.
Clues in the problem

items: The words contiguous, substring or subarray
Longest, shortest or count with a constraint
A window property that can be updated in O(1) when one element enters or leaves

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Recomputing the whole window on every move
Shrinking with if when the rule needs while
Using it for sums with negative numbers, where shrinking is not monotonic

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: When does a sliding window stop working?
blocks.text: When adding an element does not move the window's property in one direction, for example sums with negative numbers, or when the answer need not be contiguous. Prefix sums with a dictionary usually take over.

blocks.title: Fixed-size versus variable-size windows: what changes?
blocks.text: Fixed size: each step adds one element and removes one, with no inner loop. Variable size: grow on the right and shrink on the left with a while loop until the rule holds again.
The problem in plain words
Find the length of the longest stretch of consecutive characters in which no character appears twice.
Edge cases

items: A repeat that lies left of the window must be ignored ("abba")

blocks.text: Brute force
Check every substring for duplicates with a set: O(n³), or O(n²) with early exit.
Optimal approach
Sliding window. Move right one step at a time. Remember the last index of each character. If the new character was last seen inside the window, jump left to one past that index.

items: Convert to an array for O(1) indexing.
For each right index, look up the character's last index.
If that index ≥ left, set left = index + 1.
Record the new last index and update best with right − left + 1.

blocks.caption: lengthOfLongestSubstring

blocks.text: Why this complexity
right visits each character once and left only moves forward. A window with a repeat can never become valid by extending it, so skipping is safe.
Why it is correct
Invariant: chars[left...right] has no repeats. The check k ≥ left ignores stale entries from before the window. best records the largest valid window ever seen.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return the substring itself.
blocks.text: Record the window's start index whenever best improves, then build the string from that start and length.

blocks.title: Allow at most k distinct characters.
blocks.text: Keep a count per character. After adding the right character, shrink from the left while the number of distinct characters exceeds k, decreasing counts and removing zeros.

blocks.title: Why convert to Array<Character> in Swift?
blocks.text: Swift String cannot be indexed by integer in O(1); reaching offset i costs O(i). An Array<Character> gives O(1) access and still treats each user-visible character as one element.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Longest run of distinct events in a stream, for example distinct screens visited without a revisit. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 3: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters?
quiz.why: right visits each character once and left only moves forward. A window with a repeat can never become valid by extending it, so skipping is safe.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
You may change at most k characters of a string to any other letter. Find the length of the longest stretch that can be made of one repeated letter.

rows: change both As or both Bs

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: k = 0 reduces to the longest existing run
k at least the string length gives the whole string

blocks.text: Brute force
For every substring count the most common letter and test length − count ≤ k: O(n²) or worse.
Optimal approach
Sliding window. A window is fixable when its length minus the count of its most common letter is at most k. Grow on the right; while the window is not fixable, shrink from the left.

items: Add the right character to the counts and update maxCount.
While window length − maxCount > k, remove the left character and move left.

blocks.caption: characterReplacement

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Each character enters and leaves the window at most once. maxCount is never decreased; a stale larger value only keeps the window from shrinking below the best length already found, so the answer stays correct.
Why it is correct

The best answer needs a window whose true most-common count reaches a new high. Whenever that happens maxCount is updated exactly, so the window can grow to that answer. Until then the window never exceeds the best valid length seen.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is it safe not to decrease maxCount?
blocks.text: The answer only improves when a window has a higher most-common count than any before. A stale value can make the window keep its size instead of shrinking, but it never lets the window grow beyond what a real count justified.

blocks.title: Solve it with an exact maximum.
blocks.text: After removing the left character, recompute the maximum over the 26 counts. That costs O(26 · n), which is still linear.

blocks.title: What if only certain replacements are allowed?
blocks.text: Then the cost of fixing a window depends on which letters it contains, so track the cost per target letter separately, for example by running the window once per allowed target.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the longest period that could be made uniform with a limited number of corrections. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 424: Longest Repeating Character Replacement

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Longest Repeating Character Replacement?
quiz.why: Each character enters and leaves the window at most once. maxCount is never decreased; a stale larger value only keeps the window from shrinking below the best length already found, so the answer stays correct.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find the shortest stretch of one string that contains every character of a second string, counting repeats. If there is none, the answer is the empty string.

rows: the shortest stretch with an A, a B and a C

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: t needs a character more times than s has it
Several windows of the same length

blocks.text: Brute force
Check every substring against the required counts: O(n² · alphabet).
Optimal approach

Sliding window with a need table. need[c] is how many more of c the window requires; it goes negative for surplus. missing counts the characters still uncovered. Grow on the right; whenever missing is 0, record the window and shrink from the left until it stops being valid.

items: Count t into need; missing = length of t.
Add the right character: if need was positive, missing goes down; then decrease need.
While missing is 0: record the window if shorter, give the left character back, and if its need becomes positive, missing goes up.
Return the best window, or an empty string.

blocks.caption: minWindow

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each character of s enters and leaves the window at most once. The single counter missing avoids comparing whole tables.
Why it is correct
The window is valid exactly when missing is 0. For each right end the shrink loop finds the shortest valid window ending there, so the global shortest is seen.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why can need go negative?
blocks.text: A negative value records a surplus: the window holds more of that character than required. It lets the shrink step know that removing one does not break the window.

blocks.title: Return all shortest windows.
blocks.text: When a window ties the best length, add its start to a list instead of ignoring it; clear the list when a strictly shorter window is found.

blocks.title: What if the characters of t must appear in order?
blocks.text: Then it is a subsequence problem. Track for each position the latest start from which t can be matched in order, using DP or a forward and backward scan.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the shortest log excerpt that mentions every one of a set of required events. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Minimum Window Substring?
quiz.why: Each character of s enters and leaves the window at most once. The single counter missing avoids comparing whole tables.

modules.title: Fast/Slow Pointers
modules.summary: Two references move at different speeds. If there is a cycle they meet; if not, the fast one reaches the end while the slow one is at the middle.

blocks.text: Two references move at different speeds. If there is a cycle they meet; if not, the fast one reaches the end while the slow one is at the middle.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Two runners on a track: on a loop the faster one always laps the slower one.
Clues in the problem

items: Linked list cycle or middle node
A sequence defined by next = f(current)

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes
Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you find where the cycle starts?
blocks.text: After they meet, move one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's first node.

blocks.title: Why must the runners meet inside a cycle?
blocks.text: Inside the cycle the gap between them shrinks by exactly one node per round, so it must reach zero; the fast pointer cannot jump over the slow one.
The problem in plain words
Following next pointers from the head, decide whether you would ever revisit a node, that is, whether the list loops back on itself.
Edge cases

items: A single node pointing to itself
A cycle that starts at the head

blocks.text: Brute force
Store every visited node in a set and stop on a repeat: O(n) extra space.
Optimal approach
Floyd's method. Move slow one step and fast two steps. If fast runs off the end there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, fast gains one node per round and must land on slow.

items: Start slow and fast at the head.
While fast can move two steps, move slow one and fast two.
If they are the same node, return true.
If fast cannot move, return false.

blocks.caption: hasCycle

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Without a cycle fast reaches the end in n/2 rounds. With one, once both are inside the loop the gap shrinks by one each round, so they meet within one loop length.
Why it is correct
Inside a loop of length c the distance from fast to slow decreases by exactly 1 per round modulo c, so it reaches 0. Outside a loop, fast hits nil first.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Find the node where the cycle begins.
blocks.text: After the two pointers meet, move one back to the head and advance both one step at a time. They meet again at the first node of the cycle, because the distance from the head to that node equals the distance from the meeting point to it, modulo the cycle length.

blocks.title: Find the cycle length.
blocks.text: From the meeting point, keep one pointer still and step the other until it returns, counting the steps.

blocks.title: Why === and not ==?
blocks.text: === asks whether two references are the same object. Two different nodes may hold equal values, and a class is not Equatable unless you make it so.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Detecting a circular chain of references, such as a redirect that eventually points back to itself. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Linked List Cycle?
quiz.why: Without a cycle fast reaches the end in n/2 rounds. With one, once both are inside the loop the gap shrinks by one each round, so they meet within one loop length.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Return the middle node of a singly linked list. When the list has an even number of nodes, return the second of the two middle nodes.

rows: the second of the two middle nodes

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Even length returns the second middle

blocks.text: Brute force
Count the nodes in one pass, then walk count / 2 steps in a second pass.
Optimal approach
Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps at a time. When the fast pointer can go no further, the slow pointer is at the middle.

items: slow and fast start at the head.
While fast has a next node, move slow one step.

blocks.caption: middleNode

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The fast pointer covers the list in n / 2 iterations and no extra memory is used. It needs only one pass.
Why it is correct
After k iterations slow is at position k and fast at position 2k. The loop stops when fast is at or past the last node, which puts slow at position n / 2 rounded down, counting from 0.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return the first middle node for even lengths.
blocks.text: Stop one step earlier: loop while fast.next?.next exists. Slow then rests on the first of the two middle nodes.

blocks.title: Delete the middle node.
blocks.text: Keep a reference to the node before slow, and at the end link it past slow. A list with one node becomes empty.

blocks.title: Why does the loop test fast.next and not fast?
blocks.text: fast is advanced by two, so it may land on the last node or on nil. Testing fast.next covers both: optional chaining makes it nil in either case, and the loop stops.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Splitting a linked sequence in half before sorting or comparing the halves. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 876: Middle of the Linked List

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Middle of the Linked List?
quiz.why: The fast pointer covers the list in n / 2 iterations and no extra memory is used. It needs only one pass.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Rearrange a linked list so the nodes alternate from the two ends: first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on. Change the links in place; do not just change values.

rows: the middle node ends up last

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Empty list or one node: nothing to do
Two nodes stay as they are
Odd length leaves the middle node at the end

blocks.text: Brute force
Copy the nodes into an array and relink using two indices: O(n) extra memory.
Optimal approach
Three familiar steps. Find the middle with slow and fast pointers. Reverse the second half. Then weave the two halves together, taking one node from each in turn.

items: Move slow one step and fast two steps to find the middle.
Cut after slow and reverse the second half.
Take a node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half.
Repeat until the second half is used up.

blocks.caption: reorderList

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each phase is one pass over part of the list and only a few references are kept.
Why it is correct

After reversal the second half lists the last nodes in the order they are needed. Alternating from the two halves gives first, last, second, second-to-last. The first half is never shorter, so stopping when the second runs out is right.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why must the list be cut before weaving?
blocks.text: Without the cut, the first half still links into the second half, so the weave would create a cycle or lose track of where the first half ends.

blocks.title: Do it with a stack.
blocks.text: Push every node on a stack, then walk from the head taking n / 2 nodes from the stack and inserting each after the current front node. It uses O(n) extra memory.

blocks.title: Which three smaller problems does this combine?
blocks.text: Finding the middle of a list, reversing a list, and merging two lists alternately.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Interleaving the newest and oldest items of a feed without allocating a second list. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Reorder List?
quiz.why: Each phase is one pass over part of the list and only a few references are kept.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

An array of n + 1 numbers contains only values from 1 to n, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is repeated (possibly more than twice). Find it without changing the array and with constant extra memory.
Edge cases

items: The duplicate appears more than twice
The array must not be modified

blocks.text: Brute force
Use a set, or sort: O(n) extra memory or a modified array.
Optimal approach

Treat each index as a node whose arrow points to index nums[i]. Because two indices hold the same value, two arrows point at one node, which creates a cycle whose entry is the duplicate value. Find the entry with Floyd's method.

items: Move slow one arrow and fast two arrows until they meet.
Move both one arrow at a time until they meet again.
That meeting index is the duplicate value.

blocks.caption: findDuplicate

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Both phases take a number of steps proportional to n and use two integers. Binary search on the value range is O(n log n) with O(1) memory.
Why it is correct

Values lie in 1…n, so no arrow points to index 0 and the walk from 0 must enter a cycle. The cycle entry has two incoming arrows, from two indices holding its value. Floyd's second phase meets exactly at the entry.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why does the walk start at index 0?
blocks.text: Values are between 1 and n, so nothing points to index 0. That guarantees index 0 is outside the cycle, which the second phase of Floyd's method requires.

blocks.title: Solve it with binary search on the value.
blocks.text: Pick a middle value and count how many numbers are less than or equal to it. If the count exceeds the middle value, the duplicate is in the lower half; otherwise in the upper half. O(n log n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.title: What if the array may be modified?
blocks.text: Mark visits by negating the value at the index each number points to; meeting an already negative value reveals the duplicate. Or place each value at its own index by swapping.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Detecting a repeated identifier in a batch when memory is too tight for a lookup table. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 287: Find the Duplicate Number

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Find the Duplicate Number?
quiz.why: Both phases take a number of steps proportional to n and use two integers. Binary search on the value range is O(n log n) with O(1) memory.

modules.title: Prefix Sum
modules.summary: Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction.

blocks.text: Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Odometer readings: distance between two towns is one reading minus another.
Clues in the problem

items: Many range-sum queries on fixed data
Count subarrays with a given sum

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Off-by-one between prefix index and array index
Using it when the array is updated often (use a Fenwick tree instead)

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do prefix sums combine with a dictionary to count subarrays summing to k?
blocks.text: A run ending at j sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals prefix(j) − k. Keep a dictionary of prefix-sum counts, starting with [0: 1], and add the matching count at each step.

blocks.title: How does it extend to 2D?
blocks.text: Build pre[r + 1][c + 1] = cell + above + left − diagonal. Any rectangle's sum is then four lookups combined by inclusion and exclusion.

rows: O(n) to build, O(1) per query

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
An array never changes, and you will be asked many times for the sum of the values between two positions, inclusive. Answer each query in constant time.
Edge cases
Brute force
Add up the range on every query: O(n) per query.
Optimal approach
Precompute prefix sums once, with a leading 0 so that prefix[i] is the sum of the first i values. The sum of any range is then one subtraction.

items: For each value, append the previous total plus the value.

blocks.caption: NumArray

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The work is moved to construction. With q queries the total is O(n + q) instead of O(n · q).
Why it is correct
prefix[right + 1] sums positions 0 to right and prefix[left] sums positions 0 to left − 1. Their difference is exactly positions left to right.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if the array can be updated?
blocks.text: Use a Fenwick tree or a segment tree. Both support point updates and range sums in O(log n).

blocks.title: Extend it to a 2D matrix.
blocks.text: Build prefix[r + 1][c + 1] as the sum of the rectangle from the origin. A query combines four entries by inclusion and exclusion.

blocks.title: Why is the leading 0 useful?
blocks.text: It lets a range starting at index 0 use the same formula as any other, with no special case.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Answering 'total sales between day a and day b' instantly from daily figures. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 303: Range Sum Query - Immutable

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Range Sum Query - Immutable?
options: O(n) to build, O(1) per query
quiz.why: The work is moved to construction. With q queries the total is O(n + q) instead of O(n · q).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
For every position, compute the product of all the other numbers in the array, without using division.

rows: only the position holding 0 avoids multiplying by it

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: One zero: only that position is non-zero
Two or more zeros: everything is zero
Single element gives [1] with this code

blocks.text: Brute force
For each position multiply all the others: O(n²).
Optimal approach

The answer at i is (product of everything to its left) × (product of everything to its right). Sweep left to right writing the left products into the output, then sweep right to left multiplying in the right products.

items: Left to right: out[i] = prefix, then prefix *= nums[i].
Right to left: out[i] *= suffix, then suffix *= nums[i].

blocks.caption: productExceptSelf

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Two passes with two running variables. Every element must be read, so O(n) is the floor. Dividing the total product by each element would fail when a zero is present.
Why it is correct

After the first pass out[i] holds the product of nums[0..<i]. In the second pass suffix holds the product of nums[(i+1)...] when it meets index i, so the two factors together cover every element except nums[i].
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why not divide the total product by each element?
blocks.text: Division fails when any element is zero, and the problem usually forbids it. It can also lose precision or overflow differently with other number types.

blocks.title: How would you handle it if division were allowed but zeros may appear?
blocks.text: Count the zeros. With two or more, every answer is 0. With exactly one, only that position is non-zero and equals the product of the others. With none, divide the total by each element.

blocks.title: Can the same idea give prefix and suffix maximums?
blocks.text: Yes. Any operation that combines a left part and a right part works the same way: keep a running maximum from the left and another from the right.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Computing each item's share of a combined factor when that item itself must be left out. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 238: Product of Array Except Self

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Product of Array Except Self?
quiz.why: Two passes with two running variables. Every element must be read, so O(n) is the floor. Dividing the total product by each element would fail when a zero is present.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Count the contiguous runs whose values add up to exactly k. Values may be negative.
Edge cases

items: Negative numbers make a sliding window invalid
The run may start at index 0, which is why prefix sum 0 is pre-counted

blocks.text: Brute force
Sum every (start, end) pair with a running total: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Track the running sum. A run ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals sum − k. Keep a dictionary of how often each prefix sum has occurred.

items: Add the current value to sum.
Record the new sum in seen.

blocks.caption: subarraySum

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass with O(1) average dictionary operations. A sliding window cannot be used because negative values mean growing the window does not always grow the sum.
Why it is correct
sum(i…j) = prefix(j) − prefix(i − 1). For each j the lookup counts every i with prefix(i − 1) = prefix(j) − k. Counting before inserting keeps empty runs out.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is seen initialised with [0: 1]?
blocks.text: It stands for the empty prefix. Without it, runs that start at index 0, where the running sum itself equals k, would not be counted.

blocks.title: Return the longest such run instead of the count.
blocks.text: Store only the first index at which each prefix sum appears, starting with [0: −1]. The longest run ending at i has length i − firstIndex[sum − k].

blocks.title: What if all numbers are positive?
blocks.text: A sliding window then works in O(1) space, because adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting time spans whose net change equals a given amount in a ledger of credits and debits. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 560: Subarray Sum Equals K

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Subarray Sum Equals K?
quiz.why: One pass with O(1) average dictionary operations. A sliding window cannot be used because negative values mean growing the window does not always grow the sum.

modules.title: Hashing
modules.summary: Trade memory for time: a Set or Dictionary answers 'have I seen this?' in O(1) on average.

blocks.text: Trade memory for time: a Set or Dictionary answers 'have I seen this?' in O(1) on average.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A coat check: hand over a ticket (key) and get the coat (value) without searching the racks.
Clues in the problem
Template
Common mistakes

items: Assuming dictionary order is stable in Swift
Using a mutable or expensive key

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What makes a type Hashable?
blocks.text: It provides hash(into:) and ==, and equal values always produce equal hashes. Structs and enums whose members are Hashable get this synthesised.

blocks.title: When would a sorted array beat a dictionary?
blocks.text: When you need order, ranges or nearest-value queries, when memory is tight, when the data is small and static, or when you need worst-case guarantees.
The problem in plain words
You get a list of numbers and a target. Find the two positions whose values add up to the target. Each position can be used once.
Edge cases

items: The same value twice, e.g. [3, 3] with target 6
No valid pair (this solution returns an empty array)
A number that is exactly half the target must not pair with itself

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every pair (i, j) with j > i and check the sum. Two nested loops: O(n²) time, O(1) space.
Optimal approach

Walk the array once. For each value x, the partner you need is target − x. Keep a dictionary of values already seen and their index. If the partner is in the dictionary you are done; otherwise store x.

items: Create an empty dictionary value → index.
For each index i and value x, compute need = target − x.
If need is a key, return [seen[need], i].
Otherwise record seen[x] = i and continue.

blocks.caption: twoSum

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Every element is visited once and each dictionary lookup or insert is O(1) on average. You cannot do better than reading each element, so O(n) time is asymptotically best. The cost is O(n) extra memory; sorting with two pointers uses less memory but takes O(n log n).
Why it is correct

When index i is processed, every earlier index is in the dictionary. If a valid pair (j, i) with j < i exists, nums[j] is found at step i. Storing x only after the lookup prevents an element pairing with itself.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What changes if the array is already sorted?
blocks.text: Use two pointers, one at each end. Move the left pointer right when the sum is too small and the right pointer left when it is too large. O(n) time, O(1) space, no dictionary.

blocks.title: How would you return all pairs, not just one?
blocks.text: Do not return at the first hit. Store a list of indices for each value, and for every element emit a pair with each earlier index of its complement. The output itself can hold O(n²) pairs.

blocks.title: What if the same pair must not be reported twice?
blocks.text: For value pairs, sort and use two pointers, skipping over equal neighbours after each hit. Alternatively keep a set of pairs already reported, stored as (smaller, larger).

blocks.title: Why is the lookup done before the insert?
blocks.text: If the value were stored first, an element equal to half the target would find itself and be paired with its own index.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding two cart items that exactly use a gift-card balance; matching a debit to a credit in a ledger. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Two Sum?
quiz.why: Every element is visited once and each dictionary lookup or insert is O(1) on average. You cannot do better than reading each element, so O(n) time is asymptotically best. The cost is O(n) extra memory; sorting with two pointers uses less memory but takes O(n log n).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Decide whether any value appears more than once in the array.
Edge cases

items: Empty array or one element is false
The duplicate may be the last element
Large value ranges rule out a counting array

blocks.text: Brute force
Compare every pair: O(n²) time, O(1) space.
Optimal approach
Insert each value into a Set. Set.insert reports whether the value was new; the first time it is not, a duplicate exists.

items: If the insert reports it was already present, return true.
If the loop ends, return false.

blocks.caption: containsDuplicate

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass with O(1) average set operations. Sorting first needs O(1) extra space but O(n log n) time; which is better depends on whether memory or time is tighter.
Why it is correct
The set holds exactly the values seen so far, so a failed insert means the current value occurred earlier.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if duplicates must be within k positions of each other?
blocks.text: Keep a set holding only the last k values. Before inserting index i, remove nums[i − k − 1] once the window is full. A dictionary of last-seen index also works.

blocks.title: How would you do it with O(1) extra space?
blocks.text: Sort in place and compare neighbours. O(n log n) time, and it changes the input order.

blocks.title: Why use insert(_:).inserted rather than contains then insert?
blocks.text: insert returns whether the value was new, so one hash lookup does the work of contains followed by insert.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Rejecting a second submission with the same idempotency key. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Contains Duplicate?
quiz.why: One pass with O(1) average set operations. Sorting first needs O(1) extra space but O(n log n) time; which is better depends on whether memory or time is tighter.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Decide whether two strings contain exactly the same characters with the same counts, in any order.

rows: t has a c that s lacks

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Repeated letters must match in count
Unicode characters work because the key is Character

blocks.text: Brute force
Sort both strings and compare: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
Count every character of the first string. Then walk the second string, using up one count per character. A character with no count left means failure. At the end every count must be zero.

items: Count the characters of s in a dictionary.
For each character of t, fail if its count is missing or zero.
Return whether all counts are zero.

blocks.caption: isAnagram

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each character is handled once with O(1) dictionary work. Both strings must be read fully, so O(n) is the floor.
Why it is correct
The loop over t never lets a count go negative, so t uses no character more often than s has it. The final check ensures s has nothing left over, so the counts are identical.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it for lowercase letters only with a fixed array.
blocks.text: Use an array of 26 integers indexed by the letter's distance from "a", reading the strings as UTF-8 bytes. Increment for s, decrement for t, and require all zeros.

blocks.title: Why is the final all-zero check needed?
blocks.text: Without it, a t that is shorter than s would pass, because the loop only detects characters that t has too many of. Comparing lengths first is an equivalent fix.

blocks.title: How would you find all anagrams of a word inside a long text?
blocks.text: Slide a window of the word's length across the text, keeping letter counts for the window, and compare with the word's counts at each position. O(n) overall.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Checking that two inventories list the same items in the same quantities regardless of order. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Valid Anagram?
quiz.why: Each character is handled once with O(1) dictionary work. Both strings must be read fully, so O(n) is the floor.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Put words into groups so that every word in a group uses exactly the same letters the same number of times.

rows: the empty word forms its own group

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Duplicate words stay in the same group
The order of groups is not fixed, because Swift dictionary order is not fixed

blocks.text: Brute force
Compare every pair of words letter by letter: O(n² · L).
Optimal approach
Give each word a canonical key that all its anagrams share: its letters in sorted order. Use that key in a dictionary whose values are the groups.

items: Create an empty dictionary from key to list of words.
For each word, sort its letters to form the key.
Append the word to the list under that key.

blocks.caption: groupAnagrams

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting a word of length L costs L log L and there are n words. Using 26 letter counts as the key removes the log factor, giving O(n · L).
Why it is correct
Two words are anagrams exactly when their sorted letters are identical, so the key is the same for words in one group and different across groups.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How do you avoid sorting each word?
blocks.text: Count the 26 letters of each word and use the counts as the key, for example as an array of 26 integers, which is Hashable. That costs O(L) per word.

blocks.title: What if the words contain Unicode characters?
blocks.text: Sorting Characters still gives a correct key. A fixed 26-slot count no longer works, so use a dictionary of character counts or the sorted string. Decide whether accents and case should be treated as equal.

blocks.title: How would you return the groups in a stable order?
blocks.text: Remember the order in which keys first appear in a separate array and output the groups in that order, or sort the groups at the end.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding records that are the same set of tokens in a different order. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Group Anagrams?
quiz.why: Sorting a word of length L costs L log L and there are n words. Using 26 letter counts as the key removes the log factor, giving O(n · L).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
From an unsorted list of integers, find the length of the longest run of consecutive values such as 1, 2, 3, 4. The values may appear anywhere in the list.
Edge cases
Brute force
Sort and scan for runs: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
Put everything in a set. A value x starts a run only if x − 1 is absent. For each such start, count upward while the next value is present. Values that are not starts are skipped.

items: Build a set of the values.
For each x in the set, skip it if x − 1 is in the set.
Otherwise count x + 1, x + 2 and so on while they are present.

blocks.caption: longestConsecutive

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The inner loop runs only from the first value of each run, so each value is visited by it at most once. Total work is O(n) despite the nested loop.
Why it is correct
Every run has exactly one smallest value, which is the only member whose predecessor is missing. Counting upward from it measures the whole run.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is the loop not O(n²)?
blocks.text: The counting loop starts only at the smallest value of each run. Every value belongs to one run and is stepped over once, so the inner loops total at most n steps.

blocks.title: Return the run itself, not just its length.
blocks.text: Remember the starting value along with the best length, then produce start, start + 1 and so on.

blocks.title: Solve it with Union Find.
blocks.text: Union each value with value + 1 when that is also present, tracking component sizes. The largest component is the answer. It works but is heavier than the set method.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the longest unbroken streak of days from an unordered list of activity dates. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Longest Consecutive Sequence?
quiz.why: The inner loop runs only from the first value of each run, so each value is visited by it at most once. Total work is O(n) despite the nested loop.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Build a store with a fixed capacity that supports get and put in constant time. When it is full and a new key arrives, it discards the entry that was used least recently. Reading or updating an entry counts as using it.

rows: capacity 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2)
adding key 3 evicts key 2, the least recently used

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Updating an existing key must not evict anything
get on a missing key returns −1
A get changes the eviction order

blocks.text: Brute force
Keep an array ordered by recency and search it: O(n) per operation.
Optimal approach

Combine a dictionary with a doubly linked list. The dictionary finds a key's node in O(1). The list keeps nodes in recency order: most recent at the front, least recent at the back. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove edge cases.

items: get: look up the node; if missing return −1; otherwise move it to the front and return its value.
put on an existing key: update the value and move the node to the front.
put on a new key when full: unlink the node before the tail and remove its key from the dictionary.
Create the new node, store it in the dictionary and put it at the front.

blocks.caption: LRUCache

blocks.text: Why this complexity
A doubly linked node can be unlinked without searching, and the dictionary gives direct access to it. Neither structure alone can do both jobs in constant time.
Why it is correct
Every use moves a node to the front, so the list is always ordered by last use and the node before the tail is the least recently used. The dictionary and the list always contain the same keys.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why a doubly linked list and not a singly linked one?
blocks.text: Removing a node needs its predecessor. With a doubly linked list that is one step; a singly linked list would need a search from the head.

blocks.title: Why is prev declared weak?
blocks.text: Each node's next reference already owns the following node. If prev were also strong, neighbouring nodes would own each other and ARC could never free them.

blocks.title: How would you make it safe to use from several threads?
blocks.text: Guard get and put with a lock or run them on a serial queue, or make the cache an actor. Even get must be guarded because it changes the order.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Keeping recently viewed images in memory under a fixed budget. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for LRU Cache?
quiz.why: A doubly linked node can be unlinked without searching, and the dictionary gives direct access to it. Neither structure alone can do both jobs in constant time.

modules.title: Binary Search
modules.summary: Halve a search range using a yes/no test that flips exactly once across the range.

blocks.text: Halve a search range using a yes/no test that flips exactly once across the range.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Guessing a number when told higher or lower.
Clues in the problem

items: 'Smallest value such that…' or 'largest value such that…'
A monotonic feasibility check over an answer range

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Infinite loop from the wrong mid or update
Applying it when the predicate is not monotonic

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Find the first true in FFFTTT.
blocks.text: Use a half-open range: lo = 0, hi = n. While lo < hi, test mid; if true set hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. lo is the first true, or n if there is none.

blocks.title: How do you binary search on an answer rather than an index?
blocks.text: Find a yes/no test over candidate answers that flips exactly once, then binary search the candidate range for the first value that passes.
The problem in plain words
Find the position of a target in an ascending array, or report −1 if it is absent, without scanning every element.
Edge cases

items: Target smaller than the first or larger than the last element
lo + hi can overflow in fixed-width integers

blocks.text: Brute force
Linear scan: O(n).
Optimal approach
Keep a closed range [lo, hi] that must contain the target if it exists. Compare the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain it.

items: While lo ≤ hi, take mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2.
Equal: return mid. Smaller than target: lo = mid + 1. Larger: hi = mid − 1.

blocks.caption: search

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each step halves the range. In the comparison model, log₂ n comparisons are needed to distinguish n positions, so this is optimal.
Why it is correct
Invariant: if the target exists, its index is in [lo, hi]. Each branch removes only indices proven not to hold the target. The range shrinks every loop, so the loop ends.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Find the first position of a duplicated target.
blocks.text: When nums[mid] equals the target, record mid and keep searching the left half (hi = mid − 1). Equivalently, find the first index whose value is ≥ target and check it.

blocks.title: Search a rotated sorted array.
blocks.text: At every step at least one half is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half's value range; if so search there, otherwise search the other half. Still O(log n).

blocks.title: Binary search on an answer range instead of an array.
blocks.text: Define a yes/no test that is false up to some value and true after it, for example 'can the work finish at speed x'. Binary search the range of candidate answers for the first value that passes.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Looking up a timestamp in a sorted log or finding which price slab an order value falls in. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Binary Search?
quiz.why: Each step halves the range. In the comparison model, log₂ n comparisons are needed to distinguish n positions, so this is optimal.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
An ascending array of distinct numbers was rotated: some front part was moved to the back. Find the index of a target, or −1, in logarithmic time.
Edge cases
Brute force
Linear scan: O(n).
Optimal approach

Binary search still works because at least one side of the midpoint is always in normal sorted order. Check which side is sorted, test whether the target lies inside that side's range, and keep that side or the other accordingly.

items: lo = 0, hi = last index; mid = middle.
If nums[mid] is the target, return mid.
If nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] the left half is sorted: go left when the target is within [nums[lo], nums[mid]), otherwise right.
Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right when the target is within (nums[mid], nums[hi]], otherwise left.

blocks.caption: searchRotated

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The range halves every step, exactly as in plain binary search. Only the rule for choosing a half changes.
Why it is correct
The rotation point lies in at most one half, so the other half is sorted and its end values bound everything in it. The target is in that half exactly when it lies between those ends.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What changes if duplicates are allowed?
blocks.text: When nums[lo], nums[mid] and nums[hi] are all equal you cannot tell which half is sorted. Shrink the range by one from each end and continue. The worst case becomes O(n).

blocks.title: Find the minimum element instead.
blocks.text: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] is larger the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Stop when lo equals hi.

blocks.title: Why is the comparison nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] and not <?
blocks.text: When lo equals mid, which happens with two elements, the left half is a single element and counts as sorted. Using < would send that case to the wrong branch.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Looking up a value in a circular buffer whose contents are sorted but whose start has moved. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 33: Search in Rotated Sorted Array

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Search in Rotated Sorted Array?
quiz.why: The range halves every step, exactly as in plain binary search. Only the rule for choosing a half changes.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A grid of numbers has each row in ascending order, and each row starts with a value larger than the last value of the row above. Decide whether a target is in the grid.
Edge cases

items: Target smaller than the first or larger than the last value

blocks.text: Brute force
Scan every cell: O(rows × cols).
Optimal approach
Read row by row, the grid is one long sorted list. Run an ordinary binary search over positions 0 to rows × cols − 1, converting a position to a cell with division and remainder.

items: mid is a position; its cell is row mid / cols, column mid % cols.
Compare that value with the target.
Move lo or hi as in a normal binary search.

blocks.caption: searchMatrix

blocks.text: Why this complexity
It is a single binary search over rows × cols sorted values. Searching for the row first and then within it costs the same.
Why it is correct
The two ordering rules make the row-by-row reading strictly ascending, so the binary search invariant holds on the flattened positions.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if rows and columns are each sorted but rows do not chain?
blocks.text: Start at the top-right corner. Move left when the value is too large and down when it is too small. Each step discards a row or a column, giving O(rows + cols).

blocks.title: Solve it with two binary searches.
blocks.text: First binary-search the rows for the last row whose first value is ≤ target, then binary-search inside that row. The cost is log rows + log cols, the same total.

blocks.title: Why use division and remainder by cols, not rows?
blocks.text: A row holds cols values, so position p is in row p / cols at column p % cols. Dividing by rows would only be right for a square grid.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Looking up a value in a sorted table stored page by page. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Search a 2D Matrix?
quiz.why: It is a single binary search over rows × cols sorted values. Searching for the row first and then within it costs the same.

lessons.title: 153. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
An ascending array of distinct numbers was rotated. Find its smallest element in logarithmic time.
Edge cases

items: Values are assumed distinct and the array non-empty

blocks.text: Brute force
Scan for the smallest value: O(n).
Optimal approach
Compare the middle value with the last value of the range. If the middle is larger, the drop to the minimum lies to its right. Otherwise the minimum is the middle or to its left.

items: If nums[mid] > nums[hi], set lo = mid + 1.
Otherwise set hi = mid. When lo equals hi, that element is the minimum.

blocks.caption: findMin

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The range halves each step. Comparing with nums[hi] rather than nums[lo] avoids a special case when the range is not rotated.
Why it is correct

Invariant: the minimum is always inside [lo, hi]. If nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum cannot be at or left of mid. Otherwise the part right of mid is ascending from mid, so nothing there beats nums[mid].
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why hi = mid and not mid − 1?
blocks.text: mid may itself be the minimum. Setting hi = mid − 1 could discard it. Because the loop runs while lo < hi and mid is always below hi, hi = mid still shrinks the range.

blocks.title: What changes with duplicates?
blocks.text: When nums[mid] equals nums[hi] you cannot tell which side holds the minimum, so reduce hi by one. The worst case becomes O(n).

blocks.title: How do you find the rotation count?
blocks.text: It is the index of the minimum element, which this search already locates in lo.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Locating the start of data in a sorted circular buffer. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 153: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array?
quiz.why: The range halves each step. Comparing with nums[hi] rather than nums[lo] avoids a special case when the range is not rotated.

rows: O(n log m), m = largest pile

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
There are piles of bananas and a number of hours. Each hour one pile is chosen and up to k bananas are eaten from it. Find the smallest whole k that finishes every pile in time.

rows: one hour per pile, so k must cover the largest

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: h equal to the number of piles forces k = the largest pile
A pile smaller than k still costs a full hour
h is assumed to be at least the number of piles

blocks.text: Brute force
Try k = 1, 2, 3 and so on until the hours fit: O(max pile × n).
Optimal approach

Binary search on the answer. For a given speed, the hours needed are the sum of each pile divided by the speed, rounded up. More speed never needs more hours, so the speeds that work form an unbroken upper range; find its lower end.

items: Take the middle speed and compute the hours it needs.
If the hours fit, the answer is this speed or lower: hi = speed.
Otherwise lo = speed + 1. When lo equals hi, return it.

blocks.caption: minEatingSpeed

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are log m candidate speeds and each check scans the n piles. The search is over the answer range, not over the array.
Why it is correct
The test 'hours(speed) ≤ h' is false for small speeds and true from some speed onward. The loop keeps the first true inside [lo, hi] and shrinks until one value remains.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is hi = speed and not speed − 1?
blocks.text: The middle speed may itself be the smallest that works, so it must stay in the range. Because the loop runs while lo < hi and speed is below hi, the range still shrinks.

blocks.title: How do you round up with integer arithmetic?
blocks.text: Compute (pile + speed − 1) / speed. Adding speed − 1 before dividing pushes any remainder up to the next whole number.

blocks.title: Name another problem solved by searching the answer.
blocks.text: Examples: the smallest ship capacity to deliver packages within d days, splitting an array so the largest part is minimal, and the smallest divisor keeping a sum under a threshold.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Choosing the smallest processing rate that clears a set of queues before a deadline. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Koko Eating Bananas?
options: O(n log m), m = largest pile
quiz.why: There are log m candidate speeds and each check scans the n piles. The search is over the answer range, not over the array.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Two arrays are each sorted. Find the median of all their values together, in logarithmic time, without merging them.
Edge cases

items: Even total: average of the two middle values
All of one array smaller than the other

blocks.text: Brute force
Merge both arrays and read the middle: O(m + n).
Optimal approach

Split the combined values into a left half and a right half. If the left half takes i values from the shorter array it must take half − i from the other. Binary-search i until every value on the left is no larger than every value on the right.

items: Let a be the shorter array; half = (total + 1) / 2.
Pick i in the middle of the range; j = half − i.
If a's last left value exceeds b's first right value, i is too large; if b's last left value exceeds a's first right value, i is too small.
Otherwise the split is correct: the median comes from the values next to the split.

blocks.caption: findMedianSortedArrays

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The search is over the split position in the shorter array only. Sentinels for 'nothing on this side' remove the edge cases.
Why it is correct
A split is right exactly when aLeft ≤ bRight and bLeft ≤ aRight. Moving i up raises aLeft and lowers bLeft, so the two failure conditions tell which way to move, and a valid i always exists.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why search the shorter array?
blocks.text: The split in the other array is half − i. Searching the shorter one keeps that value from going negative or past the end, and makes the cost log of the smaller length.

blocks.title: Find the kth smallest of the two arrays.
blocks.text: Use the same partition idea with k in place of half, or repeatedly discard k / 2 elements from whichever array has the smaller value at that offset.

blocks.title: What do the Int.min and Int.max stand for?
blocks.text: They mean 'nothing on this side of the split'. Int.min never exceeds a right-hand value and Int.max is never below a left-hand value, so the comparisons still work at the ends.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Combining two sorted latency samples to report a median without merging them. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
