modules.title: Monotonic Stack
modules.summary: Keep a stack whose values only increase or only decrease. Popping resolves the 'next greater/smaller' for the popped item.

blocks.text: Keep a stack whose values only increase or only decrease. Popping resolves the 'next greater/smaller' for the popped item.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A queue of people where anyone shorter than a newcomer leaves, because they can no longer see ahead.
Clues in the problem

items: Spans, e.g. days until a warmer day

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Storing values when indices are needed
Forgetting items left on the stack at the end

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why is the total work O(n) despite the inner loop?
blocks.text: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so there are at most 2n stack operations in total.

blocks.title: Increasing or decreasing: how do you choose?
blocks.text: Ask which stored elements become useless when a new one arrives. For next greater, pop smaller values and keep the stack decreasing; for next smaller, pop larger values and keep it increasing.
The problem in plain words
For each day, report how many days pass until a warmer one, or 0 if none comes.
Edge cases

items: Equal temperatures do not count as warmer
Strictly falling input leaves everything at 0

blocks.text: Brute force
For each day scan forward for the first warmer day: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Keep a stack of indices of days still waiting, with temperatures decreasing from bottom to top. A new day resolves every waiting day that is colder, then waits itself.

items: answer starts as all zeros; stack is empty.
For day i, pop every index whose temperature is lower and set its answer to i − index.
Days left on the stack keep 0.

blocks.caption: dailyTemperatures

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner loop does O(n) work in total even though it is nested.
Why it is correct
The stack is always decreasing in temperature, so the first later day warmer than a waiting day is the one that pops it.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Next greater element in a circular array.
blocks.text: Loop over 2n positions using index i % n so that every element also sees the elements before it. Push indices only during the first pass.

blocks.title: Why store indices instead of temperatures?
blocks.text: The answer needs the distance between two days. An index gives both the position and, through the array, the value; a value alone gives neither position nor distance.

blocks.title: Solve it scanning from the right.
blocks.text: Go from right to left keeping a stack of candidate warmer days. Pop every candidate that is not warmer than today; if one remains, the answer is its index minus today's.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: For each price in a series, how long until a higher one appears. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Daily Temperatures?
quiz.why: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner loop does O(n) work in total even though it is nested.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Bars of width 1 and various heights stand side by side. Find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars.

rows: the bars 5 and 6 give width 2 × height 5

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Strictly increasing bars are resolved only at the end
A bar of height 0 splits the histogram

blocks.text: Brute force
For each bar, extend left and right while the bars are at least as tall: O(n²).
Optimal approach

Monotonic stack of indices with increasing heights. When a bar shorter than the top arrives, the top bar cannot extend further right. Pop it: its rectangle spans from just after the new top of the stack to just before the current index. A final height of 0 empties the stack.

items: Go through indices 0 to n, treating index n as height 0.
While the top of the stack is taller than the current height, pop it.
Its width is i − (new top index) − 1; update best with height × width.

blocks.caption: largestRectangleArea

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the nested loop is linear overall.
Why it is correct

For a popped bar, the current index is the first shorter bar to its right and the new stack top is the nearest shorter bar to its left. Between them every bar is at least as tall, so that is the widest rectangle of its height.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What does the extra height 0 at the end do?
blocks.text: It is lower than every bar, so it pops everything still on the stack and their rectangles get measured. Without it, increasing bars would never be resolved.

blocks.title: Why store indices rather than heights?
blocks.text: The width of a rectangle comes from positions. An index gives the position and, through the array, the height.

blocks.title: Use this to find the largest rectangle of 1s in a grid.
blocks.text: Treat each row as the base of a histogram whose bar heights count consecutive 1s above it, and run this algorithm on every row. O(rows × cols).

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the largest block of contiguous capacity available across adjacent time slots. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 84: Largest Rectangle in Histogram

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Largest Rectangle in Histogram?
quiz.why: Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the nested loop is linear overall.

modules.title: Monotonic Queue
modules.summary: A deque kept in decreasing order gives the maximum of a moving window at its front.

blocks.text: A deque kept in decreasing order gives the maximum of a moving window at its front.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A leaderboard that drops anyone who is both older and weaker than a new entrant.
Clues in the problem

items: Maximum or minimum of every window of size k
A DP transition that takes the best of the last k states

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Not evicting the front when it leaves the window
Using removeFirst() on Array (O(n)); keep a head index or use Deque

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why store indices rather than values?
blocks.text: The index tells you when the front has left the window; the value can always be read from the array.

blocks.title: How would you use swift-collections Deque here?
blocks.text: Import DequeModule from swift-collections and use append, popLast and popFirst, which are all O(1), in place of the array plus head index.
The problem in plain words
A window of k neighbouring values slides one step at a time from the left end to the right end. Report the largest value in the window at each position.

rows: the front leaves the window each step

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: k equal to the length gives one value
Equal values: the newer one replaces the older
Strictly falling input keeps every index until it expires

blocks.text: Brute force
Scan all k values of every window: O(n · k).
Optimal approach

Keep a queue of indices whose values decrease from front to back. A new value removes every smaller-or-equal value from the back, because those can never be a maximum again. The front is always the current maximum; drop it once it slides out of the window.

items: For index i, pop indices from the back while their value ≤ nums[i].
If the front index is ≤ i − k it has left the window; advance head.
Once i ≥ k − 1, output the value at the front.

blocks.caption: maxSlidingWindow

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Every index is appended once and removed at most once, so the inner loop totals O(n). A heap gives O(n log n). The array plus head index avoids Swift's O(n) removeFirst(); swift-collections Deque is the ready-made alternative.
Why it is correct

An index is discarded only when a later index holds a value at least as large, so it can never be the maximum of any future window. What remains is decreasing, so its front is the maximum of the window.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Sliding window minimum.
blocks.text: Keep the deque increasing instead: remove values from the back while they are greater than or equal to the new value.

blocks.title: Why store indices rather than values?
blocks.text: An index tells you when the front has left the window, and the value is still available through the array.

blocks.title: When is a heap acceptable instead?
blocks.text: When O(n log n) is acceptable and simplicity matters. Push (value, index) pairs and discard expired tops lazily before reading the maximum.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Showing the peak value over the last k samples of a live metric. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Sliding Window Maximum?
quiz.why: Every index is appended once and removed at most once, so the inner loop totals O(n). A heap gives O(n log n). The array plus head index avoids Swift's O(n) removeFirst(); swift-collections Deque is the ready-made alternative.

modules.title: BFS
modules.summary: Explore in rings of increasing distance using a queue. The first time a node is reached is by a shortest path in an unweighted graph.

blocks.text: Explore in rings of increasing distance using a queue. The first time a node is reached is by a shortest path in an unweighted graph.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Ripples from a stone dropped in a pond.
Clues in the problem

items: Shortest number of steps or moves
Spreading from several sources at once

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Marking visited when dequeued instead of when enqueued

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why does BFS give shortest paths only for unweighted graphs?
blocks.text: BFS orders nodes by number of edges. With weights, a path with more edges can be cheaper, so use Dijkstra for non-negative weights.

blocks.title: What is multi-source BFS?
blocks.text: Put every source in the queue at distance 0 before starting. Each node then receives its distance to the nearest source in one pass.
The problem in plain words
Return the node values grouped by depth: the root first, then its children left to right, then the next depth, and so on.
Edge cases
Brute force
Run a depth-first walk carrying the depth and append into result[depth]; also O(n) but not breadth-first.
Optimal approach
Breadth-first search one whole level at a time. The queue holds exactly the nodes of the current depth; build the next depth's queue while reading it.

items: Start with the root in the queue.
Read every node of the current queue into a level array.
Append the level, swap queues, repeat until empty.

blocks.caption: levelOrder

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node enters and leaves a queue once. Swapping arrays avoids removeFirst(), which is O(n) on a Swift Array.
Why it is correct
If the queue holds all nodes at depth d in left-to-right order, the children collected are all nodes at depth d + 1 in the same order.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Zigzag order.
blocks.text: Use the same BFS and reverse every second level before appending it.

blocks.title: Right side view of the tree.
blocks.text: Take the last value of each level.

blocks.title: Why not call removeFirst() in a loop?
blocks.text: removeFirst() on an Array shifts every remaining element, so each call is O(n) and the traversal becomes O(n²). Swap whole-level arrays, keep a head index, or use Deque.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Showing an organisation chart or category tree one tier at a time. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 102: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Binary Tree Level Order Traversal?
quiz.why: Each node enters and leaves a queue once. Swapping arrays avoids removeFirst(), which is O(n) on a Swift Array.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

A grid holds empty cells (0), fresh oranges (1) and rotten oranges (2). Each minute, every fresh orange next to a rotten one (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Find how many minutes pass until none are fresh, or −1 if some can never rot.

rows: rot spreads outward from the top-left corner
the bottom-left orange is cut off

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: No fresh oranges at the start: 0 minutes
No rotten oranges but some fresh: −1
Several rotten oranges spreading at once
Fresh oranges walled off by empty cells

blocks.text: Brute force
Simulate minute by minute, rescanning the whole grid each time: O((rows × cols)²).
Optimal approach
Breadth-first search from all rotten oranges at the same time. The queue holds the oranges that rotted in the latest minute; their fresh neighbours form the next minute's queue. Count the rounds.

items: Queue every rotten orange and count the fresh ones.
While fresh oranges remain and the queue is not empty, process one whole level.
Each queued orange rots its fresh neighbours; add them to the next queue and decrease fresh.
After each level add one minute. At the end return minutes if fresh is 0, otherwise −1.

blocks.caption: orangesRotting

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each cell enters the queue at most once and checks four neighbours. Starting from all sources together gives each orange its distance to the nearest rotten one.
Why it is correct
BFS reaches cells in order of distance. With every rotten orange in the first level, level d contains exactly the oranges whose nearest rotten orange is d steps away, which is the minute they rot.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why start from all rotten oranges at once?
blocks.text: Each fresh orange rots at the time of its nearest rotten orange. Starting them all at level 0 gives that minimum directly in one pass, instead of running a separate search from each.

blocks.title: How would you return the time each orange rots?
blocks.text: Keep a grid of times. When an orange is added to the next queue, record the current minute plus one in its cell.

blocks.title: What if rot also spread diagonally?
blocks.text: Use eight direction pairs instead of four. Nothing else changes.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Estimating how long an update or outage takes to spread through neighbouring nodes. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Rotting Oranges?
quiz.why: Each cell enters the queue at most once and checks four neighbours. Starting from all sources together gives each orange its distance to the nearest rotten one.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Change one word into another by altering one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must come from a given list. Find the number of words in the shortest such chain, counting both ends, or 0 if there is none.

rows: hit → cog, list [hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog]
same, but cog is not in the list

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The end word must be in the list
The start word need not be
All words have the same length

blocks.text: Brute force
DFS over all chains: explores long detours and does not find the shortest first.
Optimal approach

Breadth-first search, level by level. From each word, try every single-letter change; any result still in the set of unused words is one step further. Remove a word from the set when it is first reached.

items: Put the list in a set; return 0 if the end word is absent.
Process the queue one whole level at a time; steps counts levels.
For each word try all 25 other letters at each position.
A candidate found in the set is removed and queued for the next level.

blocks.caption: ladderLength

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each of the N words is expanded once into L × 25 candidates. Generating neighbours by changing letters avoids comparing every pair of words.
Why it is correct

BFS reaches words in order of chain length, so the first time the end word is taken from the queue the chain is shortest. Removing words on first discovery cannot lose a shorter chain, because none exists.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Search from both ends at once.
blocks.text: Run BFS from the start and from the end alternately, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stop when the two meet. It explores far fewer words.

blocks.title: Return the chain itself.
blocks.text: Record for each discovered word the word it came from, then walk back from the end word to the start and reverse the list.

blocks.title: Why remove a word when it is discovered rather than when it is processed?
blocks.text: If removal waited until processing, the same word could be queued several times from different parents within one level, wasting work.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the fewest single edits linking two valid states. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Word Ladder?
quiz.why: Each of the N words is expanded once into L × 25 candidates. Generating neighbours by changing letters avoids comparing every pair of words.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Turn a binary tree into a string, and turn that string back into an identical tree. The format is yours to choose, as long as the round trip is exact.

rows: pre-order with # for every missing child
an empty tree is a single marker

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Negative and multi-digit values need a separator
Missing children must be recorded, or the shape is lost
Deeply skewed trees make the recursion deep

blocks.text: Brute force
Store two traversals (pre-order and in-order) and rebuild from both: needs distinct values and more code.
Optimal approach
Write the tree in pre-order and write a marker for every missing child. Reading the same sequence back in pre-order rebuilds the tree, because the markers say exactly where each subtree ends.

items: serialize: write the node's value, then its left subtree, then its right subtree; write # for nil.
deserialize: read the next token; # means nil.
Otherwise create a node, then read its left subtree, then its right subtree.

blocks.caption: Codec

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node and each missing child is written and read once. The string must contain every value, so O(n) is the floor.
Why it is correct

With markers, a pre-order listing determines the tree uniquely: after reading a node, everything up to the end of its left subtree is consumed before the right subtree starts. Reading and writing follow the same order, so they agree.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it level by level instead.
blocks.text: Write values in BFS order with a marker for each missing child. To read, keep a queue of parents and give each the next two tokens as its children.

blocks.title: How would you make the string shorter?
blocks.text: Drop trailing markers, use a compact binary encoding, or for a BST store pre-order alone, since the ordering rule recovers the shape.

blocks.title: Why are the markers necessary?
blocks.text: Without them, different trees give the same sequence of values. The markers record where each subtree ends.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up

blocks.title: Convert a recursive DFS to an iterative one.
blocks.text: Use an explicit stack: push the start, then repeatedly pop, visit, and push unvisited neighbours. Post-order needs a visited flag per stack entry or a second stack.

blocks.title: Pre-order, in-order, post-order: when does each fit?
blocks.text: Pre-order when the parent must be handled before its children, such as copying a tree. In-order for sorted output from a BST. Post-order when a node needs its children's results, such as height.
The problem in plain words
Decide whether two binary trees are identical: the same shape, with the same value at every position.

rows: the 2 is a left child in one tree and a right child in the other

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Same values in a different shape
Same shape with one different value

blocks.text: Brute force
Serialise both trees including markers for missing children and compare the strings: O(n) time but extra memory.
Optimal approach
Walk both trees together. Two missing nodes match. One missing node does not. Two present nodes match when their values are equal and their left subtrees and right subtrees match.

items: If either node is nil, the answer is whether both are nil.
If the values differ, return false.
Compare the right subtrees; both must match.

blocks.caption: isSameTree

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each pair of corresponding nodes is visited once, and the recursion stops at the first difference.
Why it is correct
Two trees are identical exactly when their roots agree and their corresponding subtrees are identical, which is the recursive definition the code follows.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Check whether one tree is a subtree of another.
blocks.text: For every node of the larger tree, run the same-tree check against the smaller tree's root; return true if any succeeds. That is O(n · m) in the worst case.

blocks.title: Do it iteratively.
blocks.text: Keep a queue or stack of node pairs. Pop a pair, apply the same nil and value checks, and push the two pairs of children.

blocks.title: Check whether a tree is a mirror of itself.
blocks.text: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirror images: the roots must be equal, and each one's left must mirror the other's right.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Count the nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
Edge cases

items: A completely one-sided tree makes the recursion as deep as n

blocks.text: Brute force
Enumerate every root-to-leaf path and keep the longest: same O(n) visits, but stores paths.
Optimal approach
The depth of a node is 1 plus the larger depth of its two subtrees; an absent node has depth 0.

items: If the node is nil return 0.

blocks.caption: maxDepth

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Every node is visited once. h is the tree height: log n when balanced, n when skewed.
Why it is correct
By induction on height: the base case (nil) is 0, and a node's longest downward path goes through its deeper child.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it iteratively with BFS.
blocks.text: Run a level-order traversal and count the levels.

blocks.title: Compute the minimum depth instead.
blocks.text: A node with one child is not a leaf, so do not take the minimum with a missing child's 0. Use 1 + the minimum over existing children, or run BFS and stop at the first leaf.

blocks.title: When could recursion overflow the stack?
blocks.text: Recursion depth equals the tree height. A heavily skewed tree with tens of thousands of nodes or more can exhaust the stack; use an iterative version there.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A binary tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Decide whether a tree is balanced.

rows: no node's subtrees differ by more than 1
at the root the left side is two levels deeper

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A chain of three nodes is not
The imbalance may be deep inside, not at the root

blocks.text: Brute force
At every node compute both subtree heights from scratch: O(n²) on a skewed tree.
Optimal approach
One post-order pass in which each call returns its subtree's height, or nil as soon as any subtree is unbalanced. The nil propagates upward and stops further work.

items: Get the left and right heights; if either is nil, return nil.
If they differ by more than 1, return nil.
Otherwise return 1 + max(left, right). The tree is balanced if the root's result is not nil.

blocks.caption: isBalanced

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node is visited once and heights are reused. Returning an optional carries both the height and the verdict in one value.
Why it is correct
A tree is balanced exactly when both subtrees are balanced and their heights differ by at most one. The function checks precisely that at every node, bottom-up.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is checking only the root's two heights not enough?
blocks.text: The two subtrees can have equal heights while one of them is badly unbalanced inside. The rule must hold at every node.

blocks.title: What does the guard with two bindings do when the left result is nil?
blocks.text: guard let with two bindings evaluates them in order and stops at the first nil. If the left result is nil, the right subtree is never visited.

blocks.title: How do AVL trees use this property?
blocks.text: An AVL tree stores a height or balance factor in each node and restores this property after every insert or delete by rotating nodes, keeping operations O(log n).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Mirror a binary tree: at every node, the left and right subtrees change places.

rows: every level reads right to left

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A node with only one child: the child moves to the other side

blocks.text: Brute force
Build a new mirrored tree node by node: same time, O(n) extra memory.
Optimal approach
Recursively invert the left subtree and the right subtree, then swap the two child references of the current node.

items: If the node is nil, return nil.
Assign them back swapped and return the node.

blocks.caption: invertTree

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Every node is visited once and does O(1) work. Each node must be touched, so O(n) is the floor.
Why it is correct
By induction on height: if both subtrees are already mirrored, swapping them mirrors the tree rooted at this node.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it iteratively with a queue.
blocks.text: Put the root in a queue. Repeatedly take a node, swap its two children, and add the non-nil children to the queue.

blocks.title: Check whether a tree is symmetric.
blocks.text: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirror images: the two roots must be equal, and each one's left subtree must mirror the other's right subtree.

blocks.title: Does the order (swap first or recurse first) matter?
blocks.text: No. Swapping and then recursing into both children gives the same result as recursing first, as long as both subtrees are processed exactly once.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes of a binary tree. The path does not have to pass through the root.
Edge cases

items: Empty tree or single node gives 0
The longest path may lie entirely inside one subtree
The answer counts edges, not nodes

blocks.text: Brute force
For every node compute the heights of both subtrees separately and add them: O(n²) on a skewed tree.
Optimal approach
One post-order pass. Each call returns the height of its subtree. The longest path that bends at a node is left height + right height, so update a running best there.

items: Compute the left height and the right height.
Return 1 + max(left, right) to the parent.

blocks.caption: diameterOfBinaryTree

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node is visited once and the height is reused instead of recomputed.
Why it is correct
Every path has a single highest node where it bends. Its length is the sum of the two downward heights from that node. Taking the maximum over all nodes covers every path.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return the path itself.
blocks.text: Have each call also return the deepest leaf of its subtree, or store parent links. When best improves, record the node and the two leaves, then join the two root-to-leaf paths.

blocks.title: What if edges have weights?
blocks.text: Return the largest weighted depth instead of a count of levels, adding each edge's weight, and update best with the sum of the two largest weighted depths.

blocks.title: Why can the answer not be read from the root alone?
blocks.text: The longest path may sit entirely within one subtree, far from the root. Only checking every node as a possible bending point finds it.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given two binary trees, decide whether the second appears inside the first: some node of the first tree, together with everything below it, must be identical to the second tree.

rows: the node 4 with its children matches exactly
root = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, null, null, null, null, 0], subRoot = [4, 1, 2]

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The match must include all descendants, not just a top part
Repeated values need every candidate tried
An empty second tree counts as a subtree with this code

blocks.text: Brute force
There is no simpler correct method; the naive approach is the one below.
Optimal approach
For each node of the first tree, test whether the tree rooted there is identical to the second tree using the same-tree check. Stop at the first match.

items: If the first tree is empty, the answer is whether the second is empty too.
If the trees rooted here are identical, return true.

blocks.caption: isSubtree

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Each of the n nodes may start a comparison costing up to m. In practice most comparisons fail at the first node. Serialising both trees and using linear string matching, or hashing subtrees, gives O(n + m).
Why it is correct
A subtree is defined by its root node. Trying every node of the first tree as that root, and requiring an exact match below it, covers every possibility.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How would you make it O(n + m)?
blocks.text: Serialise both trees with markers for missing children and a separator before each value, then search for one string in the other with a linear-time matcher such as KMP. Alternatively hash every subtree bottom-up and compare hashes.

blocks.title: Why is comparing in-order traversals alone wrong?
blocks.text: Different trees can share the same in-order sequence. Without markers for missing children, and without separators between values, the sequence does not determine the shape.

blocks.title: How does this differ from checking that one tree's shape is contained in another?
blocks.text: Here the match must include every descendant down to the leaves. A containment check would allow the larger tree to continue below the matched part.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Check whether a binary tree obeys the search-tree rule: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger, at every level.

rows: 3 sits in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A node can satisfy its parent yet violate an ancestor
Values at the limits of Int, which is why the bounds are optionals

blocks.text: Brute force
For every node, scan its whole left subtree for the maximum and its right subtree for the minimum: O(n²) on a skewed tree.
Optimal approach
Pass an allowed range down the tree. Going left tightens the upper bound to the parent's value; going right tightens the lower bound. Every node must lie strictly inside its range.

items: Start at the root with no bounds.
Fail if the node is not strictly above its lower bound or strictly below its upper bound.
Check the left child with the node's value as the new upper bound.
Check the right child with the node's value as the new lower bound.

blocks.caption: isValidBST

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node is visited once with O(1) work. Every node must be examined to rule out a violation, so O(n) cannot be improved.
Why it is correct
The range passed to a node is exactly the set of values allowed by all its ancestors. If every node lies in its range, the search-tree rule holds for every ancestor and descendant pair.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is comparing each node only with its children not enough?
blocks.text: A node can be on the correct side of its parent and still break the rule for a grandparent or higher ancestor. In [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] the 3 is a valid left child of 6 but lies in the right subtree of 5.

blocks.title: Solve it with an in-order traversal.
blocks.text: Traverse left, node, right while remembering the previous value. The tree is valid exactly when each value is strictly greater than the previous one.

blocks.title: How would you allow duplicate values on one side?
blocks.text: Loosen the comparison on that side only, for example allow node.val equal to the lower bound for the right subtree, and state the convention clearly because definitions differ.

lessons.title: 230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find the kth smallest value stored in a binary search tree, counting from 1.
Edge cases

items: k equals the number of nodes

blocks.text: Brute force
Collect all values with any traversal, sort, and index: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
An in-order traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order. Do it with an explicit stack and stop at the kth value, so no more of the tree is visited than necessary.

items: Push nodes while going left as far as possible.
Pop the top: it is the next value in sorted order.
Decrease remaining; if it is 0, return that value.
Otherwise move to the popped node's right child and repeat.

blocks.caption: kthSmallest

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Reaching the smallest value costs the height h, and each further value costs O(1) amortised. The traversal stops early instead of visiting all n nodes.
Why it is correct
In-order means left subtree, node, right subtree. In a BST everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger, so nodes are popped in ascending order.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: The tree changes often and the query is frequent. How do you speed it up?
blocks.text: Store in each node the size of its left subtree. Then go left if k is at most that size, return the node if k is one more, otherwise go right with k reduced. That is O(h) per query.

blocks.title: Do it recursively.
blocks.text: Do an in-order recursion with a counter captured from the outer function; record the value when the counter reaches k and stop descending.

blocks.title: Find the kth largest.
blocks.text: Do the mirrored traversal: go right first, then the node, then left.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up

lessons.title: 235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
In a binary search tree, find the deepest node that has two given values in its subtree. A node counts as its own ancestor.

rows: 2 and 8 are on different sides of 6
4 lies under 2, and a node is its own ancestor

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: One target is an ancestor of the other
Both targets in the same subtree
Both values are assumed to be in the tree

blocks.text: Brute force
Find the path from the root to each target and take the last node the paths share: O(h) extra memory.
Optimal approach
Use the ordering. Starting at the root, if both targets are smaller go left; if both are larger go right. The first node where they split, or that equals one of them, is the answer.

items: Both values smaller than the node: move left.

blocks.caption: lowestCommonAncestor

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One downward walk with no recursion. h is about log n for a balanced tree and n for a chain.
Why it is correct

While both targets lie on the same side, every common ancestor in that direction is deeper than the current node. At the first node where they do not, the targets are in different subtrees or one is the node itself, so nothing deeper is an ancestor of both.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it for a general binary tree.
blocks.text: Use post-order recursion: return the node if it is one of the targets, otherwise search both children. If both sides return something, the current node is the answer; otherwise pass up whichever side found one.

blocks.title: What if a target may be missing?
blocks.text: First confirm that both values exist with two ordinary BST searches, or have the search report how many targets were found, and return nil if either is missing.

blocks.title: Write it recursively.
blocks.text: If both values are smaller, return the result for the left child; if both are larger, for the right child; otherwise return the node. It uses O(h) call stack.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Remove the node holding a given key from a binary search tree, if it exists, keeping the search-tree rule intact, and return the root.

rows: 4, the next larger value, takes the place of 3

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Deleting a node with one child
Deleting a node with two children

blocks.text: Brute force
Collect every value except the key and rebuild the tree: O(n).
Optimal approach

Search for the key. A node with at most one child is replaced by that child (or by nothing). A node with two children takes the value of its in-order successor, the smallest value in its right subtree, and that successor is then deleted from the right subtree.

items: Go left or right until the key is found or the path ends.
No left child: return the right child in its place. No right child: return the left child.
Two children: find the leftmost node of the right subtree.
Copy its value into the current node, then delete that value from the right subtree.

blocks.caption: deleteNode

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Finding the node and finding its successor each follow one downward path, and the second deletion removes a node with at most one child, so it does not cascade.
Why it is correct

The successor is larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything else in the right subtree, so placing its value in the node preserves the ordering. Removing the successor is one of the simple cases because it has no left child.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Could you use the predecessor instead of the successor?
blocks.text: Yes. The largest value in the left subtree works the same way: copy it into the node and delete it from the left subtree. Alternating between the two can help keep the tree from leaning.

blocks.title: Why does copying the successor's value keep the tree valid?
blocks.text: The successor is the smallest value larger than the deleted key. Everything in the left subtree is smaller than it and everything remaining in the right subtree is larger, so the ordering still holds at that node.

blocks.title: Write it without recursion.
blocks.text: Walk down keeping a reference to the parent and which side you came from. Handle the zero and one child cases by relinking the parent. For two children, find the successor and its parent, copy the value, and unlink the successor.

lessons.title: 701. Insert into a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Add a new value to a binary search tree so that the search-tree rule still holds, and return the root. The value is not already in the tree.

rows: the new node is the root

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The new value is smaller or larger than everything
Inserting sorted values one by one produces a chain, not a balanced tree

blocks.text: Brute force
Collect all values, add the new one, and rebuild the tree: O(n).
Optimal approach
Walk down from the root as if searching for the value: left when it is smaller, right otherwise. The first empty spot on that path is where the new node belongs.

items: If the tree is empty, the new node is the root.
Compare the value with the current node.
If the child on that side exists, move to it.
If it does not, attach the new node there and stop.

blocks.caption: insertIntoBST

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The walk follows one root-to-leaf path. h is about log n in a balanced tree and n in a chain. The iterative form needs no call stack.
Why it is correct
Each step moves to the only subtree that may legally contain the value. Attaching at the first empty spot therefore respects every ancestor's bound and changes nothing else.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Write it recursively.
blocks.text: If the node is nil return a new node. Otherwise assign the result of inserting into the left or right child back to that child, and return the node. It uses O(h) call stack.

blocks.title: How do self-balancing trees keep the height small?
blocks.text: They store extra information per node, such as a height or a colour, and after each insert or delete they perform rotations that restore a balance rule. That keeps the height O(log n).

blocks.title: How would you handle duplicate values?
blocks.text: Pick one convention and apply it everywhere, for example send equal values to the right subtree, or store a count in the node instead of adding a second node.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

A path is any chain of connected nodes in a binary tree; it may start and end anywhere and need not pass through the root. Find the largest possible sum of values along a path. The tree has at least one node.
Edge cases

items: All values negative: the answer is the largest single node
A path may be a single node
The best path may avoid the root
A path cannot fork: at most one node uses both children

blocks.text: Brute force
For every pair of nodes compute the sum of the path between them: O(n²) or worse.
Optimal approach

Post-order DFS. Each call returns the best sum of a downward branch starting at its node. A branch that would lose value is treated as 0 (not taken). At each node, the best path bending there is node + left branch + right branch; record it.

items: l and r are the children's branch gains, floored at 0.
Return node.val + max(l, r): the parent can extend only one side.

blocks.caption: maxPathSum

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Every node is visited once. Returning one value and recording another separates 'what the parent may use' from 'the best complete path here'.
Why it is correct

Every path has one highest node. Its sum is that node plus the best downward branch on each side, or nothing on a side where every branch is negative. Taking the maximum over all nodes covers every path.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why floor the child gains at 0?
blocks.text: A branch with a negative total would lower the sum, and a path is free to stop at the node instead of going down that side.

blocks.title: Why return max(l, r) rather than l + r?
blocks.text: A path through the parent can continue into only one child's side. Using both would make the path fork, which is not a path.

blocks.title: Return the path itself.
blocks.text: Have each call also return the nodes of its best branch, and when best improves, store the left branch reversed, the node, and the right branch.

blocks.title: How do you avoid duplicate subsets when the input has duplicates?
blocks.text: Sort the input and skip a value that equals the previous one at the same depth.

blocks.title: What is the time complexity of generating all subsets?
blocks.text: O(n · 2ⁿ): there are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each one costs up to n.
The problem in plain words
Given distinct positive numbers and a target, list every combination whose values add up to the target. A number may be used any number of times, and order does not matter.
Edge cases

items: The same set in a different order must not be repeated
Candidates are assumed positive, so the search always ends

blocks.text: Brute force
Generate every multiset up to the target size and filter: far more work without pruning.
Optimal approach

Backtracking. Keep the remaining amount. From a start index, try each candidate that still fits, recurse with the same index so it can be reused, then remove it. Never go back to earlier indices, which prevents reordered duplicates.

items: If remaining is 0, record the path.
For each index from start whose value ≤ remaining, append it.
Recurse with the same index and the reduced remaining.
Remove it and try the next index.

blocks.caption: combinationSum

blocks.text: Why this complexity

The number of combinations can itself be exponential, so no polynomial bound exists in general. Pruning values larger than the remainder cuts most dead branches; sorting first allows stopping the loop early.
Why it is correct
Indices along a path never decrease, so each multiset is generated in exactly one order. Every valid combination is reached because each allowed next value is tried.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Each number may be used only once.
blocks.text: Sort the candidates, recurse with i + 1 instead of i, and skip a candidate equal to the previous one at the same depth so equal values do not produce repeated combinations.

blocks.title: Why pass i instead of i + 1?
blocks.text: Passing i lets the same candidate be chosen again at the next level. Passing i + 1 would allow each candidate at most once.

blocks.title: Only count the combinations instead of listing them.
blocks.text: Use DP as in the coin-change counting problem: ways[0] = 1, and for each candidate add ways[a − candidate] to ways[a] for a from the candidate up to the target.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Listing the ways to fill an exact quantity from available pack sizes. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Combination Sum?
quiz.why: The number of combinations can itself be exponential, so no polynomial bound exists in general. Pruning values larger than the remainder cuts most dead branches; sorting first allows stopping the loop early.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
List every possible ordering of a set of distinct numbers.
Edge cases

items: Empty input gives one empty ordering
Output size is n!, which grows very fast

blocks.text: Brute force
There is no shortcut: every ordering has to be written out. Generating by repeated insertion costs the same.
Optimal approach
Backtracking. Build the ordering one position at a time. At each position try every number not yet used, mark it used, recurse, then undo both the append and the mark.

items: If the path holds every number, record a copy and return.
For each index that is not marked used: mark it and append its number.
Recurse to fill the next position.
Remove the number and unmark it, then try the next index.

blocks.caption: permute

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are n! orderings and copying each costs n. The recursion depth and the used array are both O(n).
Why it is correct
Each level fixes one position and tries each unused number exactly once, so every ordering is produced once. Undoing the choice restores the state for the next candidate.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Handle duplicate numbers without duplicate orderings.
blocks.text: Sort the input. At each position skip a number when it equals the previous number and that previous one is not currently used, so equal values are placed in one fixed order only.

blocks.title: Generate the next permutation in lexicographic order.
blocks.text: From the right, find the first element smaller than its right neighbour. Swap it with the smallest larger element to its right, then reverse the part after it. If no such element exists, the sequence is the last permutation.

blocks.title: How does this differ from generating subsets?
blocks.text: Subsets decide for each element whether to include it, and order does not matter, so the loop moves forward from a start index. Permutations use every element and order matters, so each level scans all unused elements.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Trying every order of a small number of stops to find the best route. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Permutations?
quiz.why: There are n! orderings and copying each costs n. The recursion depth and the used array are both O(n).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
List every selection of the given distinct numbers, including the empty selection and the full set.
Edge cases

items: Empty input still yields one subset
Output size doubles with every element
Order of the output differs between methods

blocks.text: Brute force
Count from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 and read each number's bits as include/exclude flags. Same cost; less natural to extend with pruning.
Optimal approach
Backtracking. Record the current path, then for each later index: add the number, explore deeper, remove it again.

items: Record the current path as a subset.
For each index from start onward, append that number.
Remove the number and try the next index.

blocks.caption: subsets

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each costs up to n, so no algorithm that writes them all out can be faster.
Why it is correct
Indices only increase along a path, so each subset is produced exactly once, in increasing index order. Removing after the call restores the path for the next choice.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Handle duplicate numbers without duplicate subsets.
blocks.text: Sort the input. Inside the loop, skip nums[i] when i > start and it equals nums[i − 1], so equal values are not chosen twice at the same depth.

blocks.title: Only subsets of size k.
blocks.text: Record the path only when it has k elements and stop going deeper. Prune when too few elements remain to reach size k.

blocks.title: Why does appending path store a copy in Swift?
blocks.text: Array is a value type. Appending path stores its current contents; later changes to path do not affect the stored copy.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Enumerating every combination of optional add-ons for a small configurable product. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A grid holds one letter per cell. Decide whether a word can be traced by moving between neighbouring cells (up, down, left, right), using each cell at most once.

rows: A → B → C → C → E → D
the B would have to be used twice

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A cell may not be reused within one path
The word is longer than the number of cells
Several starting cells match the first letter

blocks.text: Brute force
There is no fundamentally better method than searching; the naive version forgets to prune and copies the visited set at every step.
Optimal approach
Backtracking DFS. From every cell, try to match the word letter by letter. Mark a matched cell as used, try the four neighbours for the next letter, then restore the cell so other paths can use it.

items: If every letter is matched, return true.
Fail if the cell is outside the grid or does not hold the current letter.
Mark the cell and try the four neighbours with the next letter.
Restore the cell and report whether any neighbour succeeded.

blocks.caption: exist

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each start may branch three ways per letter (the fourth direction is the cell just used). Marking in place avoids a separate visited set.
Why it is correct
The search tries every path of matching letters that does not reuse a cell. Restoring the cell on the way back means a failed path leaves the board unchanged for the next one.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How can you prune early?
blocks.text: Check first that the board contains every letter of the word often enough. Searching from the rarer end of the word also cuts branches.

blocks.title: Search for many words at once.
blocks.text: Put the words in a trie and run one DFS per cell that walks the trie along with the board, collecting every word reached. That is the approach for Word Search II.

blocks.title: Why restore the cell after exploring?
blocks.text: The mark means 'used on the current path'. If it stayed after a failed attempt, later paths that legitimately need that cell would be blocked.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Checking whether a swipe path across a letter grid spells a valid word. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Word Search?
quiz.why: Each start may branch three ways per letter (the fourth direction is the cell just used). Marking in place avoids a separate visited set.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two share a row, column or diagonal. List every arrangement.

rows: queens in columns 1,3,0,2 and 2,0,3,1 by row
two queens always attack each other

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The number of solutions grows quickly

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every way of putting n queens on n² cells and test each: astronomically many.
Optimal approach

Backtracking row by row. Each row gets exactly one queen. Three sets record the columns and both diagonal directions already attacked, so a square is tested in O(1). Place, recurse to the next row, then remove.

items: If row equals n, record the board.
For each column not attacked (column, row − col diagonal, row + col diagonal): place the queen and record the three attacks.
Remove the queen and its three records.

blocks.caption: solveNQueens

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The first row has n choices, the next at most n − 1, and so on; pruning cuts far more in practice. Cells on one diagonal share row − col; cells on the other share row + col.
Why it is correct
One queen per row is necessary, so searching row by row loses nothing. A placement is accepted only if its column and both diagonals are free, which is exactly the no-attack rule.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Only count the solutions.
blocks.text: Keep the same search but increment a counter at row n instead of building the board strings.

blocks.title: Why do row − col and row + col identify diagonals?
blocks.text: Moving one step down-right adds 1 to both row and column, so row − col stays the same. Moving down-left adds 1 to the row and subtracts 1 from the column, so row + col stays the same.

blocks.title: Use bitmasks instead of sets.
blocks.text: Represent the attacked columns and diagonals as three integers. The free squares in a row are the zero bits of their combination, and shifting the diagonal masks moves them to the next row.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: A standard model for constraint puzzles such as assigning non-conflicting slots. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for N-Queens?
quiz.why: The first row has n choices, the next at most n − 1, and so on; pruning cuts far more in practice. Cells on one diagonal share row − col; cells on the other share row + col.

items: Sorting makes the best next choice obvious

items: Assuming greedy works without an argument

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Give an example where greedy fails and DP is needed.
blocks.text: Coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 (two coins) is optimal.

blocks.title: What is an exchange argument?

lessons.title: 121. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
You have one price per day. Pick one day to buy and a later day to sell so the profit is as large as possible. If no profit is possible the answer is 0.
Edge cases

items: The lowest price on the last day is useless

blocks.text: Brute force
Check every buy day against every later sell day: O(n²) time.
Optimal approach
Scan left to right keeping the lowest price seen so far. For each day, the best sale ending today is today's price minus that minimum.

items: Start with minPrice = Int.max and best = 0.
For each price, lower minPrice if this price is smaller.

blocks.caption: maxProfit

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass, two variables. For a fixed sell day the best buy day is the cheapest earlier day, so nothing else needs to be remembered.
Why it is correct
minPrice is always the minimum of the prefix ending at the current day, so p − minPrice is the best profit for selling on that day. best is the maximum of those over all days.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if you may make many transactions?
blocks.text: Add up every positive day-to-day rise. Any longer rise is the sum of its daily rises, so this greedy total is optimal.

blocks.title: What if there is a cooldown or a fee?
blocks.text: Use DP with a small number of states per day, such as holding and not holding (plus a cooling state for cooldown). Update each state from the previous day. O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.title: How would you also return the buy and sell days?
blocks.text: Remember the index of the minimum price. Whenever best improves, record that index and the current day.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Largest rise after a low point in any time series, such as the biggest latency regression after a baseline. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.why: One pass, two variables. For a fixed sell day the best buy day is the cheapest earlier day, so nothing else needs to be remembered.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Each position holds the longest jump allowed from there. Starting at the first position, find the fewest jumps needed to reach the last position. The last position is guaranteed to be reachable.
Edge cases

items: A first jump that already reaches the end
Zeros that must be jumped over

blocks.text: Brute force
DP: fewest jumps to each index from every earlier index that reaches it, O(n²).
Optimal approach

Greedy by levels, like BFS. All indices reachable with the current number of jumps form a range ending at 'end'. While scanning that range, track the farthest index one more jump could reach. On reaching 'end', spend a jump and extend the range.

items: For each index before the last, update farthest with i + nums[i].
When i equals end, add a jump and set end = farthest.

blocks.caption: jump

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass. Each index is examined once and belongs to exactly one level.
Why it is correct
The indices reachable in exactly k jumps form a contiguous range. The next range ends at the farthest reach from any index in the current one, so counting range boundaries counts the minimum jumps.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why does the loop stop before the last index?
blocks.text: Reaching the last index needs no further jump. If the loop included it and it happened to equal end, an extra jump would be counted.

blocks.title: Return the path of indices.
blocks.text: Remember for each index the index it was best reached from, updating whenever farthest improves, then walk back from the end.

blocks.title: What if the end might be unreachable?
blocks.text: Check whether i ever exceeds farthest, as in Jump Game, and return −1 or nil in that case.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the fewest relay hops to cover a route when each station has a limited range. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Jump Game II?
quiz.why: One pass. Each index is examined once and belongs to exactly one level.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Each position holds the longest jump you may make from there. Starting at the first position, decide whether the last position can be reached.

rows: every route ends on the 0 at index 3

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Single element is already at the end
A zero that can be jumped over
A zero that cannot be passed
Empty input returns true with this code

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every jump from every position recursively: exponential without memoisation, O(n²) with it.
Optimal approach
Greedy. Track the farthest index reachable so far. Walk left to right: if the current index is beyond that, you are stuck; otherwise extend the farthest reach using this position's jump.

items: For each index i: if i > farthest, return false.
If the loop finishes, return true.

blocks.caption: canJump

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass and one variable. Only the farthest reach matters, not how you got there, because any index up to it is also reachable.
Why it is correct
Invariant: every index from 0 to farthest is reachable. If index i is within reach, so is everything up to i + jump. If i is beyond reach, no earlier position can get past it.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Find the minimum number of jumps.
blocks.text: Track the end of the range reachable with the current number of jumps and the farthest index reachable with one more. When the scan reaches the end of the current range, add a jump and extend the range. O(n).

blocks.title: Solve it scanning from the right.
blocks.text: Keep the leftmost index known to reach the end, starting at the last index. Moving left, an index becomes the new goal if it can jump at least that far. The answer is whether the goal reaches index 0.

blocks.title: Why is DP unnecessary here?
blocks.text: The only fact needed about the past is the farthest reachable index, and it can be updated in O(1). Remembering reachability for each index separately adds nothing.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Checking whether a chain of hand-offs with limited range can cover a whole route. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Jump Game?
quiz.why: One pass and one variable. Only the farthest reach matters, not how you got there, because any index up to it is also reachable.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Stations are arranged in a circle. Each gives some fuel, and driving to the next station costs some fuel. Starting with an empty tank, find the station from which a full clockwise lap is possible, or −1 if there is none.

rows: total fuel is less than total cost

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Total fuel below total cost: impossible
The answer, when it exists, is unique in the original problem

blocks.text: Brute force
Simulate a lap from every station: O(n²).
Optimal approach

If the total gain is negative, no start works. Otherwise scan once keeping a tank. Whenever the tank goes negative at station i, no station from the current start up to i can be the answer, so restart from i + 1 with an empty tank.

items: total, tank and start begin at 0.
At each station add gas − cost to both total and tank.
If tank < 0, set start = i + 1 and tank = 0.

blocks.caption: canCompleteCircuit

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass with three variables. Every station is examined once.
Why it is correct

If starting at s fails at i, any station between s and i starts with no more fuel than s had on arriving there, so it fails by i as well. When total ≥ 0, the last candidate must succeed because the earlier deficits are covered by the surplus after it.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why can the stations between start and i be skipped?
blocks.text: Leaving the current start with an empty tank, the car reached each station in between with a tank of 0 or more. Starting at one of those with exactly 0 can only do worse, so it also fails by station i.

blocks.title: Why does total ≥ 0 guarantee an answer?
blocks.text: Split the circle at the last restart. The part before it has a net deficit and the part from it to the end never goes negative. Since the whole lap is non-negative, the surplus carried from the second part covers the first.

blocks.title: Return all valid starting stations.
blocks.text: Compute the running balance around the circle once. A station is a valid start exactly when the balance just before it is the minimum of the whole lap, so report every position that attains that minimum.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Choosing the point in a cyclic schedule from which a running balance never goes negative. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.why: One pass with three variables. Every station is examined once.

lessons.title: 1584. Min Cost to Connect All Points

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Points lie on a grid. Connecting two points costs the sum of their horizontal and vertical distance. Find the cheapest total cost that leaves every point connected to every other, directly or indirectly.
Edge cases

items: Every pair of points is a possible link, so the graph is dense

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every set of n − 1 links and keep the cheapest that connects everything: exponential.
Optimal approach

Prim's algorithm. Grow one connected group from any point. Track, for each outside point, the cheapest link into the group. Always add the outside point whose link is cheapest, then update the others using the newly added point.

items: best[0] = 0; all other entries are infinity.
Pick the point outside the tree with the smallest best value and add it; add that value to the total.
For every point still outside, lower its best value if the new point is closer.
Repeat until every point is in the tree.

blocks.caption: minCostConnectPoints

blocks.text: Why this complexity

There are n rounds and each scans n points. Because every pair of points is a potential link, the graph has about n² edges, so O(n²) is linear in the number of edges and beats a heap-based or sort-based method here.
Why it is correct
The cut property: the cheapest link crossing from the tree to the rest belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Adding it never rules out an optimal solution, so repeating the step builds one.
Alternative: Kruskal

Kruskal's algorithm. List every pair of points as an edge with its cost and sort the edges from cheapest to dearest. Take each edge in turn: if its two ends are in different groups according to Union Find, keep it and merge the groups; otherwise skip it, because it would close a cycle. Stop after n − 1 edges. O(E log E) for the sort, which is O(n² log n) here because every pair is an edge. Swift's sort is not guaranteed stable, so edges of equal cost may be processed in a different order than shown; the total is the same.

blocks.caption: minCostConnectPointsKruskal

blocks.text: Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with Kruskal's algorithm.
blocks.text: Generate every pair as an edge with its cost, sort the edges, and add each one whose endpoints are in different groups according to Union Find, until n − 1 edges are added.

blocks.title: When is Kruskal the better choice?
blocks.text: When the graph is sparse or the edges are already given as a list, since its cost is O(E log E). On a dense graph such as this one, E is about n², so array-based Prim at O(n²) is faster.

blocks.title: Why does this version not need a heap?
blocks.text: Each round already has to look at every outside point to update its best value, so finding the minimum in the same O(n) scan adds nothing. A heap helps only when there are far fewer edges than n².

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Planning the least total cable needed to link a set of sites. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

modules.title: Dynamic Programming
modules.summary: Define a state, relate it to smaller states, and compute each state once.

blocks.text: Define a state, relate it to smaller states, and compute each state once.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Filling a table of answers so you never solve the same small question twice.
Clues in the problem

items: Count the ways, or minimum/maximum cost
Choices at each step that affect later options

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes
Interview questions

blocks.title: Top-down versus bottom-up: trade-offs?
blocks.text: Top-down (memoised recursion) computes only the states it needs and is natural to write, but risks deep recursion. Bottom-up is iterative, avoids recursion and makes space reduction easy, but you must get the order right.

blocks.title: How do you reduce the table to O(1) or O(n) space?
blocks.text: If a state depends only on the previous row or the previous few entries, keep just those in rolling variables or two arrays.
The problem in plain words
You climb n steps taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the different sequences of moves that reach the top.
Edge cases

items: n = 0 gives 1 with this code (one way: do nothing)
Large n overflows fixed-width integers eventually

blocks.text: Brute force
Recursion ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2) without memory: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach
The last move was 1 or 2 steps, so ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2). Keep only the last two values and roll them forward.

items: Repeat n times: (a, b) = (b, a + b).

blocks.caption: climbStairs

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each state depends on the two before it, so two variables suffice. (Matrix exponentiation gives O(log n) but is rarely expected.)
Why it is correct
After k iterations a = ways(k) and b = ways(k + 1); the tuple assignment preserves this.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Allow steps of 1, 2 or 3.
blocks.text: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2) + ways(n − 3). Roll three variables instead of two.

blocks.title: Each step has a cost; minimise it.
blocks.text: Let dp[i] be the cheapest cost to stand on step i: dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2]). The answer is the smaller of the last two.

blocks.title: Why is the plain recursion exponential?
blocks.text: It recomputes the same sub-problems again and again; the call tree has roughly 1.6ⁿ nodes. Memoising each result makes it O(n).

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting the ways to fill a slot of n units with pieces of size 1 and 2. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
