quiz.why: Each state depends on the two before it, so two variables suffice. (Matrix exponentiation gives O(log n) but is rarely expected.)

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find the longest stretch of consecutive characters in a string that reads the same forwards and backwards.

rows: "aba" is equally long; this code returns the first found

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Even-length palindromes have their centre between two characters
Several answers of the same length

blocks.text: Brute force
Check every substring: O(n³).
Optimal approach
Expand around centres. A string of length n has 2n − 1 centres: each character and each gap between two characters. From each centre, widen while the two ends match and remember the longest stretch.

items: For centre index c, start with l = c / 2 and r = l + c % 2.
While l and r are in range and the characters match, move l left and r right.
The palindrome found has length r − l − 1 and starts at l + 1.
Keep it if it is longer than the best so far.

blocks.caption: longestPalindrome

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are 2n − 1 centres and each expansion is at most n steps. Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n) but is rarely expected in interviews.
Why it is correct
Every palindrome has a centre, and expanding from that centre reaches its full extent. Trying all centres therefore finds the longest one.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with DP. What does the table mean?
blocks.text: dp[i][j] is true when s[i...j] is a palindrome: the end characters match and dp[i + 1][j − 1] is true (or the length is under 3). Fill by increasing length. O(n²) time and space.

blocks.title: Count all palindromic substrings.
blocks.text: Use the same centre expansion and add 1 for every successful match instead of tracking the longest.

blocks.title: What does Manacher's algorithm do differently?
blocks.text: It reuses the palindrome radii already computed to the left of the current position, using symmetry inside the widest palindrome found so far, so most expansions start from a known length. Total O(n).

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding symmetric patterns in sequences such as DNA strings. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Longest Palindromic Substring?
quiz.why: There are 2n − 1 centres and each expansion is at most n steps. Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n) but is rarely expected in interviews.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Among all contiguous runs of at least one element, find the largest possible sum.
Edge cases

items: All negative values: the answer is the largest single element, not 0
Input is assumed non-empty (the code reads nums[0])

blocks.text: Brute force
Sum every (start, end) pair with a running total: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Kadane's algorithm. cur is the best sum of a run that ends at the current element. Either extend the previous run or start fresh at this element.

items: For each later x: cur = max(x, cur + x).

blocks.caption: maxSubArray

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The best run ending at i depends only on the best run ending at i − 1, so one variable carries all needed state.
Why it is correct
A run ending at i is either x alone or x appended to a run ending at i − 1; the best such is max(x, cur + x). The global best is the maximum over all end positions.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return the start and end indices.
blocks.text: Keep a candidate start that resets whenever a new run begins. When best improves, record the candidate start and the current index.

blocks.title: Solve it with divide and conquer.
blocks.text: The best run lies entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or crosses the middle. The crossing case is the best suffix of the left plus the best prefix of the right. That gives O(n log n), or O(n) if each call returns total, best prefix, best suffix and best.

blocks.title: What about a circular array?
blocks.text: The answer is the larger of the normal maximum and (total − minimum subarray), which represents a run that wraps around. If every value is negative, return the normal maximum.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the strongest contiguous period in a series of daily gains and losses. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Maximum Subarray?
quiz.why: The best run ending at i depends only on the best run ending at i − 1, so one variable carries all needed state.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A robot starts in the top-left cell of an m × n grid and can move only right or down. Count the different routes to the bottom-right cell.
Edge cases

items: A single row or column has exactly one route
Large grids overflow fixed-width integers eventually

blocks.text: Brute force
Recursion paths(r, c) = paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1) without memory: exponential.
Optimal approach
Every cell is entered from above or from the left, so its count is the sum of those two. The top row and left column are all 1. One row of storage is enough, updated in place left to right.

items: For each further grid row, go through columns 1 to n − 1.
row[c] += row[c − 1]: the old row[c] is the cell above, row[c − 1] is the cell to the left.
The last entry is the answer.

blocks.caption: uniquePaths

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each cell is computed once. The closed form C(m + n − 2, m − 1) gives the answer in O(min(m, n)) multiplications, but the table extends to grids with obstacles.
Why it is correct
Before the update row[c] holds the count for the cell above; after updating row[c − 1] it holds the count for the cell to the left in the current row. Their sum is the count for the current cell.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if some cells are blocked?
blocks.text: Set a blocked cell's count to 0 instead of adding. The first row and column can no longer be assumed to be 1; a block there cuts off everything after it.

blocks.title: Give the combinatorial formula and explain it.
blocks.text: Every route is a sequence of m − 1 downs and n − 1 rights. Choosing which positions are downs gives C(m + n − 2, m − 1).

blocks.title: Find the path with the smallest sum of cell values.
blocks.text: Use the same table but take the minimum of the cell above and the cell to the left, plus the current cell's value.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting the distinct ways through a staged process where each step advances one of two counters. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

items: Reducing a 2D table to one row

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Unique Paths?
quiz.why: Each cell is computed once. The closed form C(m + n − 2, m − 1) gives the answer in O(min(m, n)) multiplications, but the table extends to grids with obstacles.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Letters are coded as numbers: A is 1, B is 2, up to Z as 26. Given a string of digits, count how many different letter sequences it could stand for.
Edge cases

items: A 0 is only valid as part of 10 or 20
Two zeros in a row give 0

blocks.text: Brute force
Try splitting off one or two digits recursively: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach

Let ways(i) be the count for the first i digits. The last letter used either one digit (allowed if that digit is not 0) or two digits (allowed if they form 10 to 26). Add the counts of the two shorter prefixes that apply. Two variables are enough.

items: Return 0 if the string is empty or starts with 0.
For each further digit: add cur if the digit is not 0; add prev if the last two digits are 10…26.
Shift the two variables and continue. Return cur.

blocks.caption: numDecodings

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each digit is processed once and depends only on the two previous counts.
Why it is correct
Every decoding ends with a one-digit letter or a two-digit letter, and removing it leaves a decoding of a shorter prefix. The two cases cannot coincide, so their counts add.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Add a wildcard character that stands for any digit 1–9.
blocks.text: Count the choices per position: a wildcard alone has 9 options; as the first of two digits it can be 1 or 2 depending on the second; as the second it has 9 options after 1 and 6 after 2. Multiply the earlier counts by those factors.

blocks.title: Return the decodings themselves.
blocks.text: Use backtracking: at each position try one digit and, if valid, two digits, appending the letter and recursing. The number of results can be exponential.

blocks.title: Why does 0 need special care?
blocks.text: 0 has no letter of its own. It is valid only as the second digit of 10 or 20, so a 0 after any other digit, or at the start, makes the count 0.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting the ways an unpunctuated numeric code can be split into valid tokens. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Decode Ways?
quiz.why: Each digit is processed once and depends only on the two previous counts.

rows: O(n² · L) with substring cost L

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Decide whether a string can be cut into pieces so that every piece is a word from a given dictionary. Words may be reused.
Edge cases

items: A greedy longest-match can fail where another split works

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every way of cutting the string recursively: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach
dp[i] says whether the first i characters can be built from dictionary words. dp[end] is true if some earlier start has dp[start] true and the substring from start to end is a word.

items: For each end from 1 to n, look at every start before it with dp[start] true.
If chars[start..<end] is in the set, mark dp[end] true and stop looking.

blocks.caption: wordBreak

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are n end positions and up to n starts each; building and hashing a substring costs its length. Limiting start to the longest word length tightens this.
Why it is correct
A prefix can be segmented exactly when it ends with a dictionary word whose preceding prefix can be segmented. dp[start] is final before any larger end is computed.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return one valid segmentation.
blocks.text: Store, for each reachable end, the start that made it reachable. Walk back from the end of the string following those starts to read off the words.

blocks.title: Return all segmentations.
blocks.text: Use backtracking with memoisation: for each start position return every list of words that segments the rest. The number of results can be exponential.

blocks.title: How would a trie help?
blocks.text: Insert the dictionary into a trie. From each reachable start, walk the trie along the string and mark every position where a word ends. This avoids building and hashing substrings.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Splitting a run-together search query into known terms. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Word Break?
options: O(n² · L) with substring cost L
quiz.why: There are n end positions and up to n starts each; building and hashing a substring costs its length. Limiting start to the longest word length tightens this.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Among all contiguous runs of at least one element, find the largest product. Values may be negative or zero.

rows: two negatives multiply to a positive

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: An even number of negatives can give the best answer

blocks.text: Brute force
Multiply out every (start, end) pair with a running product: O(n²).
Optimal approach

Track both the largest and the smallest product of a run ending at the current element. A negative value turns the smallest into the largest, so both are needed. Each new value is one of: the element alone, largest × element, smallest × element.

items: For each later x, form the three candidates x, hi × x and lo × x.
hi is their maximum and lo their minimum.

blocks.caption: maxProduct

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass with three variables. Unlike the maximum-sum problem, one running value is not enough because sign flips matter.
Why it is correct
The extreme products of runs ending at i come from extending an extreme run ending at i − 1 or starting fresh at i. Keeping both extremes covers the sign of x in every case.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is tracking only the maximum wrong?
blocks.text: A large negative product becomes a large positive one when multiplied by another negative. If only the maximum is kept, that information is lost.

blocks.title: Return the subarray itself.
blocks.text: Track the start index of the runs behind hi and lo along with their values. When best improves, record the start of the hi run and the current index.

blocks.title: How do zeros affect the state?
blocks.text: After a zero, both hi and lo become 0, and the next element starts a fresh run because the candidate 'x alone' wins or ties. So a zero splits the array into independent parts.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the best compounded growth over a contiguous period when some factors are negative. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Maximum Product Subarray?
quiz.why: One pass with three variables. Unlike the maximum-sum problem, one running value is not enough because sign flips matter.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Houses in a row each hold some money. You may not take from two neighbouring houses. Find the largest total you can take.
Edge cases

items: Greedy 'take every other house' fails, e.g. [2, 1, 1, 2]

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every valid subset recursively: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach
For each house choose the better of skipping it (keep the best so far) or taking it (best up to two houses back plus this one). Two variables carry everything needed.

items: prev = best up to two houses back, cur = best up to the previous house; both 0.
For each house x, new cur = max(cur, prev + x).

blocks.caption: rob

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each state depends only on the previous two, so the full table collapses to two variables.
Why it is correct
An optimal plan for the first i houses either excludes house i (so it is optimal for i − 1) or includes it (so the rest is optimal for i − 2).
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: The houses form a circle.
blocks.text: The first and last houses are now neighbours. Solve the row without the first house and the row without the last house, and take the better. Handle a single house separately.

blocks.title: Return which houses were chosen.
blocks.text: Keep the full dp array. Walk back from the end: if dp[i] differs from dp[i − 1], house i was taken, so jump to i − 2; otherwise step to i − 1.

blocks.title: The houses form a binary tree.
blocks.text: Do a post-order DFS that returns two values per node: the best total if the node is taken and the best if it is not.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Choosing non-adjacent time slots to maximise total value. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for House Robber?
quiz.why: Each state depends only on the previous two, so the full table collapses to two variables.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Houses stand in a circle, each with some money. You may not take from two neighbouring houses, and the first and last houses are neighbours. Find the largest total.

rows: the two 2s are neighbours, so take the 3

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The first and last cannot both be taken

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every valid subset: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach

The first and last house cannot both be used. So the answer is the better of two straight-row problems: the row without the last house and the row without the first. Each is the ordinary House Robber.

items: If there is one house, return it.

blocks.caption: robCircle

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Two linear passes with two variables each. ArraySlice avoids copying the array.
Why it is correct

Any valid plan omits the first house or omits the last (or both). The best plan omitting the last is the optimum for the first row; the best omitting the first is the optimum for the second. The larger covers all cases.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why are two passes enough?
blocks.text: Every valid plan leaves out the first house or the last house. Solving once without each covers all plans, and a plan that leaves out both is included in either pass.

blocks.title: Why does a single house need its own case?
blocks.text: With one house both slices are empty and would give 0, but the house can be taken. With two or more houses the slices handle everything.

blocks.title: What if the houses form a tree?
blocks.text: Use DFS returning two values per node: the best total taking the node and the best not taking it.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Scheduling non-adjacent slots in a rotating weekly cycle where the last slot touches the first. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for House Robber II?
quiz.why: Two linear passes with two variables each. ArraySlice avoids copying the array.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Pick elements from the array, keeping their order but skipping any you like, so that each picked value is strictly larger than the one before. Find the greatest number of elements you can pick.
Edge cases

items: Equal values do not extend a run
The elements need not be adjacent

blocks.text: Brute force
Check every subset of positions: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach
Let dp[i] be the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. It is 1 plus the best dp[j] over all earlier j with a smaller value. The answer is the largest entry.

items: Every dp[i] starts at 1: the element alone.
For each i, look at every earlier j.
If nums[j] < nums[i], dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).

blocks.caption: lengthOfLIS

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each pair (j, i) is examined once. This is the clearest version but not the fastest: keeping the smallest tail value for each length and binary-searching it gives O(n log n).
Why it is correct
Any increasing subsequence ending at i is either the element alone or an increasing subsequence ending at some earlier, smaller element with nums[i] appended. dp[i] takes the best of those.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Describe the O(n log n) method.
blocks.text: Keep an array where entry i is the smallest tail value of any increasing subsequence of length i + 1. For each number, binary-search the first entry that is not smaller and overwrite it, or append if there is none. The array's length is the answer.

blocks.title: How do you recover the subsequence itself?
blocks.text: Alongside dp, store for each index the previous index that gave its best value. Start at the index with the largest dp and follow the stored links backwards.

blocks.title: Count how many longest increasing subsequences there are.
blocks.text: Keep a second array of counts. When dp[j] + 1 beats dp[i], copy count[j]; when it ties, add count[j]. Sum the counts of all indices whose dp equals the maximum.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the longest run of improving results in a history, allowing gaps. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Longest Increasing Subsequence?
quiz.why: Each pair (j, i) is examined once. This is the clearest version but not the fastest: keeping the smallest tail value for each length and binary-searching it gives O(n log n).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given coin values (unlimited supply of each) and an amount, find the fewest coins that sum to the amount, or −1 if it cannot be made.
Edge cases

items: Greedy (largest coin first) fails, e.g. coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every combination recursively: exponential.
Optimal approach
Bottom-up DP. dp[a] is the fewest coins for amount a. For each a, try each coin c ≤ a: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a − c] + 1).

items: Fill dp with amount + 1 (acts as infinity); dp[0] = 0.
For a from 1 to amount, try each usable coin.
If dp[amount] is still above amount, return −1.

blocks.caption: coinChange

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are amount + 1 states and each tries every coin once. amount + 1 is a safe sentinel because no answer can use more than amount coins.
Why it is correct
An optimal solution for a ends with some coin c; removing it leaves an optimal solution for a − c. All smaller amounts are solved before a.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Count the number of ways instead.
blocks.text: Set dp[0] = 1. Loop over coins on the outside and amounts on the inside, adding dp[a − coin] to dp[a]. Coins outside counts combinations rather than orderings.

blocks.title: Return the coins used.
blocks.text: For each amount also store the coin that produced the best value. Walk back from the target subtracting the stored coin each time.

blocks.title: When does greedy work?
blocks.text: It works for so-called canonical systems such as 1, 5, 10, 25. There is no simple general test, so use DP unless the system is known to be canonical; [1, 3, 4] with amount 6 is a counter-example.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Choosing the fewest pack sizes to fulfil an exact quantity. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Coin Change?
quiz.why: There are amount + 1 states and each tries every coin once. amount + 1 is a safe sentinel because no answer can use more than amount coins.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Decide whether a list of positive integers can be split into two groups with the same total.
Edge cases

items: An odd total is impossible immediately
An element larger than half the total makes it impossible

blocks.text: Brute force
Try assigning each number to one of the two groups: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach

The question is whether some subset sums to half the total. This is 0/1 knapsack: reach[s] says whether sum s can be formed. For each number, mark s reachable when s − x already was, scanning s downward so each number is used at most once.

items: Compute the total; if odd return false. target = total / 2.
For each number x, for s from target down to x: if reach[s − x], set reach[s].

blocks.caption: canPartition

blocks.text: Why this complexity

There are target + 1 states and each number scans them once. This is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the size of the sum, not only on n. The general problem is NP-complete, so no method polynomial in n alone is known.
Why it is correct
After processing some numbers, reach[s] is true exactly when a subset of them sums to s. Scanning downward means reach[s − x] still describes subsets without x, so x is never counted twice.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why must the inner loop run downward?
blocks.text: Scanning upward would let reach[s − x] already include x from earlier in the same pass, so x could be used more than once. That is the unbounded knapsack, which is a different problem.

blocks.title: Return the actual subset.
blocks.text: Keep, for each reachable sum, the number that first made it reachable, or keep the full two-dimensional table. Walk back from target subtracting the recorded number each time.

blocks.title: How does this relate to Coin Change?
blocks.text: Both are knapsack problems over sums. Coin Change lets each coin be used any number of times, so its inner loop runs upward and it minimises a count. Here each number is used at most once, so the loop runs downward and the table holds true or false.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given two strings, find the length of the longest sequence of characters that appears in both in the same order, not necessarily next to each other.

rows: a, c, e appear in order in both

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Subsequence is not the same as substring

blocks.text: Brute force
Generate every subsequence of one string and test it against the other: O(2ⁿ · m).
Optimal approach

Fill a table where dp[i][j] is the answer for the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other. If the two last characters match, extend the diagonal by one. Otherwise take the better of dropping a character from either string.

items: Create an (m + 1) × (n + 1) table of zeros; row 0 and column 0 stand for an empty prefix.
For each cell, compare the characters a[i − 1] and b[j − 1].
No match: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i − 1][j], dp[i][j − 1]). The bottom-right cell is the answer.

blocks.caption: longestCommonSubsequence

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) cells and each is filled in O(1). Space can be cut to two rows because a row depends only on the one above it.
Why it is correct

If the last characters match, some optimal answer uses that match, leaving the two shorter prefixes. If they differ, at least one of them is unused, so the answer equals the better of the two cases with one character removed.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Recover the subsequence, not just its length.
blocks.text: Walk back from the bottom-right cell. If the characters match, take that character and move diagonally. Otherwise move to whichever neighbour, up or left, holds the larger value. Reverse what you collected.

blocks.title: Reduce the space to O(min(m, n)).
blocks.text: Each row depends only on the row above, so keep two rows, or one row plus a saved diagonal value. Put the shorter string on the column axis.

blocks.title: How does edit distance differ?
blocks.text: Edit distance counts the fewest insertions, deletions and replacements to turn one string into the other. Its table takes a minimum over three operations instead of a maximum over two, and its first row and column are 0, 1, 2 and so on rather than zeros.

quiz.why: The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) cells and each is filled in O(1). Space can be cut to two rows because a row depends only on the one above it.

modules.title: Heap / Top K
modules.summary: A heap gives the smallest (or largest) item in O(log n) per update. Keep a heap of size k to track the k best.

blocks.text: A heap gives the smallest (or largest) item in O(log n) per update. Keep a heap of size k to track the k best.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A tournament bracket that always knows the current champion.
Clues in the problem

items: Top k, kth largest or smallest
Repeatedly take the best remaining item

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Sorting everything when only k items are needed
Swift's standard library has no heap; write one or use swift-collections

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why a min-heap for the k largest?
blocks.text: The root is the weakest of the k items kept, so a new item only needs comparing with the root, and the weakest is evicted in O(log k).

blocks.title: Heap versus quickselect: trade-offs?
blocks.text: A heap is O(n log k), works on streams and needs O(k) memory. Quickselect is O(n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case, and needs all the data in memory.

lessons.title: 703. Kth Largest Element in a Stream

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Numbers arrive one at a time. After each arrival, report the kth largest number seen so far.

rows: the third largest after each addition

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Fewer than k numbers at the start
A new number smaller than the current kth largest changes nothing

blocks.text: Brute force
Keep everything sorted and re-sort on each addition: O(n log n) per add.
Optimal approach

Keep only the k largest numbers in a min-heap. Its root is the smallest of them, which is the kth largest overall. On each arrival, push the number and, if the heap now holds more than k, remove the root.

items: Append the value and sift it up.
If the heap has more than k values, remove the minimum: move the last value to the root and sift it down.

blocks.caption: KthLargest

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The heap never holds more than k + 1 values, so each sift is at most log k steps. Older, smaller numbers can never become the kth largest again, so discarding them loses nothing.
Why it is correct
Invariant: the heap holds the k largest values seen (or all of them if fewer). A removed value is smaller than k others, and later arrivals only add larger competition.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why a min-heap and not a max-heap?
blocks.text: The value needed is the smallest of the k largest. A min-heap has exactly that at its root, and it is also the one to discard when a larger number arrives.

blocks.title: What if k can change between calls?
blocks.text: Keep all values in two heaps or a balanced tree so the boundary can move, since a heap of size k has discarded what a larger k would need.

blocks.title: How would you track the median instead?
blocks.text: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size. The median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Showing the score needed to stay in the top k of a live leaderboard. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

lessons.title: 215. Kth Largest Element in an Array

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Find the value that would sit in position k if the array were sorted from largest to smallest. Duplicates count as separate positions.
Edge cases
Brute force
Sort the whole array and read position n − k: O(n log n).
Optimal approach

Keep a min-heap holding the k largest values seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those, which is the kth largest overall. A new value only matters if it beats the root; then it replaces the root and sinks to its place.

items: While the heap has fewer than k values, append and sift up.
Otherwise compare the new value with the root.
If it is larger, overwrite the root and sift down.
At the end the root is the answer.

blocks.caption: findKthLargest

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Each of the n values causes at most one sift along a path of length log k. Quickselect achieves O(n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case and needs the whole array in memory; the heap also works on a stream.
Why it is correct
Invariant: the heap holds the k largest values seen so far. A value no larger than the root cannot be among them. A larger value displaces the root, which is the weakest member.
Alternative: Quickselect

Quickselect. Pick a pivot (here the last element of the range), move everything smaller to its left, and put the pivot between the two groups: it is now in its final sorted position. If that position is the one wanted, stop; otherwise repeat on the side that contains it. O(n) time on average and O(n²) in the worst case, for example on already sorted input with this pivot choice; choosing a random pivot makes the worst case unlikely. O(1) extra space beyond the working copy.

blocks.caption: findKthLargestQuick

blocks.text: Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with quickselect. What are the trade-offs?
blocks.text: Partition around a pivot as in quicksort, then continue only in the side that contains position n − k. O(n) on average and O(1) extra space, but O(n²) in the worst case, it reorders the array, and it needs all the data up front.

blocks.title: How do the sift-up and sift-down index formulas work?
blocks.text: With the heap stored in an array from index 0, the children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and the parent is at (i − 1) / 2. Sift up swaps with the parent while smaller; sift down swaps with the smaller child while larger.

blocks.title: What changes if the numbers arrive as an endless stream?
blocks.text: The heap approach works unchanged, since it only keeps k values. Quickselect and sorting do not apply because the data never ends.

blocks.text: Finding the cut-off score for the top k results without sorting everything. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.why: Each of the n values causes at most one sift along a path of length log k. Quickselect achieves O(n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case and needs the whole array in memory; the heap also works on a stream.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Return the k values that occur most often in the array. Any order is accepted.
Edge cases

items: k equals the number of distinct values
Swift dictionary iteration order is not stable, so tied values can come out in any order

blocks.text: Brute force
Count, then sort all distinct values by frequency: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
Count with a dictionary, then bucket values by frequency. A frequency is at most n, so an array of n + 1 buckets covers every case; read buckets from high to low.

items: Place each value in buckets[its frequency].
Walk buckets from n down to 1 collecting values until k are taken.

blocks.caption: topKFrequent

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Counting, bucketing and the final walk are each linear. A size-k heap gives O(n log k), which is the usual alternative when memory matters.
Why it is correct
Values in a higher bucket are strictly more frequent than those in lower buckets, so reading downward yields the k most frequent.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Use a heap instead; compare costs.
blocks.text: Count, then keep a min-heap of size k ordered by frequency: O(n log k) time and O(k) for the heap. The bucket method is O(n) but allocates n + 1 buckets.

blocks.title: Handle a stream where counts change.
blocks.text: Keep counts in a dictionary and recompute the top k on demand, or maintain an ordered structure. For very large streams use an approximate method such as Space-Saving or a Count-Min Sketch.

blocks.title: Return results in a deterministic order.
blocks.text: Sort by frequency descending and then by value ascending, or sort the values inside each bucket.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Showing the most searched terms or the most ordered products in a period. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Several linked lists are each in ascending order. Combine all their nodes into one ascending list.
Edge cases
Brute force
Collect every value, sort, and rebuild: O(N log N) for N total nodes.
Optimal approach
Keep the current head of every list in a min-heap. Repeatedly take the smallest node, attach it to the result, and put that node's successor into the heap in its place.

items: Push the head of each non-empty list into the heap.
Take the root: it is the smallest remaining node. Attach it to the result.
If it has a successor, put the successor at the root; otherwise move the last heap entry to the root and shrink.
Sift down and repeat until the heap is empty.

blocks.caption: mergeKLists

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The heap never holds more than k nodes, so each of the N nodes costs log k. Merging the lists in pairs, round by round, has the same bound without a heap.
Why it is correct
The smallest remaining node overall must be the head of some list, and all heads are in the heap, so the root is the global minimum each time.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it by merging pairs of lists.
blocks.text: Merge lists in pairs so the number of lists halves each round. There are log k rounds and each touches all N nodes: O(N log k), with no heap.

blocks.title: Why is merging one list at a time into the result slower?
blocks.text: The growing result is rescanned for every list, so early nodes are compared again and again: O(N · k) in total.

blocks.title: How would this work with files too large for memory?
blocks.text: Read one block from each file, keep the current smallest items in a heap, and write output in blocks. This is the merge phase of external sorting.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Merging time-ordered event streams from several sources into one timeline. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.why: The heap never holds more than k nodes, so each of the N nodes costs log k. Merging the lists in pairs, round by round, has the same bound without a heap.

rows: O(log n) per add, O(1) per median

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Numbers arrive one at a time. At any moment, report the median of all numbers seen so far.

rows: average of 1 and 2; then the middle of 1, 2, 3

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Even count: average of the two middle values
findMedian is assumed to be called after at least one add

blocks.text: Brute force
Keep a sorted array and insert each number in place: O(n) per add.
Optimal approach

Keep the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, with the smaller half holding the same number of values or one more. The median is at the top of one heap or the average of both tops.

items: Push the new number into the smaller half.
Move the largest value of the smaller half into the larger half, so every value in low is ≤ every value in high.
If the larger half now has more values, move its smallest back.
Median: top of low if it has more values, otherwise the average of both tops.

blocks.caption: MedianFinder

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Only the two middle values are ever needed, and heaps keep exactly those at their tops. Each add performs at most three heap operations.
Why it is correct
Passing a value through low and then across guarantees low's maximum ≤ high's minimum. The size rule keeps the middle of the sorted order at the tops.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why does every number go through low first?
blocks.text: It guarantees the ordering between the halves: the value that crosses to high is the largest of low after the new number joined, so nothing in low exceeds anything in high.

blocks.title: What if numbers can also be removed?
blocks.text: Use two balanced trees or heaps with lazy deletion: mark removed values and discard them when they reach a top, tracking the real sizes separately.

blocks.title: What if all numbers are between 0 and 100?
blocks.text: Keep 101 counters. Adding is O(1), and the median is found by walking the counters to the middle position, which is a constant amount of work.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Reporting a running median response time. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

options: O(log n) per add, O(1) per median
quiz.why: Only the two middle values are ever needed, and heaps keep exactly those at their tops. Each add performs at most three heap operations.

blocks.text: Model items as nodes and relations as edges, then visit with BFS/DFS or process in dependency order.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A city map of junctions and roads.
Clues in the problem

items: Grids where cells connect to neighbours

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes
Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle?
blocks.text: If fewer than n nodes are output, the remaining nodes all still have incoming edges, which is only possible if they lie on or behind a cycle.

blocks.title: Adjacency list versus matrix?
blocks.text: A list uses O(V + E) memory and suits sparse graphs. A matrix uses O(V²) memory but answers 'is there an edge' in O(1), which suits dense graphs.
The problem in plain words
Given one node of a connected undirected graph, build a completely separate copy of the whole graph and return the copy of that node.

rows: a new graph with the same four links
no node object is shared with the original

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Cycles: the copy must not loop forever
Every copy must be a new object

blocks.text: Brute force
There is no simpler correct approach; forgetting the dictionary leads to infinite recursion on any cycle.
Optimal approach

DFS with a dictionary from each original node to its copy. On reaching a node: if it already has a copy, return it. Otherwise create the copy, record it immediately, then copy each neighbour recursively and attach the results.

items: If this node was already copied, return that copy.
Create a new node and store it in the dictionary before going further.
For each neighbour, clone it and append the result to the copy's neighbours.

blocks.caption: cloneGraph

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node is copied once and each link is followed once from each end.
Why it is correct

Recording the copy before visiting neighbours means a cycle leads back to the existing copy instead of creating another. Every neighbour link in the original is reproduced between the corresponding copies.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it with BFS.
blocks.text: Put the start node in a queue and its copy in the dictionary. For each node taken from the queue, look at its neighbours: create and queue copies for unseen ones, and append each neighbour's copy to the current copy.

blocks.title: Why must the copy be registered before the loop?
blocks.text: A cycle leads back to a node whose neighbours are still being copied. If its copy were not yet registered, the recursion would create another copy and never finish.

blocks.title: How would you copy a linked list that has random pointers?
blocks.text: Use a dictionary from original node to copy in two passes: first create all the copies, then set each copy's next and random through the dictionary.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Duplicating an object graph such as a document with cross-references. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Clone Graph?
quiz.why: Each node is copied once and each link is followed once from each end.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A grid holds land ("1") and water ("0"). Land cells that touch up, down, left or right belong to the same island. Count the islands.
Edge cases

items: A very large island makes the recursion deep

blocks.text: Brute force
For each land cell, search the whole grid for its component without marking: revisits cells repeatedly.
Optimal approach
Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill from it, marking each reached cell as water so it is never counted again.

items: Copy the grid so it can be marked.
On a "1": count += 1, then sink the whole island with DFS.

blocks.caption: numIslands

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each cell is sunk at most once and examined a constant number of times.
Why it is correct
A flood fill reaches exactly the cells connected to its start. Because those are erased, each island triggers the counter exactly once.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Use BFS to avoid deep recursion.
blocks.text: Replace the recursion with a queue. Mark a cell when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued, so it is never queued twice.

blocks.title: Solve it with Union Find.
blocks.text: Treat each land cell as a node. Union each land cell with its right and down land neighbours. The answer is the number of land cells minus the number of successful unions.

blocks.title: Return the largest island's area.
blocks.text: Have the flood fill return how many cells it sank and keep the maximum.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting connected regions, such as separate clusters of occupied seats or touching delivery zones on a map grid. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Number of Islands?
quiz.why: Each cell is sunk at most once and examined a constant number of times.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

Courses are numbered from 0. Some pairs say one course must be taken before another. Decide whether every course can be completed, which is possible exactly when the requirements contain no circular dependency.

rows: each course waits for the other

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A cycle that does not involve course 0
In each pair [a, b], b comes before a

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every ordering of the courses and check it against the requirements: O(n!).
Optimal approach

Kahn's algorithm. Count how many prerequisites each course still needs. Courses needing none are ready. Take a ready course, reduce the count of every course it unlocks, and add any that reach zero. If all courses get taken there is no cycle.

items: Build the list of courses each course unlocks and each course's prerequisite count.
Collect every course whose count is 0.
Take one ready course and lower the count of each course it unlocks.
A course whose count reaches 0 becomes ready. Finish when none are ready and compare the number taken with the total.

blocks.caption: canFinish

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each course is taken once and each prerequisite pair is processed once. The input itself has V + E items, so this is linear in the input.
Why it is correct

A course in a cycle can never reach count 0, because another course in the same cycle must be taken first. Conversely, if there is no cycle, some untaken course always has all its prerequisites taken, so the process never stalls early.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Return a valid order of courses instead of true or false.
blocks.text: Append each course to a list at the moment it is taken. If the list ends with every course it is a valid order; otherwise there is a cycle and no order exists.

blocks.title: Solve it with DFS.
blocks.text: Mark each node as unvisited, in progress or finished. Reaching an in-progress node means a cycle. Appending nodes as they finish and reversing the list gives a valid order.

blocks.title: How would you find the smallest number of terms needed if courses can be taken in parallel?
blocks.text: Process the ready courses one whole layer at a time, like BFS levels. The number of layers is the minimum number of terms; it equals the longest chain of prerequisites.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Ordering build steps or database migrations so each runs after the ones it depends on. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Course Schedule?
quiz.why: Each course is taken once and each prerequisite pair is processed once. The input itself has V + E items, so this is linear in the input.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Courses are numbered from 0, and some must be taken before others. Return one order in which all courses can be taken, or an empty list if the requirements are circular.
Edge cases

items: Several valid orders exist; this code returns one
A cycle anywhere makes the answer empty

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every ordering and check it: O(n!).
Optimal approach

Kahn's algorithm with the queue doubling as the answer. Courses with no remaining prerequisites enter the queue. Reading the queue from the front, each course lowers the count of the courses it unlocks, and those reaching zero are appended.

items: Build unlock lists and prerequisite counts.
queue = every course with count 0; head = 0.
Take queue[head], advance head, and lower the counts of the courses it unlocks.
Append any that reach 0. At the end, the queue is the order if it contains every course.

blocks.caption: findOrder

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each course is appended once and each prerequisite pair is processed once. A head index avoids removeFirst().
Why it is correct

A course is appended only after all its prerequisites were appended earlier, so the queue is a valid order. Courses on a cycle never reach count 0, so the queue falls short exactly when a cycle exists.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How do you produce the lexicographically smallest order?
blocks.text: Replace the queue with a min-heap so the smallest available course number is always taken next.

blocks.title: Solve it with DFS.
blocks.text: Run a DFS with three states per node. Append a node after all the nodes that depend on it are finished, then reverse the list. Meeting an in-progress node means a cycle.

blocks.title: Why is the queue itself the answer?
blocks.text: Courses are appended only when all their prerequisites are already in the queue, and nothing is ever removed, so the final contents are in a valid order.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Producing an install order for packages that depend on each other. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Course Schedule II?
quiz.why: Each course is appended once and each prerequisite pair is processed once. A head index avoids removeFirst().

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

A grid gives the height of each cell of an island. The Pacific touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right edges. Water flows from a cell to a neighbour of equal or lower height. Find the cells from which water can reach both oceans.

rows: the cell with height 1 cannot reach the Atlantic

blocks.text: Edge cases
Brute force
From every cell, search downhill to see which oceans are reachable: O((rows × cols)²).
Optimal approach
Reverse the direction. Start from each ocean's edge cells and climb to neighbours of equal or greater height, marking what that ocean can be reached from. The answer is the cells marked for both.

items: Keep one marked grid per ocean.
From every Pacific edge cell climb uphill, marking cells; do the same from every Atlantic edge cell.
A climb continues only to unmarked neighbours at least as high as the current cell.
Collect the cells marked in both grids.

blocks.caption: pacificAtlantic

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each cell is marked at most once per ocean. Two searches from the edges replace one search per cell.
Why it is correct
Water can flow from cell x to the ocean exactly when the ocean's edge can be reached from x by non-increasing steps, which is the same as reaching x from the edge by non-decreasing steps.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why search from the oceans instead of from each cell?
blocks.text: A search from each cell repeats work for neighbouring cells. Two searches from the edges visit every cell at most twice in total.

blocks.title: Do it with BFS.
blocks.text: Put all of one ocean's edge cells in a queue and expand to unmarked neighbours that are at least as high; repeat for the other ocean.

blocks.title: What changes if water also flows diagonally?
blocks.text: Use eight directions in the climb. Nothing else changes.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Working out which regions drain to both of two outlets in a height map. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Pacific Atlantic Water Flow?
quiz.why: Each cell is marked at most once per ocean. Two searches from the edges replace one search per cell.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A grid holds land (1) and water (0). Land cells touching up, down, left or right form an island. Find the number of cells in the largest island.

rows: the top-left island has three cells

blocks.text: Edge cases
Brute force
For each land cell, flood-fill without marking and count: revisits the same island once per cell.
Optimal approach
Scan the grid. On unvisited land, flood-fill with DFS that erases each cell as it counts it and returns the count. Keep the largest count.

items: Copy the grid so cells can be erased.
area(r, c) returns 0 outside the grid or on water.
Otherwise erase the cell and return 1 plus the areas in the four directions.
Scan every cell and keep the largest area returned.

blocks.caption: maxAreaOfIsland

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each cell is erased at most once, and each is examined a constant number of times.
Why it is correct
A flood fill visits exactly the cells of one island and counts each once, because a cell is erased before its neighbours are explored.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How does this differ from Number of Islands?
blocks.text: Number of Islands only counts how many flood fills start. Here each flood fill also returns how many cells it erased, and the largest is kept.

blocks.title: Avoid deep recursion.
blocks.text: Use an explicit stack or a queue of cells in place of recursion, marking a cell when it is added.

blocks.title: Count the perimeter of an island instead.
blocks.text: For each land cell add 4, then subtract 1 for every neighbouring land cell on its four sides.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the largest contiguous block of occupied cells in a floor or seating plan. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Max Area of Island?
quiz.why: Each cell is erased at most once, and each is examined a constant number of times.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A signal starts at one node of a network of one-way links, each with a travel time. Find how long it takes until every node has received it, or report −1 if some node is unreachable.

rows: node 4 is reached last, at time 2
node 1 cannot be reached from node 2

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A longer path with more links that is still faster
Nodes are numbered from 1, so index 0 is unused

blocks.text: Brute force
Explore every path from the source with DFS, keeping the best time per node: exponential in the worst case.
Optimal approach

Dijkstra's algorithm. Repeatedly settle the unsettled node with the smallest known time; its time is final because all link times are non-negative. Then try to improve its neighbours through it. The answer is the largest settled time.

items: Set the source's time to 0 and every other time to infinity.
Pick the unsettled reachable node with the smallest time and settle it.
For each link out of it, update the neighbour if going through this node is faster.
Repeat until no reachable node is unsettled. Return the largest time, or −1 if any is still infinity.

blocks.caption: networkDelayTime

blocks.text: Why this complexity

This version finds the next node by scanning an array, which costs O(V) per round. That is simple and efficient for dense graphs. With a min-heap the cost becomes O((V + E) log V), which is better for large sparse graphs.
Why it is correct

When the node with the smallest tentative time is chosen, any other route to it would pass through a node with a time at least as large and then add a non-negative link, so it cannot be shorter. This argument fails with negative weights.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Rewrite it with a priority queue. What changes?
blocks.text: Push (time, node) pairs into a min-heap and pop the smallest, skipping entries whose time is worse than the recorded one. The cost becomes O((V + E) log V), which is better on sparse graphs. Swift needs a hand-written heap or swift-collections.

blocks.title: What if some link times are negative?
blocks.text: Dijkstra is no longer correct, because a settled time could later be improved. Use Bellman–Ford, which relaxes every link V − 1 times in O(V · E) and can detect a negative cycle.

blocks.title: How would you return the actual route to a node?
blocks.text: Record for each node the node it was last improved from. Follow those predecessors back from the target to the source and reverse the list.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the fastest delivery time from a depot to every drop point over a road network. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Network Delay Time?
quiz.why: This version finds the next node by scanning an array, which costs O(V) per round. That is simple and efficient for dense graphs. With a min-heap the cost becomes O((V + E) log V), which is better for large sparse graphs.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Cities are linked by one-way flights with prices. Find the cheapest way to travel from a start city to a destination using at most k intermediate stops, or report −1 if it cannot be done.

rows: only the direct flight is allowed

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: k stops means at most k + 1 flights
The cheapest route overall may use too many stops

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every route with DFS, stopping at k + 1 flights: exponential in k.
Optimal approach

Bellman–Ford limited to k + 1 rounds. In each round, try every flight once, but read prices only from the previous round. After round r the table holds the cheapest price to each city using at most r flights.

items: cost[src] = 0; every other city is infinity.
Repeat k + 1 times: copy cost into next.
For each flight from a reachable city, lower next[to] if cost[from] + price is cheaper.
Replace cost with next. At the end return cost[dst], or −1 if it is still infinity.

blocks.caption: findCheapestPrice

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are k + 1 rounds and each looks at every flight once. Plain Dijkstra does not respect the stop limit without also tracking the number of flights in its state.
Why it is correct

By induction on rounds: a cheapest route with at most r flights ends with one flight added to a cheapest route with at most r − 1 flights. Copying the array is what stops one round from chaining two flights.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why is the copy of the cost array needed?
blocks.text: Without it, a price improved earlier in the same round could be used by a later flight in that round, chaining two or more flights and breaking the 'at most r flights after round r' guarantee.

blocks.title: How does full Bellman–Ford detect a negative cycle?
blocks.text: Run V − 1 rounds, then one more. If any distance still improves in the extra round, a negative cycle is reachable from the source.

blocks.title: Could you solve this with Dijkstra?
blocks.text: Yes, if the state is (city, flights used) rather than the city alone, so that a dearer route with fewer flights is not discarded. The heap then holds (cost, city, flights) entries.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the cheapest shipment route when the number of hand-offs is capped. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Cheapest Flights Within K Stops?
quiz.why: There are k + 1 rounds and each looks at every flight once. Plain Dijkstra does not respect the stop limit without also tracking the number of flights in its state.

items: Skipping path compression or union by size
Using it when edges are removed

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What do path compression and union by size each buy you?
blocks.text: Path compression flattens the tree during find. Union by size keeps trees shallow when merging. Together they give near-constant amortised time per operation.

blocks.title: Union Find versus DFS for components?
blocks.text: For a fixed graph both are linear and DFS is simpler. Union Find is better when edges arrive over time with connectivity queries in between. It cannot remove edges.

lessons.title: 323. Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
There are n nodes numbered from 0 and a list of undirected links. Count the separate groups, where nodes are in one group if a chain of links joins them.
Edge cases
Brute force
Run a full search from every node without remembering visits.
Optimal approach
Union Find. Start with n groups. For each link, find the leaders of both ends; if they differ, merge the groups and reduce the count by one.

items: For each edge find the two leaders.
If they differ, point one at the other and decrement count.

blocks.caption: countComponents

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Each edge costs two finds and at most one union. This version uses path halving only; union by size gives the near-constant bound formally. DFS over an adjacency list is an equally good O(n + E) alternative.
Why it is correct
Each successful union joins two different groups into one, so count always equals the number of groups. An edge inside a group changes nothing.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with DFS.
blocks.text: Build an adjacency list, then run DFS from every unvisited node, counting how many times a search starts.

blocks.title: Edges arrive over time: report the count after each.
blocks.text: Union Find handles this directly: process each edge as it arrives and report the current count.

blocks.title: How do you tell whether the graph is a tree?
blocks.text: It must have exactly n − 1 edges and a single component. Equivalently, no edge may join two nodes that are already connected, and the final count must be 1.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting separate clusters of linked accounts or devices. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
