rows: O(n²) table scan; finds are O(log n) worst case here

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A square 0/1 table says which pairs of cities are directly connected. Cities linked directly or through others form one group. Count the groups.
Edge cases

items: The table is symmetric, so only the upper triangle is read

blocks.text: Brute force
Run a full search from every city without remembering visits: repeats work for each member of a group.
Optimal approach
Union Find. Every city starts as its own group. For each connected pair, find both group leaders; if they differ, merge them and reduce the count by one.

items: parent[i] = i for every city; count = n.
For each pair (i, j) with a 1 in the table, find both leaders.
If the leaders differ, point one at the other and decrement count.

blocks.caption: findCircleNum

blocks.text: Why this complexity

Reading the table is already n² and cannot be avoided. This version uses path halving only; adding union by size brings each find to near-constant amortised time. A DFS over the table is equally good at O(n²).
Why it is correct
Two cities share a leader exactly when a chain of merges links them. Each successful merge joins two distinct groups, so count always equals the number of groups.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Add union by size; what does it buy?
blocks.text: Attach the smaller tree under the larger one. Together with path compression this keeps trees almost flat, so each operation is near-constant amortised time.

blocks.title: Solve it with DFS instead.
blocks.text: Keep a visited array. For each unvisited city, add one to the count and DFS through every city its row connects to. O(n²).

blocks.title: Connections arrive one at a time; report the count after each.
blocks.text: That is the natural use of Union Find: union each connection as it arrives, decrement the count when the two leaders differ, and report the count.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Grouping devices or accounts that are linked to each other directly or through intermediaries. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Number of Provinces?
options: O(n²) table scan; finds are O(log n) worst case here
quiz.why: Reading the table is already n² and cannot be avoided. This version uses path halving only; adding union by size brings each find to near-constant amortised time. A DFS over the table is equally good at O(n²).

blocks.text: The problem in plain words

A graph started as a tree on n nodes numbered 1 to n, then one extra edge was added, creating exactly one cycle. Given the edges in order, return the edge that can be removed to restore a tree; if several qualify, the one that appears last.

rows: 1, 2 and 3 are already connected when [2,3] arrives

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: The cycle may not include node 1
Edges after the redundant one still exist
Nodes are numbered from 1, so index 0 is unused

blocks.text: Brute force
For each edge, remove it and check with DFS whether the rest is still connected: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Union Find. Process edges in order. If the two ends already have the same leader they are already connected, so this edge closes the cycle. Otherwise merge their groups.

items: For each edge find the leaders of both ends.
Different: point one leader at the other.

blocks.caption: findRedundantConnection

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each edge costs two finds and at most one union. This version uses path halving only; adding union by size gives the near-constant bound formally.
Why it is correct

Before the cycle closes, the edges form a forest and every edge joins two separate groups. The first edge whose ends share a group is the one that completes the single cycle, and it is the last edge of that cycle in input order.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What changes for a directed graph?
blocks.text: A directed version has two failure cases: a node with two parents, and a cycle. You record the two candidate edges for the double parent and use Union Find to see which one must go.

blocks.title: Solve it with DFS.
blocks.text: Before adding each edge, run DFS from one end to see whether the other end is already reachable. If it is, that edge is the answer. This is O(n²) overall.

blocks.title: Why is the first edge that fails also the last edge of the cycle?
blocks.text: Until the cycle closes, the edges form a forest. The first edge whose ends are already connected completes the cycle, so every other edge of that cycle came earlier in the input.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the link that introduced a loop in a network that should be loop-free. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Redundant Connection?
quiz.why: Each edge costs two finds and at most one union. This version uses path halving only; adding union by size gives the near-constant bound formally.

modules.title: Trie
modules.summary: A tree keyed by characters. Shared prefixes share nodes, so prefix queries cost only the prefix length.

blocks.text: A tree keyed by characters. Shared prefixes share nodes, so prefix queries cost only the prefix length.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A filing cabinet whose drawers are labelled by first letter, then second letter, and so on.
Clues in the problem

items: Many words checked against one text or board

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes
Interview questions

blocks.title: Trie versus a sorted array with binary search for prefixes?
blocks.text: A sorted array finds a prefix range in O(L log n), is compact and cache-friendly, but inserting is O(n). A trie does lookup and insert in O(L) and uses more memory.

blocks.title: How do you delete a word?
blocks.text: Clear the end-of-word flag on the last node, then optionally remove nodes on the way back up that have no children and end no word.

rows: O(L) per operation, L = length of the word or prefix

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Build a word store with three operations: add a word, ask whether an exact word was added, and ask whether any added word begins with a given prefix.

rows: the full word and its prefix are both on the path
the path exists but "app" was never added as a word

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A word that is a prefix of another word
Searching a prefix that was never marked as a word

blocks.text: Brute force
Keep words in an array and scan it: O(total characters) per query. A Set answers exact search in O(length) but cannot answer prefix queries without scanning.
Optimal approach
A tree where each edge is a character. Words that share a prefix share the same path from the root. Each node carries a flag saying whether a word ends there.

items: insert: walk from the root, creating missing child nodes, then set isWord on the last node.
walk: follow the characters; return nil as soon as a child is missing.
startsWith: walk and require only that the path exists.

blocks.caption: Trie

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each operation touches one node per character, regardless of how many words are stored. Every character must be read, so O(L) is the floor.
Why it is correct
A path from the root spells exactly one string. insert guarantees the path exists and marks its end; search and startsWith differ only in whether that mark is required.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Support a wildcard character in search.
blocks.text: At a wildcard, try every child recursively; at a normal character follow the single matching child. The worst case visits many nodes.

blocks.title: Delete a word.
blocks.text: Walk to the last node and clear its isWord flag. Optionally walk back up, removing nodes that have no children and are not word ends.

blocks.title: Dictionary children versus a fixed array of 26: trade-offs?
blocks.text: A fixed array of 26 is fast and predictable for lowercase a–z but wastes memory in sparse nodes. A dictionary handles any Character and saves memory when nodes are sparse, at the cost of hashing.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Suggesting completions as a user types a product name. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)?
options: O(L) per operation, L = length of the word or prefix
quiz.why: Each operation touches one node per character, regardless of how many words are stored. Every character must be read, so O(L) is the floor.

lessons.title: 211. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

rows: O(L) for add; search is O(L) without dots and up to O(26^d · L) with d dots

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Build a word store that supports adding words and searching, where a search pattern may contain dots and each dot matches any single letter.

rows: the dot matches b, d or m

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A pattern that is all dots
A pattern shorter or longer than every word
A prefix of a word is not a match

blocks.text: Brute force
Keep a list and compare the pattern with every word: O(words × length) per search.
Optimal approach
Store the words in a trie. Search walks the trie along the pattern: a letter follows its one child; a dot tries every child of the current node.

items: addWord: walk from the root creating missing children; mark the last node.
search: at the end of the pattern, the answer is the node's word mark.
At a dot, succeed if any child matches the rest of the pattern.
At a letter, follow that child or fail.

blocks.caption: WordDictionary

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Without dots a search touches one node per character. Each dot can fan out across all children, so many dots make it slower.
Why it is correct
A trie path spells a stored prefix. A pattern matches a word exactly when a root path exists whose letters agree with the pattern at every non-dot position and which ends on a marked node.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How would you speed up patterns with many dots?
blocks.text: Group stored words by length so a pattern only meets words of its own length, or keep counts of what lies below each node so impossible branches can be skipped.

blocks.title: Support * matching any number of letters.
blocks.text: At a star, try matching zero letters (stay on this node and advance the pattern) or one letter (move to each child and keep the star). Memoise on node and pattern position.

blocks.title: Why not use a hash set?
blocks.text: A hash set answers exact lookups only. A pattern with dots would have to be compared with every stored word.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Matching crossword-style patterns such as c.t against a word list. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

links.title: Open LeetCode 211: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Design Add and Search Words Data Structure?
options: O(L) for add; search is O(L) without dots and up to O(26^d · L) with d dots
quiz.why: Without dots a search touches one node per character. Each dot can fan out across all children, so many dots make it slower.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given a grid of letters and a list of words, report every word that can be traced through neighbouring cells without reusing a cell within that word.

rows: board oaan / etae / ihkr / iflv, words [oath, pea, eat, rain]
pea and rain cannot be traced

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A word that is a prefix of another
The same word reachable by several paths must be reported once

blocks.text: Brute force
Run the single-word search once per word: repeats the same board walks for every word.
Optimal approach

Put all the words in a trie and walk the board once. A DFS step moves to a neighbouring cell only if the current trie node has a child for that letter, so every shared prefix is explored once for all words.

items: Build the trie; store the full word at its last node.
From each cell, follow the trie child for that cell's letter; stop if there is none.
If the node holds a word, report it and clear it so it is not reported again.
Mark the cell, try the four neighbours, restore the cell.

blocks.caption: findWords

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The trie prunes any path that is not a prefix of some word, which in practice removes almost all of the search.
Why it is correct
A DFS path spells a prefix exactly when the matching trie path exists, so every word traceable on the board is reached, and clearing the stored word prevents duplicates.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Remove finished words from the trie to speed things up.
blocks.text: When a word is reported and its node has no children left, delete the node from its parent. Dead branches then stop attracting the search.

blocks.title: Why store the whole word at the node?
blocks.text: The DFS then knows the word as soon as it reaches the node, without rebuilding it from the path, and clearing it marks the word as already reported.

blocks.title: How does this differ from Word Search?
blocks.text: Word Search looks for one word, guided by its letters. Here many words are searched in a single pass, guided by the trie, so shared prefixes are walked once.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding all dictionary words in a letter-grid game. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Word Search II?
quiz.why: The trie prunes any path that is not a prefix of some word, which in practice removes almost all of the search.

modules.title: Bit Manipulation
modules.summary: Use the binary form of integers directly: XOR to cancel pairs, masks to test and set flags.

blocks.text: Use the binary form of integers directly: XOR to cancel pairs, masks to test and set flags.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: A row of light switches, each flipped independently.
Clues in the problem

items: Powers of two, parity, counting set bits

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes
Interview questions

blocks.title: Why does x & (x − 1) clear the lowest set bit?
blocks.text: Subtracting 1 turns the lowest set bit to 0 and the zeros below it to 1. ANDing with the original clears that bit and leaves the higher bits unchanged.

blocks.title: How do you enumerate all subsets with a mask?
blocks.text: Loop mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; element i is in the subset when bit i of mask is set.
The problem in plain words
Every value appears exactly twice except one. Find the one that appears once, without extra memory.
Edge cases

items: The guarantee (pairs plus one) must hold

blocks.text: Brute force
Count occurrences in a dictionary: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimal approach
XOR every value together. x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and order does not matter, so each pair cancels and the single value remains.

blocks.caption: singleNumber

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass and one integer of state. Every element must be read, so O(n) time is the floor.
Why it is correct
XOR is associative and commutative, so the total equals the XOR of all pairs (each 0) with the single value.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What if every other value appears three times?
blocks.text: Count the set bits at each bit position modulo 3; the remainders form the answer. O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.title: What if two values appear once?
blocks.text: XOR everything to get a ^ b. Pick any set bit of that result, split the numbers by whether they have that bit, and XOR each group separately.

blocks.title: Why does order not matter?
blocks.text: XOR is commutative and associative, so the values can be regrouped into pairs that cancel no matter where they sit.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding the one unmatched ID when every open event should have a matching close event. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Single Number?
quiz.why: One pass and one integer of state. Every element must be read, so O(n) time is the floor.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Take the 32-bit binary form of a number and write its bits in the opposite order: the lowest bit becomes the highest, and so on.

rows: the single low bit moves to position 31

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Leading zeros matter: they become trailing zeros
The result needs all 32 positions, so exactly 32 rounds are run

blocks.text: Brute force
Convert to a 32-character string, reverse it and parse: slower and allocates.
Optimal approach
Repeat 32 times: shift the result left by one, copy in the lowest bit of the input, and shift the input right by one.

blocks.caption: reverseBits

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The work is fixed by the word size. Swapping halves, quarters and so on with masks does it in five steps; a lookup table per byte is fastest for repeated calls.
Why it is correct
In round i the bit at position i of the input is appended to the result. After 32 rounds it has been shifted left 31 − i more times, landing at position 31 − i.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How would you speed it up for many calls?
blocks.text: Precompute the reversal of every byte in a 256-entry table, then reverse a 32-bit value by reversing its four bytes and swapping their order.

blocks.title: Do it with masks and swaps.
blocks.text: Swap the two 16-bit halves, then the 8-bit halves of each, then 4-bit, 2-bit and 1-bit groups, using a mask and two shifts at each stage. Five steps in total.

blocks.title: Why loop exactly 32 times instead of until x is 0?
blocks.text: Stopping when x reaches 0 would leave the result short by the number of leading zeros, which must appear as trailing zeros in the answer.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Converting bit order when two devices number bits from opposite ends. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Reverse Bits?
quiz.why: The work is fixed by the word size. Swapping halves, quarters and so on with masks does it in five steps; a lookup table per byte is fastest for repeated calls.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Count how many bits are set to 1 in the binary form of a non-negative integer.
Edge cases

items: Powers of two have exactly one
The code assumes a non-negative value

blocks.text: Brute force
Test each of the 64 bit positions with a shift and a mask: fixed 64 steps.
Optimal approach
x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit. Repeat until x is zero and count the repetitions.

items: While x is not zero, replace x with x & (x − 1).

blocks.caption: hammingWeight

blocks.text: Why this complexity
The loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position. Swift's built-in nonzeroBitCount does this in one hardware instruction where available.
Why it is correct
Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and all lower bits to 1. ANDing with x keeps the higher bits and clears that bit and everything below it, so exactly one set bit disappears each round.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: What does Swift provide for this?
blocks.text: Every integer type has nonzeroBitCount, along with leadingZeroBitCount and trailingZeroBitCount.

blocks.title: Count the bits for every number from 0 to n.
blocks.text: Use DP: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1), or bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1. O(n) in total.

blocks.title: How do you test whether a number is a power of two?
blocks.text: It must be positive and satisfy x & (x − 1) == 0, meaning it has exactly one set bit.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Counting how many feature flags are switched on in a bitmask. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Number of 1 Bits?
quiz.why: The loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position. Swift's built-in nonzeroBitCount does this in one hardware instruction where available.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
An array of length n holds distinct numbers from the range 0 to n, so exactly one number of that range is absent. Find it.

rows: the missing one is n itself

blocks.text: Edge cases
Brute force
Sort and look for the gap, or use a set: O(n log n) time or O(n) space.
Optimal approach
XOR every index 0 to n with every value. Each present number appears once as an index and once as a value and cancels. Only the missing number is left.

items: acc = n (the one index the loop does not visit).
For each index i and value x, acc = acc XOR i XOR x.

blocks.caption: missingNumber

blocks.text: Why this complexity
One pass and one integer. The sum formula n(n + 1) / 2 − sum works too; XOR cannot overflow.
Why it is correct
The XOR of all numbers 0 to n, combined with the XOR of the array, pairs up every present number with itself. x ^ x is 0, so the result is the single unpaired number.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with a sum.
blocks.text: Subtract the sum of the array from n(n + 1) / 2. In languages with fixed-width integers watch for overflow on large n.

blocks.title: What if two numbers are missing?
blocks.text: XOR alone gives a ^ b. Use the sum and the sum of squares to form two equations, or split the numbers by a set bit of a ^ b and XOR each group separately.

blocks.title: Why start acc at n?
blocks.text: The loop covers indices 0 to n − 1, but the range of numbers goes up to n. Starting acc at n includes that last number.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Finding which sequence number never arrived in a batch. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Missing Number?
quiz.why: One pass and one integer. The sum formula n(n + 1) / 2 − sum works too; XOR cannot overflow.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
For every number from 0 to n, report how many 1 bits its binary form has, as a list.
Edge cases

items: Powers of two have exactly one bit

blocks.text: Brute force
Count the bits of each number separately: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
Dropping the last binary digit of i gives i >> 1, a smaller number whose answer is already known. The dropped digit is i & 1. So bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

items: For i from 1 to n, look up bits[i >> 1].

blocks.caption: countBits

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each entry is one lookup and one addition. The output has n + 1 entries, so O(n) is the floor.
Why it is correct
i and i >> 1 have the same bits except for the lowest one, which is i & 1. The smaller index is always filled in first.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Use the recurrence based on i & (i − 1).
blocks.text: bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1, because i & (i − 1) is i with its lowest set bit removed.

blocks.title: Why is this dynamic programming?
blocks.text: Each answer is built from the answer to a smaller sub-problem that was stored earlier, which is the definition of bottom-up DP.

blocks.title: What is the total number of 1 bits from 0 to n?
blocks.text: Sum the list, or count per bit position: for each position, full cycles of 2^(p+1) contribute 2^p ones each, plus the remainder.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Precomputing a lookup table of bit counts for fast use later. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Counting Bits?
quiz.why: Each entry is one lookup and one addition. The output has n + 1 entries, so O(n) is the floor.

modules.title: Intervals
modules.summary: Sort ranges by start (or end), then sweep once, comparing each range with the last one kept.

blocks.text: Sort ranges by start (or end), then sweep once, comparing each range with the last one kept.

blocks.title: Picture it
blocks.text: Laying strips of tape on a ruler and seeing where they overlap.
Clues in the problem

items: Resources needed at the busiest moment

blocks.text: Template
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting nested ranges (use max for the end)

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Sort by start or by end: when does it matter?
blocks.text: Sort by start for merging and inserting. Sort by end when choosing the most non-overlapping intervals, because finishing earliest leaves the most room.

blocks.title: How do you find the maximum number of overlapping ranges?
blocks.text: Sweep: +1 at each start and −1 at each end in sorted order, tracking the running maximum. Decide whether an end at the same time as a start counts as overlap.
The problem in plain words
Given start and end times of meetings, decide whether one person could attend all of them, meaning no two overlap. A meeting may start exactly when another ends.

rows: the first meeting covers the other two

blocks.text: Edge cases
Brute force
Compare every pair of meetings: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Sort by start time. Then only neighbours can overlap: a meeting clashes exactly when it starts before the previous one ends.

items: For each meeting after the first, compare its start with the previous end.
If it starts earlier, return false.
Otherwise return true at the end.

blocks.caption: canAttendMeetings

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting dominates; the scan is linear.
Why it is correct
After sorting, if any two meetings overlap then some adjacent pair overlaps too, because the later of the two starts before the earlier one ends and so does everything between them.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How many rooms are needed if they do overlap?
blocks.text: That is Meeting Rooms II: the answer is the largest number of meetings running at the same time.

blocks.title: Return the conflicting pair.
blocks.text: Return the two neighbours at the point where the check fails; after sorting they are a genuine overlapping pair.

blocks.title: What if meetings arrive one at a time?
blocks.text: Keep the meetings in a structure ordered by start time. On insertion, compare only with the neighbour before and the neighbour after.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Checking a calendar for double bookings. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Meeting Rooms?
quiz.why: Sorting dominates; the scan is linear.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
You get a list of [start, end] ranges. Combine every group of ranges that overlap or touch into one range.
Edge cases

items: Ranges that only touch at an endpoint

blocks.text: Brute force
Compare every pair and merge until nothing changes: O(n²) or worse.
Optimal approach
Sort by start. Then each range either overlaps the last merged range (extend its end) or starts a new one.

items: For each range, compare its start with the end of the last output range.
Overlap: extend that end with max. Otherwise append the range.

blocks.caption: merge

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting dominates; the sweep is linear. After sorting, anything that overlaps an earlier range must overlap the most recent merged one.
Why it is correct
With starts in order, a range that starts after the last merged end cannot overlap any earlier range. Using max keeps the end right when a range is nested.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Insert one range into an already merged list.
blocks.text: Copy every interval that ends before the new one starts. Merge all that overlap it by taking the smallest start and largest end. Then copy the rest. O(n).

blocks.title: Minimum meeting rooms needed.
blocks.text: Sort starts and ends separately and sweep, or keep a min-heap of end times. The answer is the largest number of meetings in progress at once. O(n log n).

blocks.title: Minimum removals to make ranges non-overlapping.
blocks.text: Sort by end. Keep an interval when its start is not before the end of the last one kept. The removals are the total minus the number kept.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Combining overlapping delivery slots or busy calendar blocks into continuous windows. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Merge Intervals?
quiz.why: Sorting dominates; the sweep is linear. After sorting, anything that overlaps an earlier range must overlap the most recent merged one.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A list of non-overlapping ranges is sorted by start. Add one new range, merging wherever it overlaps, so the result is still sorted and non-overlapping.
Edge cases

items: New range before everything or after everything
Ranges that only touch count as overlapping

blocks.text: Brute force
Append the new range, sort, and run the merge-intervals sweep: O(n log n).
Optimal approach
The list is already sorted, so three linear phases suffice: copy the ranges that end before the new one starts, absorb every range that overlaps it, then copy the rest.

items: Copy ranges whose end < new start.
While a range's start ≤ current end, widen current to cover it.

blocks.caption: insert

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each range is examined once. Sorting is unnecessary because the input order is already correct.
Why it is correct
Ranges ending before the new start cannot overlap it. Once a range starts after the current end, no later range can overlap either, because starts are ascending.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Could binary search speed this up?
blocks.text: Binary search can find where the overlap begins and ends in O(log n), but building the output array is still O(n). It helps only with a structure that supports cheap splicing.

blocks.title: Do it in place.
blocks.text: Find the first and last overlapping positions, replace that span with the single merged range using replaceSubrange, and return. Array shifting keeps it O(n).

blocks.title: How does this relate to Merge Intervals?
blocks.text: Merge Intervals sorts first and then sweeps. Here the input is already sorted and only one new range can cause merging, so a single linear sweep is enough.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Adding a booking to a sorted calendar of busy blocks. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)
Prerequisites

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the optimal solution for Insert Interval?
quiz.why: Each range is examined once. Sorting is unnecessary because the input order is already correct.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given start and end times of meetings, find the smallest number of rooms so that every meeting can take place. A room is free again the moment its meeting ends.

rows: at most two meetings run at once

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A meeting starting exactly when another ends can reuse the room

blocks.text: Brute force
For every moment a meeting starts, count how many meetings are running: O(n²).
Optimal approach

Sort the start times and the end times separately. Walk through the starts; before taking a room for a start, release a room for every end time that is not later than it. Track the largest number of rooms in use.

items: Sort starts and ends into two arrays.
For each start, release rooms while the next end ≤ this start.

blocks.caption: minMeetingRooms

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting dominates. Each end is consumed once by the inner loop, so the sweep is linear.
Why it is correct

The rooms needed equal the largest number of meetings in progress at once. Processing ends before a start at the same time frees the room first, matching the rule that touching meetings do not overlap.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Solve it with a min-heap of end times.
blocks.text: Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use. For each meeting, pop the earliest end if it is not later than the start, then push this meeting's end. The largest heap size is the answer.

blocks.title: Why may starts and ends be sorted independently?
blocks.text: Only the number of meetings in progress matters, not which start pairs with which end. Sorted separately, the two lists still give the correct count at every moment.

blocks.title: Assign an actual room number to each meeting.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given a list of ranges, find the smallest number to remove so that none of the remaining ranges overlap. Ranges that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap.
Edge cases

items: One long range covering many short ones

blocks.text: Brute force
Try every subset and keep the largest compatible one: O(2ⁿ).
Optimal approach
Greedy. Sort by end. Walk through and keep a range whenever it starts at or after the end of the last kept range; otherwise count it as removed. Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest.

items: lastEnd starts below every possible start.
If a range starts at or after lastEnd, keep it and set lastEnd to its end.

blocks.caption: eraseOverlapIntervals

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Sorting dominates and the sweep is linear. Minimising removals is the same as maximising the ranges kept.
Why it is correct
Exchange argument: in any best solution the first kept range can be swapped for the one that ends earliest without creating an overlap, so the greedy choice is always safe.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why sort by end and not by start?
blocks.text: Sorting by start can keep a long range that begins early and blocks many short ones. The range that ends earliest always leaves the most room.

blocks.title: How many meeting rooms would avoid any removal?
blocks.text: Sweep the sorted start and end times and track how many ranges are open at once; the maximum is the number of rooms needed.

blocks.title: Return the ranges that are kept.
blocks.text: Collect each range at the point where it is kept instead of only updating lastEnd.

lessons.title: 105. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
You are given two listings of the same binary tree with distinct values: one in pre-order (node, left, right) and one in in-order (left, node, right). Rebuild the tree.

rows: 3 is the root; 9 is left of it in the in-order list

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: A tree that leans entirely left or right
Values must be distinct for the listings to determine the tree

blocks.text: Brute force
Search the in-order list for each root with a linear scan: O(n²).
Optimal approach

The next value in pre-order is always the root of the current subtree. Its position in the in-order list splits the remaining values into the left subtree (before it) and the right subtree (after it). A dictionary gives that position in O(1).

items: Record every value's index in the in-order list.
build(lo, hi): if the range is empty return nil.
Take the next pre-order value as the node; find its in-order index mid.
Build the left subtree from lo…mid − 1, then the right from mid + 1…hi.

blocks.caption: buildTree

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node is created once and its split point is found in constant time. Without the dictionary the search would cost O(n) per node.
Why it is correct

Pre-order lists a subtree's root before anything else in it, and in-order places the whole left subtree before the root. Building the left side first consumes pre-order values in exactly the right sequence.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Use in-order and post-order instead.
blocks.text: The last value in post-order is the root. Process post-order from the end and build the right subtree before the left.

blocks.title: Why are pre-order and post-order alone not enough?
blocks.text: Both list the root at an end but neither shows where the left subtree stops, so a node with a single child could be on either side.

blocks.title: What breaks with duplicate values?
blocks.text: A value's position in the in-order list is no longer unique, so the split point is ambiguous and several trees fit.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Sort a linked list in ascending order in O(n log n) time.
Edge cases
Brute force
Copy values to an array, sort, write back: O(n) extra memory.
Optimal approach
Merge sort suits linked lists: splitting needs only a walk to the middle, and merging relinks nodes without extra arrays. Split in half with slow and fast pointers, sort each half, and merge.

items: A list of 0 or 1 nodes is sorted.
Find the node before the middle and cut the list there.
Merge them by repeatedly attaching the smaller head.

blocks.caption: sortList

blocks.text: Why this complexity
There are log n levels of splitting and each level relinks n nodes. Quicksort is awkward on lists because it needs random access for good pivots.
Why it is correct
By induction: both halves come back sorted, and merging two sorted lists by taking the smaller head produces a sorted list of all nodes.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it with O(1) extra space.
blocks.text: Use bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of length 1, then 2, then 4, relinking nodes with a loop instead of recursion. No call stack is needed.

blocks.title: Why start fast one node ahead of slow?
blocks.text: With fast one ahead, slow stops at the last node of the first half, which is the node whose next must be cut. For two nodes this splits them one and one instead of looping forever.

blocks.title: Why is merge sort preferred for linked lists?
blocks.text: Merging relinks nodes without extra arrays, and splitting needs no random access. Quicksort and heapsort both rely on indexing.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Put the numbers in ascending order without calling the built-in sort, in O(n log n) time.
Edge cases

items: Empty or single-element input is already sorted
Already sorted or reverse-sorted input (merge sort is unaffected)

blocks.text: Brute force
Selection or insertion sort: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Merge sort. Split the array in half, sort each half the same way, then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.

items: An array of 0 or 1 elements is returned as is.
Split at the midpoint and sort each half recursively.
Merge: compare the fronts of the two halves and append the smaller.
Append whatever remains of the unfinished half.

blocks.caption: sortArray

blocks.text: Why this complexity

There are log n levels of splitting and each level merges n elements in total. Comparison sorting cannot beat n log n in the worst case. This version copies sub-arrays for clarity; an in-place buffer version reduces allocations but not the O(n) extra space.
Why it is correct

By induction on length: both halves come back sorted, and merging two sorted sequences by always taking the smaller front yields a sorted sequence containing every element. Using <= keeps equal elements in their original order.

blocks.title: Merge sort versus quicksort versus heapsort.
blocks.text: Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space. Quicksort: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, in place, usually fastest in practice, not stable. Heapsort: O(n log n) worst case, in place, not stable, weaker cache behaviour.

blocks.title: Sort a linked list in O(1) extra space.
blocks.text: Use bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of length 1, 2, 4 and so on by relinking nodes, which needs no recursion stack.

blocks.title: What does 'stable' mean and why does <= matter?
blocks.text: Stable means equal elements keep their original order, which matters when sorting records by one key after another. <= takes from the left half on ties, which preserves that order.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
A string contains only bracket characters. Decide whether every opening bracket is closed by the same kind of bracket, in the correct nesting order.

rows: ] arrives while ( is the most recent open bracket

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: Odd length can never be valid

blocks.text: Brute force
Repeatedly delete adjacent matching pairs "()", "[]", "{}" until nothing changes; valid if the string becomes empty. Up to O(n²) time.
Optimal approach
Use a stack. Push each opener. On a closer, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; pop it. At the end the stack must be empty.

items: Map each closer to its opener.
For each character: if it is a closer, pop and compare; if the pop fails or mismatches, return false.
If it is an opener, push it.
Return whether the stack is empty.

blocks.caption: isValid

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each character is pushed and popped at most once. The most recent unclosed opener is the only one a closer may match, which is exactly last-in-first-out.
Why it is correct

The stack always holds the unclosed openers in order. A closer is legal only if it matches the newest one. popLast() returns nil on an empty stack, which never equals an opener, so a stray closer fails.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: How would you report the index of the first error?
blocks.text: Push indices along with the characters. On a mismatch or a closer with an empty stack, the current index is the error. If openers remain at the end, report the index of the earliest unclosed one.

blocks.title: What if the string also contains letters?
blocks.text: Skip any character that is neither an opener nor a closer and process the rest exactly as before.

blocks.title: Can you do it in O(1) space if there is only one bracket type?
blocks.text: Yes. Keep a counter: add one for an opener, subtract one for a closer, fail if it ever goes negative, and require zero at the end.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Checking that tags or braces balance in a template or JSON-like input before parsing. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

quiz.why: Each character is pushed and popped at most once. The most recent unclosed opener is the only one a closer may match, which is exactly last-in-first-out.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Build a first-in-first-out queue using only stack operations: push to the top, pop from the top, look at the top, and check for empty.

rows: 1 arrived first so it leaves first

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: pop and peek are assumed to be called on a non-empty queue
Refilling must wait until the outbox is empty

blocks.text: Brute force
Move every element to a second stack and back on each pop: O(n) per pop.
Optimal approach
Keep two stacks. New elements go on the inbox. To pop or peek, use the outbox; only when it is empty, pour the whole inbox into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top.

items: pop and peek first refill: if outbox is empty, move everything from inbox to outbox.
Then pop or read the top of outbox.
The queue is empty when both stacks are.

blocks.caption: MyQueue

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each element is pushed to inbox once, moved once, and popped once: at most three stack operations over its lifetime, even though a single pop may move many.
Why it is correct

Pouring reverses arrival order, so the outbox top is the oldest element. Everything in the inbox arrived after everything in the outbox, so refilling only when the outbox is empty keeps the order right.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why refill only when the outbox is empty?
blocks.text: If elements were poured while the outbox still held some, the newer elements would land on top of older ones and leave first, breaking arrival order.

blocks.title: Explain the amortised O(1) bound.
blocks.text: Charge each element three units when it is pushed: one for the push, one for its single move to the outbox, one for its pop. No element is moved twice, so n operations cost O(n) in total.

blocks.title: Implement a stack using queues.
blocks.text: Use one queue. After each push, rotate the queue by moving the elements in front of the new one to the back, so the newest is at the front. Push is O(n) and pop is O(1).

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Buffering incoming work on one side while consumers drain the other side in arrival order. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Evaluate an arithmetic expression written in postfix form, where each operator comes after its two operands. Division drops any fractional part.
Edge cases

items: Negative numbers such as "-2" are operands, not operators

blocks.text: Brute force
Repeatedly search the list for an operator preceded by two numbers and replace the three tokens: O(n²).
Optimal approach
Use a stack. Push numbers. On an operator, pop the right operand and then the left operand, apply the operator, and push the result.

items: For each token, if it parses as an integer, push it.
Otherwise pop b, then pop a.
Compute a op b and push it.
The single value left on the stack is the answer.

blocks.caption: evalRPN

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each token causes a constant number of stack operations.
Why it is correct
In postfix form an operator always applies to the two most recently completed values, which is exactly what the top two stack entries are.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Why must b be popped before a?
blocks.text: The right operand was pushed last, so it comes off first. For subtraction and division the order changes the result.

blocks.title: How would you convert an infix expression to postfix?
blocks.text: Use the shunting-yard method: output numbers directly, keep operators on a stack, and pop operators of higher or equal precedence before pushing a new one. Parentheses are pushed and popped as markers.

blocks.title: How would you report a malformed expression?
blocks.text: Check that at least two values are on the stack before applying an operator, that a divisor is not zero, and that exactly one value remains at the end. Throw or return nil otherwise.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Build a stack that supports push, pop and top as usual, and can also report its current smallest value, with every operation in constant time.

rows: push −2, push 0, push −3, getMin, pop, top, getMin
after the pop the minimum goes back to −2
a duplicate minimum survives one pop

blocks.text: Edge cases

items: pop, top and getMin are assumed to be called only on a non-empty stack

blocks.text: Brute force
Scan the whole stack on every getMin: O(n) per call.
Optimal approach

Store, with every element, the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed. The minimum for the whole stack is then just the value stored with the top element, and popping restores the previous minimum automatically.

items: push: the new minimum is min(value, minimum stored with the current top).
top and getMin: read the two halves of the last pair.

blocks.caption: MinStack

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each operation touches only the last array element. The cost is one extra integer per element.
Why it is correct

The stored minimum for an entry depends only on the entries below it, which do not change while it is on the stack. So after any sequence of pushes and pops the top pair still holds the correct minimum.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Use a second stack that stores only the minimums. How does it save space?
blocks.text: Push onto the second stack only when the new value is less than or equal to its top, and pop it only when the value removed equals its top. It stores fewer entries when the minimum rarely changes.

blocks.title: Can it be done with O(1) extra space?
blocks.text: Yes, by storing an encoded value such as 2 × value − min when a new minimum is pushed and decoding on pop. It is fragile because of overflow and is rarely worth it.

blocks.title: How would you add getMax as well?
blocks.text: Store the maximum so far in each entry as well. Each entry becomes (value, min so far, max so far) and every operation stays O(1).

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up

modules.summary: Linked List problems.

blocks.text: The problem in plain words
Given the head of a singly linked list, return the head of the same nodes linked in the opposite order.
Edge cases

items: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next too early

blocks.text: Brute force
Copy values to an array, then rebuild or overwrite in reverse: O(n) extra space.
Optimal approach
Walk the list with three references: prev, the current node, and the saved next. Point the current node back at prev, then advance.

items: Advance prev = node, cur = next. When cur is nil, prev is the new head.

blocks.caption: reverseList

blocks.text: Why this complexity
Each node's pointer is rewritten exactly once and no extra structure is allocated.
Why it is correct
Invariant: prev heads the already reversed part and cur heads the untouched part. Saving next before rewriting keeps the untouched part reachable.
Interview follow-ups

blocks.title: Do it recursively; what is the stack cost?
blocks.text: Reverse the rest of the list first, then make the old second node point back to the head and set head.next to nil. It uses O(n) call stack.

blocks.title: Reverse only positions m to n.
blocks.text: Walk to the node just before position m. Then, n − m times, detach the node after the sublist's first node and re-insert it at the front of the sublist. A dummy head handles m = 1.

blocks.title: Reverse in groups of k.
blocks.text: Check that k nodes remain. Reverse those k, connect the previous group's tail to the new group head, and continue. A final group shorter than k is left as it is.

blocks.title: Where the idea shows up
blocks.text: Undoing the order of a chain of linked records without allocating a second chain. (An illustration of the technique, not a claim about any company's code.)

questions.q: What do Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta mean?
questions.a: Big-O is an upper bound on growth, Big-Omega a lower bound, and Big-Theta a tight bound (both at once). In interviews 'O(n)' is usually used loosely to mean the tight bound for the worst case; say which case you mean.

questions.q: What is amortised analysis?
questions.a: The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations. Appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortised: most appends are cheap and the occasional O(n) resize is paid for by the cheap ones before it.

questions.q: What is the difference between best, average and worst case?
questions.a: They describe different inputs of the same size. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average and O(n²) in the worst case. A hash table lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case. State the case you are quoting.

questions.q: How do you analyse a recursive algorithm?
questions.a: Write a recurrence: the number of sub-calls, the size of each, and the extra work per call. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n); T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) gives O(log n); T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + O(1) gives O(2ⁿ). Drawing the recursion tree and summing each level also works.

questions.q: Where does O(log n) come from?
questions.a: From repeatedly cutting the problem by a constant factor, as in binary search, or from the height of a balanced tree, as in a heap or balanced BST.

questions.q: How do you count space complexity?
questions.a: Count the extra memory beyond the input: auxiliary arrays, hash tables, and the recursion stack. A recursive DFS on a tree of height h uses O(h) stack even if it allocates nothing else. Say whether you count the output.

questions.q: What does 'in place' mean?
questions.a: The algorithm uses O(1) extra memory, or at most O(log n) for a recursion stack, and rearranges the input directly rather than building a copy.

questions.q: How do input limits hint at the expected complexity?
questions.a: As a rule of thumb, n up to about 20 allows exponential search, a few thousand allows O(n²), around 10⁵ to 10⁶ needs O(n log n) or O(n), and larger needs O(n) or O(log n). Use the limits to rule approaches out early.

questions.q: What is a time–space trade-off? Give an example.
questions.a: Spending memory to save time or the reverse. Two Sum with a dictionary is O(n) time and O(n) space; sorting with two pointers is O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space. Memoisation is the same trade in DP.

questions.q: When would you choose an array over a linked list?
questions.a: An array gives O(1) access by index and is cache-friendly, but inserting or removing in the middle is O(n). A linked list gives O(1) insert and remove at a known node but O(n) access and worse locality. Arrays win in most practical cases.

questions.q: How does a dynamic array grow?
questions.a: When full it allocates a larger buffer, typically by a constant factor such as double, and copies the elements across. Geometric growth is what makes append O(1) amortised; growing by a fixed amount would make it O(n).

questions.q: How do you rotate an array by k positions in place?
questions.a: Reduce k modulo n. Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n − k. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you check whether two strings are anagrams?
questions.a: Compare character counts: count the characters of one, subtract for the other, and require every count to be zero. O(n) time. Sorting both and comparing is O(n log n).

questions.q: How do you sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in one pass?
questions.a: The Dutch national flag method: keep three pointers low, mid and high. Swap 0s to the front and 2s to the back while mid scans. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: How do you find an element that appears more than n/2 times?
questions.a: Boyer–Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter, incrementing on a match and decrementing otherwise, replacing the candidate when the counter reaches zero. O(n) time, O(1) space. Verify the candidate with a second pass if a majority is not guaranteed.

questions.q: How do you find the longest palindromic substring?
questions.a: Expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres (each character and each gap) while the two sides match, tracking the longest. O(n²) time, O(1) space. Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n) but is rarely expected.

questions.q: How do you decide between two pointers, a sliding window and prefix sums?
questions.a: Two pointers for sorted data or pairs from both ends. A sliding window for a contiguous range whose validity changes in one direction as it grows. Prefix sums when the range property is a sum and values can be negative, or when there are many range queries.

questions.q: How do you search a row- and column-sorted matrix?
questions.a: Start at the top-right corner. If the value is too large move left; if too small move down. Each step removes a row or column, so it is O(rows + cols).

questions.q: What is the difference between singly and doubly linked lists?
questions.a: A singly linked node stores one next pointer; a doubly linked node also stores prev. Doubly linked lists allow O(1) removal of a known node and backward traversal, at the cost of more memory and more pointer updates.

questions.q: Why use a dummy (sentinel) head node?
questions.a: It removes the special case for inserting or deleting at the head, because every real node then has a predecessor. Return dummy.next at the end.

questions.q: How do you find the middle of a linked list in one pass?
questions.a: Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

questions.q: How do you remove the nth node from the end in one pass?
questions.a: Advance a lead pointer n steps, then move lead and a trailing pointer together until lead reaches the end. The trailing pointer is then just before the node to remove. A dummy head handles removing the first node.

questions.q: Why is binary search not useful on a linked list?
questions.a: Reaching the middle element takes O(n), so the halving saves comparisons but not time. The total is still O(n).

questions.q: How would you design an LRU cache?
questions.a: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. A get moves the node to the front; a put inserts at the front and evicts from the back when over capacity. Both are O(1).

questions.q: How do you check whether a linked list is a palindrome in O(1) space?
questions.a: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, compare the two halves node by node, and restore the list if required.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
questions.a: A stack is last-in-first-out; a queue is first-in-first-out. Stacks suit nested structure, undo and DFS. Queues suit processing in arrival order and BFS.

questions.q: How do you build a queue from two stacks?
questions.a: Push onto an input stack. To dequeue, pop from an output stack, refilling it by moving everything from the input stack only when it is empty. Each element moves at most once, so operations are O(1) amortised.

questions.q: How do you design a stack that returns its minimum in O(1)?
questions.a: Keep a second stack of minimums, or store with each element the minimum at the time it was pushed. Pop both together.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an expression in reverse Polish notation?
questions.a: Scan the tokens. Push numbers; on an operator pop two operands, apply it with the correct order, and push the result. The final stack entry is the answer.

questions.q: What is a deque and when is it useful?
questions.a: A double-ended queue with O(1) insert and remove at both ends. It supports sliding-window maximum, 0–1 BFS and work-stealing queues.

questions.q: How does recursion relate to the call stack?
questions.a: Each call pushes a frame holding its parameters, locals and return address. Deep recursion can overflow the stack; converting to an explicit stack on the heap avoids that.

questions.q: How does a hash table work?
questions.a: A hash function maps a key to a bucket index in an array. Lookups go straight to that bucket, giving O(1) on average. Different keys can land in the same bucket, which is a collision that must be resolved.

questions.q: How are collisions handled?
questions.a: Separate chaining keeps a list of entries in each bucket. Open addressing stores entries in the array itself and probes for another slot, for example linearly. Chaining degrades gently; open addressing is more cache-friendly but sensitive to load.

questions.q: What is the load factor and why does a table resize?
questions.a: The load factor is entries divided by buckets. As it rises, collisions rise, so the table grows and rehashes every entry once it passes a threshold. Resizing is O(n) but amortises to O(1) per insert.

questions.q: Why can a hash table operation take O(n)?
questions.a: If many keys collide, a single bucket or probe sequence holds most of the entries. That happens with a poor hash function or adversarial keys; randomised hashing reduces the risk.

questions.q: What makes a good hash key?
questions.a: It is immutable while stored, equal keys always hash equally, the hash spreads keys evenly, and it is cheap to compute.

questions.q: When would you use a tree-based map instead of a hash map?
questions.a: When you need keys in sorted order, range queries, or the nearest key above or below a value, or when you need guaranteed O(log n) rather than average O(1).

questions.q: What is the difference between a binary tree and a binary search tree?
questions.a: A binary tree only limits each node to two children. A BST also orders them: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is larger. That ordering gives search, insert and delete in O(height).

questions.q: What are the tree traversals and when is each used?
questions.a: Pre-order (node, left, right) to copy or serialise a tree. In-order (left, node, right) to read a BST in sorted order. Post-order (left, right, node) when a node needs its children's results. Level-order (BFS) for anything by depth.

questions.q: Why do balanced trees matter?
questions.a: A BST's operations cost O(height). An unbalanced BST can degrade to a linked list with height n. Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height O(log n) with rotations.

questions.q: How do you validate a BST?
questions.a: Pass down an allowed range: every node must lie strictly between the bounds inherited from its ancestors. Checking only each node against its direct children is wrong. Alternatively, an in-order traversal must be strictly increasing.

questions.q: How do you find the lowest common ancestor?
questions.a: In a BST, walk from the root: go left if both values are smaller, right if both are larger, otherwise the current node is the answer. In a general binary tree, use post-order recursion: a node is the LCA if the two targets are found in different subtrees, or it is one of them.

questions.q: What is the difference between height and depth?
questions.a: Depth is the number of edges from the root down to a node. Height is the number of edges on the longest path from a node down to a leaf. Some problems count nodes instead of edges, so confirm the convention.

questions.q: What are full, complete and perfect binary trees?
questions.a: Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Complete: every level is filled except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. Perfect: all internal nodes have 2 children and all leaves are at the same depth.

questions.q: How do you serialise and deserialise a binary tree?
questions.a: Write a pre-order or level-order traversal that includes a marker for missing children. Rebuild by reading the values in the same order and consuming a marker wherever a child is absent.

questions.q: How do you delete a node from a BST?
questions.a: With no children, remove it. With one child, replace it by that child. With two, copy in its in-order successor (the smallest value in the right subtree) and delete that successor node instead.

questions.q: How do BFS and DFS differ in memory on a tree?
questions.a: DFS uses O(height) memory for the stack. BFS uses O(width) for the queue, which can be about n/2 on the last level of a balanced tree.

questions.q: What is a binary heap and how is it stored?
questions.a: A complete binary tree in which every parent is no larger than its children (min-heap) or no smaller (max-heap). It is stored in an array: for index i the children are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and the parent at (i − 1) / 2.

questions.q: What are the costs of heap operations?
questions.a: Peek is O(1). Insert and remove-top are O(log n) because an element sifts along one root-to-leaf path. Building a heap from n elements is O(n) when done bottom-up.

questions.q: Why is building a heap O(n) and not O(n log n)?
questions.a: Bottom-up heapify sifts each node down by at most its height. Most nodes are near the bottom with small heights, and the sum of heights over all nodes is O(n).

questions.q: How does heapsort work?
questions.a: Build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap by one and sift the new root down. O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, not stable.

questions.q: How do you find the running median of a stream?
questions.a: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops. O(log n) per insert.

questions.q: When would you use a heap rather than a balanced BST?
questions.a: A heap when you only need the minimum or maximum repeatedly: it is simpler, array-based and has small constants. A balanced BST when you also need search, ordered iteration, or removal of arbitrary elements.

questions.q: How can a graph be represented?
questions.a: An adjacency list stores each node's neighbours and uses O(V + E) memory. An adjacency matrix uses O(V²) memory and answers 'is there an edge' in O(1). An edge list suits algorithms that sort edges, such as Kruskal's.

questions.q: When do you use BFS and when DFS?
questions.a: BFS for the shortest path in an unweighted graph and anything level by level. DFS for reachability, cycle detection, topological order, connected components and exhaustive search. Both are O(V + E).

questions.q: How do you detect a cycle?
questions.a: Undirected: DFS and look for an edge to a visited node that is not the parent, or use Union Find and look for an edge joining two nodes already connected. Directed: DFS with three states and look for an edge to a node still on the current path, or run Kahn's algorithm and check whether every node was output.

questions.q: What is topological sorting?
questions.a: An ordering of a directed acyclic graph in which every edge goes from earlier to later. Use Kahn's algorithm with in-degree counts, or DFS and reverse the finishing order. It exists only if there is no cycle.

questions.q: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work, and what is its limitation?
questions.a: It repeatedly settles the unsettled node with the smallest known distance and relaxes its edges, using a min-heap. O((V + E) log V). It requires non-negative edge weights, because a settled distance is assumed final.

questions.q: What do you use when edge weights can be negative?
questions.a: Bellman–Ford: relax every edge V − 1 times, O(V · E). One more pass that still improves a distance reveals a negative cycle. For all pairs on a small graph, Floyd–Warshall is O(V³).

questions.q: What is a minimum spanning tree and how do you build one?
questions.a: A set of edges connecting all nodes with the smallest total weight and no cycle. Kruskal sorts edges and adds each one that joins two different components, using Union Find: O(E log E). Prim grows a tree from one node using a min-heap: O(E log V).

questions.q: How do you check whether a graph is bipartite?
questions.a: Colour it with two colours using BFS or DFS, giving each neighbour the opposite colour. It is bipartite exactly when no edge joins two nodes of the same colour.

questions.q: How do you treat a grid as a graph?
questions.a: Each cell is a node with edges to its valid neighbours in four (or eight) directions. Use a direction array, check bounds, and mark cells visited in the grid itself or a separate array.

questions.q: How do you count connected components?
questions.a: Run BFS or DFS from every unvisited node, counting how many times you start. Or use Union Find and count the distinct roots.

questions.q: How do the common sorting algorithms compare?
questions.a: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²); insertion sort is fast on small or nearly sorted input. Merge sort is O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) space. Quicksort is O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, in place. Heapsort is O(n log n) worst, in place, not stable.

questions.q: What does it mean for a sort to be stable, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Equal elements keep their original relative order. It matters when sorting records by several keys in turn, for example by name and then by date.

questions.q: Can sorting be faster than O(n log n)?
questions.a: Not by comparisons alone; n log n is a proven lower bound for comparison sorts. Counting sort is O(n + k) for integers in a range of size k, and radix sort is O(d · (n + k)) for d digits, because they do not compare elements.

questions.q: How does quicksort work and how do you avoid its worst case?
questions.a: Pick a pivot, partition the array into smaller and larger elements, and recurse on both sides. The worst case arises from consistently bad pivots, such as the first element of sorted input. Use a random pivot or median-of-three, and three-way partitioning when there are many duplicates.

questions.q: What is quickselect?
questions.a: Quicksort's partition step used to find the kth smallest element: after partitioning, recurse only into the side that contains position k. O(n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case.

questions.q: What are the common binary search variants?
questions.a: Exact match, first position not less than the target (lower bound), first position greater than the target (upper bound), search in a rotated sorted array, peak finding, and binary search over a range of answers using a yes/no test.

questions.q: What are the usual binary search bugs?
questions.a: Mixing closed and half-open ranges, an update that fails to shrink the range and loops forever, overflow in (lo + hi) / 2 in fixed-width languages, and returning the wrong boundary. Fix an invariant and test with one and two elements.

questions.q: What does every recursive function need?
questions.a: A base case that returns without recursing, and recursive calls that move toward that base case. It helps to state what the function returns and trust that definition for the sub-calls.

questions.q: When do you convert recursion to iteration?
questions.a: When the depth could overflow the stack, as with a skewed tree or long list, or when performance matters. Use an explicit stack, or a loop if the recursion is a simple tail call. Swift does not guarantee tail-call optimisation.

questions.q: What is the general backtracking template?
questions.a: If the partial solution is complete, record it and return. Otherwise, for each valid choice: make the choice, recurse, then undo the choice. Check constraints before recursing to prune.

questions.q: How many subsets, permutations and combinations are there?
questions.a: A set of n distinct items has 2ⁿ subsets, n! permutations, and n! / (k! (n − k)!) combinations of size k. These counts set the minimum cost of generating them.

questions.q: What is pruning?
questions.a: Abandoning a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a valid or better answer, for example when the running sum already exceeds the target. Sorting the input first often makes pruning more effective.

questions.q: What is memoisation?
questions.a: Caching the result of a function for each distinct argument set so that repeated sub-problems are computed once. It turns many exponential recursions into polynomial ones and is top-down dynamic programming.

questions.q: When does dynamic programming apply?
questions.a: When the problem has optimal substructure, meaning the best answer is built from best answers to sub-problems, and overlapping sub-problems, meaning the same sub-problems recur. Typical signals: count the ways, minimum or maximum cost, or is it possible.

questions.q: How do you design a DP solution?
questions.a: Define the state precisely in words. Write the transition from smaller states. Set the base cases. Choose an order in which dependencies are computed first. State where the answer is. Then consider reducing space.

questions.q: What is the difference between 0/1 knapsack and unbounded knapsack?
questions.a: In 0/1 each item is used at most once; with a one-dimensional table, iterate capacity downward so an item is not reused. In unbounded, items can repeat; iterate capacity upward. Coin Change is the unbounded form.

questions.q: How do you find the longest increasing subsequence?
questions.a: The basic DP lets dp[i] be the longest increasing subsequence ending at i and checks all earlier j: O(n²). The faster method keeps, for each length, the smallest possible tail value and binary-searches where each new element goes: O(n log n).

questions.q: How do longest common subsequence and edit distance work?
questions.a: Both fill a two-dimensional table over prefixes of the two strings. For LCS, matching characters extend the diagonal by one; otherwise take the better of dropping a character from either string. Edit distance takes the minimum of insert, delete and replace. Both are O(m · n).

questions.q: How do DP, greedy and divide and conquer differ?
questions.a: Divide and conquer splits into independent sub-problems. DP handles overlapping sub-problems by storing results and considers all choices. Greedy commits to one choice at each step and needs a proof that the choice is safe.

questions.q: What are common DP families?
questions.a: Linear sequences (House Robber), grid paths, knapsack and subset sum, two-string tables (LCS, edit distance), interval DP, DP on trees, and bitmask DP over small sets.

questions.q: When is a greedy algorithm correct?
questions.a: When the problem has the greedy-choice property: some optimal solution contains the locally best choice, and what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem. Justify it with an exchange argument or by showing greedy stays ahead.

questions.q: What is the activity selection problem?
questions.a: Choose the largest number of non-overlapping intervals. Sort by end time and take each interval that starts no earlier than the last chosen one ends. Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest.

questions.q: What is Huffman coding?
questions.a: A greedy method for building an optimal prefix code. Repeatedly merge the two least frequent symbols into one node using a min-heap; frequent symbols end up with shorter codes. O(n log n).

questions.q: What is a trie and when is it better than a hash set?
questions.a: A tree keyed by characters in which shared prefixes share nodes. Use it for prefix queries, autocomplete, and matching many words against a text or board. A hash set is simpler and smaller when only exact lookups are needed.

questions.q: How does KMP string matching work?
questions.a: It precomputes, for each prefix of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch it uses that table to shift the pattern without re-reading text characters. O(n + m).

questions.q: What is a rolling hash?
questions.a: A hash of a window that can be updated in O(1) when the window slides by one character, by removing the outgoing character's contribution and adding the incoming one. Rabin–Karp uses it to find substring matches; confirm candidate matches to rule out collisions.

questions.q: How do you group words that are anagrams of each other?
questions.a: Map each word to a canonical key, either its sorted characters or its 26 letter counts, and collect words by key in a dictionary.

questions.q: What are the essential bit operations?
questions.a: Test bit i with x & (1 << i). Set it with x | (1 << i). Clear it with x & ~(1 << i). Toggle it with x ^ (1 << i). x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit and x & −x isolates it.

questions.q: How do you check whether a number is a power of two?
questions.a: It must be positive and have exactly one set bit: x > 0 and x & (x − 1) equals 0.

questions.q: What properties of XOR are useful?
questions.a: x ^ x is 0, x ^ 0 is x, and XOR is commutative and associative. Together these cancel pairs, which finds a single unpaired value or a missing number.

questions.q: When do you use a bitmask to represent a set?
questions.a: When the set has at most about 20 to 30 elements. An integer then stores membership compactly, set operations become single instructions, and the mask can index a DP table.

questions.q: What is Union Find and what does it cost?
questions.a: A structure that tracks which elements belong to the same group, with find to get a group's representative and union to merge two groups. With path compression and union by size or rank, each operation is near-constant amortised time.

questions.q: What is Union Find used for?
questions.a: Counting connected components, detecting a cycle in an undirected graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, and answering connectivity queries while edges are being added.

questions.q: How should you approach a problem you have not seen before?
questions.a: Restate it in your own words and confirm with an example. Ask about input size, value ranges and edge cases. Describe a brute-force solution and its cost. Look for the bottleneck and improve it. Agree the approach, then code, then test by hand, then state complexity.

questions.q: What clarifying questions are worth asking?
questions.a: How large is the input? Can values be negative, zero or duplicated? Is the input sorted? Can it be empty? What should be returned when there is no answer? May the input be modified? Is one answer enough or are all needed?

questions.q: Should you start with the brute-force solution?
questions.a: Yes, state it briefly with its complexity even if you do not code it. It shows you understand the problem, gives a baseline, and often reveals the repeated work that the better solution removes.

questions.q: How do you choose a data structure?
questions.a: Start from the operations you need to be fast. Membership or counting: hash set or map. Most recent first: stack. Arrival order: queue. Repeated minimum or maximum: heap. Ordered or range queries: sorted array or balanced tree. Prefixes: trie. Merging groups: Union Find.

questions.q: What do you do when you are stuck?
questions.a: Say what you have tried and where it fails. Work a small example by hand and look for a pattern. Try sorting the input, a hash map, or solving a simpler version first. Thinking aloud lets the interviewer give a useful hint.

questions.q: How do you recognise which pattern a problem needs?
questions.a: Read the signals: sorted input suggests binary search or two pointers; contiguous range suggests a sliding window or prefix sums; top k suggests a heap; shortest steps suggests BFS; all combinations suggests backtracking; count the ways or best cost suggests DP; dependencies suggest topological sort.

questions.q: How do you manage time in a 45-minute interview?
questions.a: Roughly 5 minutes to understand and clarify, 5 to 10 to settle the approach, 15 to 20 to code, and 5 to 10 to test and discuss complexity. If the best approach is not coming, implement a correct simpler one and explain how you would improve it.

questions.q: How should you talk while coding?
questions.a: Explain the plan before you start, name what each block does as you write it, and say when you are making an assumption or leaving something to fix later. Avoid long silences; a quiet interviewer cannot give you credit for reasoning they did not hear.

questions.q: How do you test your code in an interview?
questions.a: Trace a small normal case line by line, tracking variable values. Then try edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, all equal, negatives, and the largest size. Fix bugs you find and say what you changed.

questions.q: How do you present complexity?
questions.a: Give time and space separately, define what n means, state which case you are quoting, and justify it in a sentence, for example 'each element is pushed and popped at most once'. Mention the recursion stack if there is one.

questions.q: What should you do when the interviewer points out a bug or gives a hint?
questions.a: Treat it as information. Acknowledge it, re-trace the relevant case, fix the cause rather than patching the symptom, and re-test. Taking hints well counts in your favour.

questions.q: What if you have seen the problem before?
questions.a: Say so. Most interviewers will either move to a different problem or ask you to go ahead and then extend it. Reciting a memorised answer while pretending to discover it tends to show and reflects badly.

questions.q: What are interviewers evaluating?
questions.a: Problem solving, correct and readable code, communication, testing habits, knowledge of data structures and complexity, and how you respond to hints and changes in requirements. A clear, correct simpler solution usually scores better than an unfinished clever one.
