questions.q: What Swift-specific points help in a coding interview?
questions.a: Convert a String to Array(s) before indexing. Remember the standard library has no heap, so be ready to write one. Avoid removeFirst() in loops. Use guard for early exits, dictionary default subscripts for counting, and value semantics to your advantage when copying paths in backtracking.

questions.q: What questions can you ask at the end?
questions.a: Ask about the team's current technical challenges, how work is planned and reviewed, what success looks like in the first months, and how the team handles on-call and quality. Specific questions show real interest.

questions.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class?
questions.a: A struct is a value type: assigning or passing it makes an independent copy. A class is a reference type: assignments share one object. Classes support inheritance, deinit and identity (===) and are managed by ARC. Structs get a memberwise initialiser and have no inheritance. Prefer structs unless you need shared identity or inheritance.

questions.q: What is copy-on-write?
questions.a: Array, Dictionary, Set and String share their storage after a copy and duplicate it only when one copy is mutated while the storage is shared. Copies are therefore cheap until a write happens. A custom type can do the same using isKnownUniquelyReferenced on a class that holds its storage.

questions.q: What do let and var mean for a struct and for a class instance?
questions.a: let makes the value constant. For a struct that freezes every property. For a class instance it freezes only the reference; the object's var properties can still change.

questions.q: What does mutating mean?
questions.a: A method on a struct or enum that changes self must be marked mutating. It cannot be called on a value declared with let.

questions.q: What is the difference between raw values and associated values in an enum?
questions.a: Raw values are one fixed value of a single type per case, set at compile time, and give you init(rawValue:). Associated values are data attached to a case each time it is created, and can differ in type and count between cases.

questions.q: When would you use a tuple instead of a struct?
questions.a: For a small, short-lived grouping such as returning two values from a function. Use a struct once the data needs a name, methods, protocol conformances, or is passed around widely.

questions.q: What is the difference between static and class members?
questions.a: Both belong to the type rather than an instance. A class member can be overridden by a subclass; a static member cannot. Structs and enums only have static.

questions.q: What is a lazy property?
questions.a: A stored property whose initial value is computed on first access. It must be a var. Its initialisation is not thread-safe by default, so concurrent first access needs protection.

questions.q: What are property observers?
questions.a: willSet runs just before a stored property changes and didSet just after. They are not called when the property is first set inside its own type's initialiser.

questions.q: What is the difference between a stored and a computed property?
questions.a: A stored property holds a value in memory. A computed property has no storage; it runs a getter (and optionally a setter) every time it is accessed, so keep it cheap or document its cost.

questions.q: What does inout do?
questions.a: It lets a function modify the caller's variable. The argument is passed with &. Semantically the value is copied in and copied back out, and Swift's exclusivity rule forbids overlapping access to the same variable during the call.

questions.q: What is the difference between == and ===?
questions.a: == compares values using Equatable. === checks whether two class references point to the same object. Linked-list and graph problems usually need ===.

questions.q: What is an Optional?
questions.a: An enum with two cases: none, and some holding a wrapped value. T? is shorthand for Optional<T>. It makes the absence of a value explicit in the type.

questions.q: What are the ways to unwrap an optional?
questions.a: if let and guard let, the nil-coalescing operator ??, optional chaining with ?., pattern matching in a switch, and force unwrapping with !, which crashes on nil. Since Swift 5.7, 'if let x' can shadow an existing optional x without repeating the name.

questions.q: When do you use guard let instead of if let?
questions.a: guard let requires the else branch to leave the scope and keeps the unwrapped value available afterwards. It suits early exits and keeps the main path unindented. if let limits the value to its own block.

questions.q: What is an implicitly unwrapped optional?
questions.a: A type written T!. It is an optional that is force-unwrapped automatically where a non-optional is needed, so it crashes if it is nil at that point. It is used when a value is set shortly after initialisation, such as outlets.

questions.q: What does optional chaining return?
questions.a: An optional of the final result type. If any link in the chain is nil the whole expression is nil and the rest is not evaluated.

questions.q: What is the difference between map and flatMap on an Optional?
questions.a: map applies a function to the wrapped value and re-wraps the result. If the function itself returns an optional, map gives a double optional; flatMap flattens it to a single optional.

questions.q: What are the costs of common Array, Set and Dictionary operations?
questions.a: Array: index access O(1), append amortised O(1), insert or remove at the front or middle O(n), contains O(n). Set and Dictionary: insert, lookup and remove O(1) on average, with elements or keys that are Hashable and no defined order.

questions.q: Why can you not index a String with an Int?
questions.a: A Character is a grapheme cluster that can span several Unicode scalars, so characters have variable width. Reaching the nth character means walking from the start, which is O(n). Swift makes that cost visible through String.Index; count is also O(n). For algorithms, convert to Array(s) first.

questions.q: What do map, filter, reduce, compactMap and flatMap do?
questions.a: map transforms each element. filter keeps the elements that pass a test. reduce combines all elements into one value. compactMap transforms and drops nil results. flatMap transforms each element into a sequence and concatenates the results.

questions.q: What is an ArraySlice?
questions.a: A view onto part of an array that shares the array's storage and keeps the original indices, so it may not start at 0. Creating it is O(1). Convert with Array(slice) for long-term storage, because a slice keeps the whole original buffer alive.

questions.q: Is a Dictionary ordered?
questions.a: No. The order is unspecified and can differ between runs because hashing is seeded per process. Sort the keys when order matters, or use OrderedDictionary from swift-collections.

questions.q: What is the difference between sort and sorted, and is the sort stable?
questions.a: sort() reorders in place; sorted() returns a new array. Both are O(n log n). The documentation does not guarantee stability, so do not rely on equal elements keeping their order even though the current implementation behaves stably.

questions.q: What does .lazy do?
questions.a: It defers map, filter and similar operations until elements are actually consumed, so no intermediate arrays are built. It helps when you only need the first few results or the chain is long.

questions.q: What is reserveCapacity for?
questions.a: It allocates room for a known number of elements up front, avoiding repeated reallocation and copying as an array grows.

questions.q: Why is removeFirst() a problem in loops, and what do you use instead?
questions.a: It shifts every remaining element, so each call is O(n). For a queue, keep a head index, swap whole-level arrays in BFS, or use Deque from swift-collections.

questions.q: Does Swift have a built-in heap or priority queue?
questions.a: Not in the standard library. Use Heap from swift-collections, or write a small binary heap over an array, which interviewers often accept or expect.

questions.q: What happens on integer overflow?
questions.a: Arithmetic traps at runtime instead of wrapping silently. Use &+, &- and &* for wrapping arithmetic, or addingReportingOverflow to detect overflow. Computing a midpoint as lo + (hi − lo) / 2 avoids overflow.

questions.q: What are Character, Unicode.Scalar and UTF-8 bytes, and which should an algorithm use?
questions.a: Character is a user-visible character, Unicode.Scalar is one code point, and utf8 exposes raw bytes. For input known to be ASCII, Array(s.utf8) is the fastest to index and compare. Use Array(s) of Character when user-visible characters matter.

questions.q: How does ARC work?
questions.a: The compiler inserts retain and release calls. An object is freed as soon as its strong reference count reaches zero. It is not a tracing garbage collector and does not detect reference cycles.

questions.q: What is a retain cycle and how do you break it?
questions.a: Two or more objects hold strong references to each other, so none of their counts reach zero and they leak. Break the cycle by making one of the references weak or unowned.

questions.q: What is the difference between weak and unowned?
questions.a: A weak reference is an optional var that becomes nil when the object is freed. An unowned reference is non-optional and assumes the object outlives it; using it after the object is freed crashes. Use weak when unsure.

questions.q: When do you need [weak self] in a closure?
questions.a: When an escaping closure that captures self is stored, directly or indirectly, by something self owns, which would form a cycle. It is not needed for non-escaping closures, and often not for closures that run once and are then released.

questions.q: What is the difference between escaping and non-escaping closures?
questions.a: A non-escaping closure, the default for parameters, is guaranteed to run before the function returns. An @escaping closure may be stored or run later, so it can extend the lifetime of what it captures and requires explicit self for class instances.

questions.q: How do closures capture variables?
questions.a: By default a closure captures the variable itself, so it sees later changes. A capture list such as [x] copies the value at the moment the closure is created.

questions.q: What is protocol-oriented programming?
questions.a: Describing behaviour with protocols and supplying shared implementations through protocol extensions, instead of through a class hierarchy. A type can adopt many protocols, and structs and enums can take part.

questions.q: What is an associated type?
questions.a: A placeholder type inside a protocol that each conforming type fills in, such as Element in Sequence. Since Swift 5.7 a protocol can declare primary associated types, which lets you write constraints like some Collection<Int>.

questions.q: What is the difference between some and any?
questions.a: some P is an opaque type: one specific concrete type that the compiler knows and the caller does not. any P is an existential: a box that can hold any conforming type and may change at runtime, at the cost of dynamic dispatch. Prefer some unless you need to mix types.

questions.q: Why use generics instead of Any?
questions.a: Generics keep full type information at compile time, so there is no casting, errors are caught early, and the compiler can specialise the code for speed.

questions.q: What are Equatable, Hashable, Comparable and Codable?
questions.a: Equatable provides ==, Hashable allows use in a Set or as a Dictionary key, Comparable provides ordering with <, and Codable provides encoding and decoding. The compiler synthesises Equatable, Hashable and Codable when all stored properties conform; Comparable is synthesised only for enums.

questions.q: What can and cannot an extension do?
questions.a: It can add methods, computed properties, initialisers, nested types and protocol conformances. It cannot add stored properties or override existing members.

questions.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic dispatch?
questions.a: With static dispatch the call target is fixed at compile time, as for struct methods and final or private members, which allows inlining. With dynamic dispatch it is looked up at runtime: class methods through a table, protocol requirements through a witness table. A method defined only in a protocol extension, and not declared in the protocol, is dispatched statically.

questions.q: How does error handling work in Swift?
questions.a: A function marked throws can throw an Error. Call it with try inside do and handle failures in catch. try? converts an error to nil and try! crashes on an error. Swift 6 adds typed throws, written throws(MyError).

questions.q: What is the Result type for?
questions.a: An enum with success and failure cases. It stores or passes on an outcome when throwing directly is not possible, such as in completion handlers or collections of outcomes.

questions.q: What does defer do?
questions.a: It schedules a block to run when the current scope exits, however it exits. Several defer blocks run in reverse order of declaration. It is typical for cleanup.

questions.q: What is the difference between assert, precondition and fatalError?
questions.a: assert is checked only in debug builds. precondition is checked in debug and normal release builds. fatalError always stops the program and can be used where a value must be returned.

questions.q: What does async/await do?
questions.a: An async function can suspend at an await without blocking its thread, and resumes later. Code reads top to bottom, and errors use normal throws.

questions.q: What is the difference between async let, a task group and Task?
questions.a: async let starts a fixed number of child tasks in parallel. A task group starts a dynamic number. Both are structured: children finish or are cancelled before the scope ends. Task { } starts unstructured work that is not tied to the current scope.

questions.q: What is an actor?
questions.a: A reference type that protects its mutable state by letting only one task run its isolated code at a time. Access from outside uses await. Actors are re-entrant: state can change across an await inside an actor method, so re-check assumptions after suspending.

questions.q: What is @MainActor?
questions.a: A global actor that represents the main thread. Marking a type or function with it guarantees it runs on the main thread, which UI code requires.

questions.q: What is Sendable?
questions.a: A marker protocol for types that are safe to pass between concurrency domains: value types whose members are Sendable, actors, and immutable final classes. The Swift 6 language mode reports data-race violations as errors.

questions.q: How does task cancellation work?
questions.a: It is cooperative. Cancelling sets a flag; the task must check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() and stop itself. Many system async functions check for you.

questions.q: How does Swift concurrency differ from GCD?
questions.a: GCD schedules closures on queues, and correctness is up to you. Swift concurrency adds structured tasks, built-in cancellation and priority handling, and compiler checks for data races. Do not block its cooperative threads with locks or semaphores that wait.

questions.q: Why is it safe to discard an element when you move a pointer?
questions.a: With sorted input, the element at the pointer fails even with the most favourable partner still available, so it cannot be part of any answer.

questions.q: How do you skip duplicates in a three-sum?
questions.a: Sort first. Skip the fixed element when it equals the previous one, and after each hit move both inner pointers past equal values.

questions.q: When does a sliding window stop working?
questions.a: When adding an element does not move the window's property in one direction, for example sums with negative numbers, or when the answer need not be contiguous. Prefix sums with a dictionary usually take over.

questions.q: Fixed-size versus variable-size windows: what changes?
questions.a: Fixed size: each step adds one element and removes one, with no inner loop. Variable size: grow on the right and shrink on the left with a while loop until the rule holds again.

questions.q: How do you find where the cycle starts?
questions.a: After they meet, move one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's first node.

questions.q: Why must the runners meet inside a cycle?
questions.a: Inside the cycle the gap between them shrinks by exactly one node per round, so it must reach zero; the fast pointer cannot jump over the slow one.

questions.q: How do prefix sums combine with a dictionary to count subarrays summing to k?
questions.a: A run ending at j sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals prefix(j) − k. Keep a dictionary of prefix-sum counts, starting with [0: 1], and add the matching count at each step.

questions.q: How does it extend to 2D?
questions.a: Build pre[r + 1][c + 1] = cell + above + left − diagonal. Any rectangle's sum is then four lookups combined by inclusion and exclusion.

questions.q: What makes a type Hashable?
questions.a: It provides hash(into:) and ==, and equal values always produce equal hashes. Structs and enums whose members are Hashable get this synthesised.

questions.q: When would a sorted array beat a dictionary?
questions.a: When you need order, ranges or nearest-value queries, when memory is tight, when the data is small and static, or when you need worst-case guarantees.

questions.q: Find the first true in FFFTTT.
questions.a: Use a half-open range: lo = 0, hi = n. While lo < hi, test mid; if true set hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. lo is the first true, or n if there is none.

questions.q: How do you binary search on an answer rather than an index?
questions.a: Find a yes/no test over candidate answers that flips exactly once, then binary search the candidate range for the first value that passes.

questions.q: Why is the total work O(n) despite the inner loop?
questions.a: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so there are at most 2n stack operations in total.

questions.q: Increasing or decreasing: how do you choose?
questions.a: Ask which stored elements become useless when a new one arrives. For next greater, pop smaller values and keep the stack decreasing; for next smaller, pop larger values and keep it increasing.

questions.q: Why store indices rather than values?
questions.a: The index tells you when the front has left the window; the value can always be read from the array.

questions.q: How would you use swift-collections Deque here?
questions.a: Import DequeModule from swift-collections and use append, popLast and popFirst, which are all O(1), in place of the array plus head index.

questions.q: Why does BFS give shortest paths only for unweighted graphs?
questions.a: BFS orders nodes by number of edges. With weights, a path with more edges can be cheaper, so use Dijkstra for non-negative weights.

questions.q: What is multi-source BFS?
questions.a: Put every source in the queue at distance 0 before starting. Each node then receives its distance to the nearest source in one pass.

questions.q: Convert a recursive DFS to an iterative one.
questions.a: Use an explicit stack: push the start, then repeatedly pop, visit, and push unvisited neighbours. Post-order needs a visited flag per stack entry or a second stack.

questions.q: Pre-order, in-order, post-order: when does each fit?
questions.a: Pre-order when the parent must be handled before its children, such as copying a tree. In-order for sorted output from a BST. Post-order when a node needs its children's results, such as height.

questions.q: How do you avoid duplicate subsets when the input has duplicates?
questions.a: Sort the input and skip a value that equals the previous one at the same depth.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of generating all subsets?
questions.a: O(n · 2ⁿ): there are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each one costs up to n.

questions.q: Give an example where greedy fails and DP is needed.
questions.a: Coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 (two coins) is optimal.

questions.q: What is an exchange argument?
questions.a: A proof technique: take any optimal solution, show that swapping its first non-greedy choice for the greedy one never makes it worse, and repeat until it matches the greedy solution.

questions.q: Top-down versus bottom-up: trade-offs?
questions.a: Top-down (memoised recursion) computes only the states it needs and is natural to write, but risks deep recursion. Bottom-up is iterative, avoids recursion and makes space reduction easy, but you must get the order right.

questions.q: How do you reduce the table to O(1) or O(n) space?
questions.a: If a state depends only on the previous row or the previous few entries, keep just those in rolling variables or two arrays.

questions.q: Why a min-heap for the k largest?
questions.a: The root is the weakest of the k items kept, so a new item only needs comparing with the root, and the weakest is evicted in O(log k).

questions.q: Heap versus quickselect: trade-offs?
questions.a: A heap is O(n log k), works on streams and needs O(k) memory. Quickselect is O(n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case, and needs all the data in memory.

questions.q: How does Kahn's algorithm detect a cycle?
questions.a: If fewer than n nodes are output, the remaining nodes all still have incoming edges, which is only possible if they lie on or behind a cycle.

questions.q: Adjacency list versus matrix?
questions.a: A list uses O(V + E) memory and suits sparse graphs. A matrix uses O(V²) memory but answers 'is there an edge' in O(1), which suits dense graphs.

questions.q: What do path compression and union by size each buy you?
questions.a: Path compression flattens the tree during find. Union by size keeps trees shallow when merging. Together they give near-constant amortised time per operation.

questions.q: Union Find versus DFS for components?
questions.a: For a fixed graph both are linear and DFS is simpler. Union Find is better when edges arrive over time with connectivity queries in between. It cannot remove edges.

questions.q: Trie versus a sorted array with binary search for prefixes?
questions.a: A sorted array finds a prefix range in O(L log n), is compact and cache-friendly, but inserting is O(n). A trie does lookup and insert in O(L) and uses more memory.

questions.q: How do you delete a word?
questions.a: Clear the end-of-word flag on the last node, then optionally remove nodes on the way back up that have no children and end no word.

questions.q: Why does x & (x − 1) clear the lowest set bit?
questions.a: Subtracting 1 turns the lowest set bit to 0 and the zeros below it to 1. ANDing with the original clears that bit and leaves the higher bits unchanged.

questions.q: How do you enumerate all subsets with a mask?
questions.a: Loop mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; element i is in the subset when bit i of mask is set.

questions.q: Sort by start or by end: when does it matter?
questions.a: Sort by start for merging and inserting. Sort by end when choosing the most non-overlapping intervals, because finishing earliest leaves the most room.

questions.q: How do you find the maximum number of overlapping ranges?
questions.a: Sweep: +1 at each start and −1 at each end in sorted order, tracking the running maximum. Decide whether an end at the same time as a start counts as overlap.

questions.q: Derive O(n log n) for merge sort.
questions.a: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). There are log₂ n levels and each level does O(n) work in total.

questions.q: Merge sort versus quicksort in practice?
questions.a: Merge sort is stable and always O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space. Quicksort is in place and usually faster in practice but has an O(n²) worst case and is not stable.

questions.q: What changes if the array is already sorted?
questions.a: Use two pointers, one at each end. Move the left pointer right when the sum is too small and the right pointer left when it is too large. O(n) time, O(1) space, no dictionary.

questions.q: How would you return all pairs, not just one?
questions.a: Do not return at the first hit. Store a list of indices for each value, and for every element emit a pair with each earlier index of its complement. The output itself can hold O(n²) pairs.

questions.q: What if the same pair must not be reported twice?
questions.a: For value pairs, sort and use two pointers, skipping over equal neighbours after each hit. Alternatively keep a set of pairs already reported, stored as (smaller, larger).

questions.q: Why is the lookup done before the insert?
questions.a: If the value were stored first, an element equal to half the target would find itself and be paired with its own index.

questions.q: How would you report the index of the first error?
questions.a: Push indices along with the characters. On a mismatch or a closer with an empty stack, the current index is the error. If openers remain at the end, report the index of the earliest unclosed one.

questions.q: What if the string also contains letters?
questions.a: Skip any character that is neither an opener nor a closer and process the rest exactly as before.

questions.q: Can you do it in O(1) space if there is only one bracket type?
questions.a: Yes. Keep a counter: add one for an opener, subtract one for a closer, fail if it ever goes negative, and require zero at the end.

questions.topic: Problem · Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.q: What if you may make many transactions?
questions.a: Add up every positive day-to-day rise. Any longer rise is the sum of its daily rises, so this greedy total is optimal.

questions.topic: Problem · Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.q: What if there is a cooldown or a fee?
questions.a: Use DP with a small number of states per day, such as holding and not holding (plus a cooling state for cooldown). Update each state from the previous day. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.topic: Problem · Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.q: How would you also return the buy and sell days?
questions.a: Remember the index of the minimum price. Whenever best improves, record that index and the current day.

questions.q: Find the first position of a duplicated target.
questions.a: When nums[mid] equals the target, record mid and keep searching the left half (hi = mid − 1). Equivalently, find the first index whose value is ≥ target and check it.

questions.q: Search a rotated sorted array.
questions.a: At every step at least one half is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half's value range; if so search there, otherwise search the other half. Still O(log n).

questions.q: Binary search on an answer range instead of an array.
questions.a: Define a yes/no test that is false up to some value and true after it, for example 'can the work finish at speed x'. Binary search the range of candidate answers for the first value that passes.

questions.q: Return the start and end indices.
questions.a: Keep a candidate start that resets whenever a new run begins. When best improves, record the candidate start and the current index.

questions.q: Solve it with divide and conquer.
questions.a: The best run lies entirely in the left half, entirely in the right half, or crosses the middle. The crossing case is the best suffix of the left plus the best prefix of the right. That gives O(n log n), or O(n) if each call returns total, best prefix, best suffix and best.

questions.q: What about a circular array?
questions.a: The answer is the larger of the normal maximum and (total − minimum subarray), which represents a run that wraps around. If every value is negative, return the normal maximum.

questions.topic: Problem · Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.q: Return the substring itself.
questions.a: Record the window's start index whenever best improves, then build the string from that start and length.

questions.topic: Problem · Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.q: Allow at most k distinct characters.
questions.a: Keep a count per character. After adding the right character, shrink from the left while the number of distinct characters exceeds k, decreasing counts and removing zeros.

questions.topic: Problem · Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.q: Why convert to Array<Character> in Swift?
questions.a: Swift String cannot be indexed by integer in O(1); reaching offset i costs O(i). An Array<Character> gives O(1) access and still treats each user-visible character as one element.

questions.q: Do it recursively; what is the stack cost?
questions.a: Reverse the rest of the list first, then make the old second node point back to the head and set head.next to nil. It uses O(n) call stack.

questions.q: Reverse only positions m to n.
questions.a: Walk to the node just before position m. Then, n − m times, detach the node after the sublist's first node and re-insert it at the front of the sublist. A dummy head handles m = 1.

questions.q: Reverse in groups of k.
questions.a: Check that k nodes remain. Reverse those k, connect the previous group's tail to the new group head, and continue. A final group shorter than k is left as it is.

questions.q: Merge k sorted lists.
questions.a: Put the head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push its successor. O(N log k). Merging the lists pairwise in rounds gives the same bound.

questions.q: Write it recursively.
questions.a: If either list is empty return the other. Otherwise take the smaller head and set its next to the merge of the remainder. It uses O(n + m) call stack.

questions.q: Why does <= keep the merge stable?
questions.a: On a tie it takes the node from the first list, so equal elements keep their original relative order.

questions.topic: Problem · Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.q: Do it iteratively with BFS.
questions.a: Run a level-order traversal and count the levels.

questions.topic: Problem · Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.q: Compute the minimum depth instead.
questions.a: A node with one child is not a leaf, so do not take the minimum with a missing child's 0. Use 1 + the minimum over existing children, or run BFS and stop at the first leaf.

questions.topic: Problem · Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
questions.q: When could recursion overflow the stack?
questions.a: Recursion depth equals the tree height. A heavily skewed tree with tens of thousands of nodes or more can exhaust the stack; use an iterative version there.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.q: Zigzag order.
questions.a: Use the same BFS and reverse every second level before appending it.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.q: Right side view of the tree.
questions.a: Take the last value of each level.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.q: Why not call removeFirst() in a loop?
questions.a: removeFirst() on an Array shifts every remaining element, so each call is O(n) and the traversal becomes O(n²). Swap whole-level arrays, keep a head index, or use Deque.

questions.q: Use BFS to avoid deep recursion.
questions.a: Replace the recursion with a queue. Mark a cell when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued, so it is never queued twice.

questions.q: Solve it with Union Find.
questions.a: Treat each land cell as a node. Union each land cell with its right and down land neighbours. The answer is the number of land cells minus the number of successful unions.

questions.q: Return the largest island's area.
questions.a: Have the flood fill return how many cells it sank and keep the maximum.

questions.q: Allow steps of 1, 2 or 3.
questions.a: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2) + ways(n − 3). Roll three variables instead of two.

questions.q: Each step has a cost; minimise it.
questions.a: Let dp[i] be the cheapest cost to stand on step i: dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2]). The answer is the smaller of the last two.

questions.q: Why is the plain recursion exponential?
questions.a: It recomputes the same sub-problems again and again; the call tree has roughly 1.6ⁿ nodes. Memoising each result makes it O(n).

questions.q: Count the number of ways instead.
questions.a: Set dp[0] = 1. Loop over coins on the outside and amounts on the inside, adding dp[a − coin] to dp[a]. Coins outside counts combinations rather than orderings.

questions.q: Return the coins used.
questions.a: For each amount also store the coin that produced the best value. Walk back from the target subtracting the stored coin each time.

questions.q: When does greedy work?
questions.a: It works for so-called canonical systems such as 1, 5, 10, 25. There is no simple general test, so use DP unless the system is known to be canonical; [1, 3, 4] with amount 6 is a counter-example.

questions.q: Insert one range into an already merged list.
questions.a: Copy every interval that ends before the new one starts. Merge all that overlap it by taking the smallest start and largest end. Then copy the rest. O(n).

questions.q: Minimum meeting rooms needed.
questions.a: Sort starts and ends separately and sweep, or keep a min-heap of end times. The answer is the largest number of meetings in progress at once. O(n log n).

questions.q: Minimum removals to make ranges non-overlapping.
questions.a: Sort by end. Keep an interval when its start is not before the end of the last one kept. The removals are the total minus the number kept.

questions.q: Use a heap instead; compare costs.
questions.a: Count, then keep a min-heap of size k ordered by frequency: O(n log k) time and O(k) for the heap. The bucket method is O(n) but allocates n + 1 buckets.

questions.q: Handle a stream where counts change.
questions.a: Keep counts in a dictionary and recompute the top k on demand, or maintain an ordered structure. For very large streams use an approximate method such as Space-Saving or a Count-Min Sketch.

questions.q: Return results in a deterministic order.
questions.a: Sort by frequency descending and then by value ascending, or sort the values inside each bucket.

questions.q: What if duplicates must be within k positions of each other?
questions.a: Keep a set holding only the last k values. Before inserting index i, remove nums[i − k − 1] once the window is full. A dictionary of last-seen index also works.

questions.q: How would you do it with O(1) extra space?
questions.a: Sort in place and compare neighbours. O(n log n) time, and it changes the input order.

questions.q: Why use insert(_:).inserted rather than contains then insert?
questions.a: insert returns whether the value was new, so one hash lookup does the work of contains followed by insert.

questions.q: Do it without building a second array.
questions.a: Use two String.Index values. Advance or retreat past characters that are not letters or digits, then compare the lowercased characters. O(1) extra space.

questions.q: Allow deleting at most one character.
questions.a: On the first mismatch, check whether the remainder is a palindrome after skipping the left character or after skipping the right one.

questions.q: How do Unicode characters affect this?
questions.a: A Character is a whole grapheme cluster, isLetter and isNumber accept non-ASCII characters, and case mapping can change the number of characters in some scripts. For ASCII input none of this matters; say which you assume.

questions.topic: Problem · Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
questions.q: Extend it to three numbers.
questions.a: Fix one index and run the two-pointer search on the part to its right. O(n²) overall; skip equal neighbours to avoid repeated triples.

questions.topic: Problem · Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
questions.q: What if the array were not sorted?
questions.a: Use the dictionary method in O(n) time and O(n) space, or sort first in O(n log n), keeping the original indices if they are needed.

questions.topic: Problem · Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
questions.q: Why is this better than the dictionary approach here?
questions.a: It needs no extra memory and no hashing, and it uses the sorted order that the input already guarantees.

questions.q: Find the node where the cycle begins.
questions.a: After the two pointers meet, move one back to the head and advance both one step at a time. They meet again at the first node of the cycle, because the distance from the head to that node equals the distance from the meeting point to it, modulo the cycle length.

questions.q: Find the cycle length.
questions.a: From the meeting point, keep one pointer still and step the other until it returns, counting the steps.

questions.q: Why === and not ==?
questions.a: === asks whether two references are the same object. Two different nodes may hold equal values, and a class is not Equatable unless you make it so.

questions.q: Why is seen initialised with [0: 1]?
questions.a: It stands for the empty prefix. Without it, runs that start at index 0, where the running sum itself equals k, would not be counted.

questions.q: Return the longest such run instead of the count.
questions.a: Store only the first index at which each prefix sum appears, starting with [0: −1]. The longest run ending at i has length i − firstIndex[sum − k].

questions.q: What if all numbers are positive?
questions.a: A sliding window then works in O(1) space, because adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it.

questions.q: Next greater element in a circular array.
questions.a: Loop over 2n positions using index i % n so that every element also sees the elements before it. Push indices only during the first pass.

questions.q: Why store indices instead of temperatures?
questions.a: The answer needs the distance between two days. An index gives both the position and, through the array, the value; a value alone gives neither position nor distance.

questions.q: Solve it scanning from the right.
questions.a: Go from right to left keeping a stack of candidate warmer days. Pop every candidate that is not warmer than today; if one remains, the answer is its index minus today's.

questions.q: Handle duplicate numbers without duplicate subsets.
questions.a: Sort the input. Inside the loop, skip nums[i] when i > start and it equals nums[i − 1], so equal values are not chosen twice at the same depth.

questions.q: Only subsets of size k.
questions.a: Record the path only when it has k elements and stop going deeper. Prune when too few elements remain to reach size k.

questions.q: Why does appending path store a copy in Swift?
questions.a: Array is a value type. Appending path stores its current contents; later changes to path do not affect the stored copy.

questions.q: What if every other value appears three times?
questions.a: Count the set bits at each bit position modulo 3; the remainders form the answer. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: What if two values appear once?
questions.a: XOR everything to get a ^ b. Pick any set bit of that result, split the numbers by whether they have that bit, and XOR each group separately.

questions.q: Why does order not matter?
questions.a: XOR is commutative and associative, so the values can be regrouped into pairs that cancel no matter where they sit.

questions.q: The houses form a circle.
questions.a: The first and last houses are now neighbours. Solve the row without the first house and the row without the last house, and take the better. Handle a single house separately.

questions.q: Return which houses were chosen.
questions.a: Keep the full dp array. Walk back from the end: if dp[i] differs from dp[i − 1], house i was taken, so jump to i − 2; otherwise step to i − 1.

questions.q: The houses form a binary tree.
questions.a: Do a post-order DFS that returns two values per node: the best total if the node is taken and the best if it is not.

questions.q: Add union by size; what does it buy?
questions.a: Attach the smaller tree under the larger one. Together with path compression this keeps trees almost flat, so each operation is near-constant amortised time.

questions.q: Solve it with DFS instead.
questions.a: Keep a visited array. For each unvisited city, add one to the count and DFS through every city its row connects to. O(n²).

questions.q: Connections arrive one at a time; report the count after each.
questions.a: That is the natural use of Union Find: union each connection as it arrives, decrement the count when the two leaders differ, and report the count.

questions.q: Sliding window minimum.
questions.a: Keep the deque increasing instead: remove values from the back while they are greater than or equal to the new value.

questions.q: Why store indices rather than values?
questions.a: An index tells you when the front has left the window, and the value is still available through the array.

questions.q: When is a heap acceptable instead?
questions.a: When O(n log n) is acceptable and simplicity matters. Push (value, index) pairs and discard expired tops lazily before reading the maximum.

questions.q: Support a wildcard character in search.
questions.a: At a wildcard, try every child recursively; at a normal character follow the single matching child. The worst case visits many nodes.

questions.q: Delete a word.
questions.a: Walk to the last node and clear its isWord flag. Optionally walk back up, removing nodes that have no children and are not word ends.

questions.q: Dictionary children versus a fixed array of 26: trade-offs?
questions.a: A fixed array of 26 is fast and predictable for lowercase a–z but wastes memory in sparse nodes. A dictionary handles any Character and saves memory when nodes are sparse, at the cost of hashing.

questions.q: Merge sort versus quicksort versus heapsort.
questions.a: Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space. Quicksort: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, in place, usually fastest in practice, not stable. Heapsort: O(n log n) worst case, in place, not stable, weaker cache behaviour.

questions.q: Sort a linked list in O(1) extra space.
questions.a: Use bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of length 1, 2, 4 and so on by relinking nodes, which needs no recursion stack.

questions.q: What does 'stable' mean and why does <= matter?
questions.a: Stable means equal elements keep their original order, which matters when sorting records by one key after another. <= takes from the left half on ties, which preserves that order.

questions.q: Return a valid order of courses instead of true or false.
questions.a: Append each course to a list at the moment it is taken. If the list ends with every course it is a valid order; otherwise there is a cycle and no order exists.

questions.q: Solve it with DFS.
questions.a: Mark each node as unvisited, in progress or finished. Reaching an in-progress node means a cycle. Appending nodes as they finish and reversing the list gives a valid order.

questions.q: How would you find the smallest number of terms needed if courses can be taken in parallel?
questions.a: Process the ready courses one whole layer at a time, like BFS levels. The number of layers is the minimum number of terms; it equals the longest chain of prerequisites.

questions.q: Rewrite it with a priority queue. What changes?
questions.a: Push (time, node) pairs into a min-heap and pop the smallest, skipping entries whose time is worse than the recorded one. The cost becomes O((V + E) log V), which is better on sparse graphs. Swift needs a hand-written heap or swift-collections.

questions.q: What if some link times are negative?
questions.a: Dijkstra is no longer correct, because a settled time could later be improved. Use Bellman–Ford, which relaxes every link V − 1 times in O(V · E) and can detect a negative cycle.

questions.q: How would you return the actual route to a node?
questions.a: Record for each node the node it was last improved from. Follow those predecessors back from the target to the source and reverse the list.

questions.topic: Problem · Min Cost to Connect All Points
questions.q: Solve it with Kruskal's algorithm.
questions.a: Generate every pair as an edge with its cost, sort the edges, and add each one whose endpoints are in different groups according to Union Find, until n − 1 edges are added.

questions.topic: Problem · Min Cost to Connect All Points
questions.q: When is Kruskal the better choice?
questions.a: When the graph is sparse or the edges are already given as a list, since its cost is O(E log E). On a dense graph such as this one, E is about n², so array-based Prim at O(n²) is faster.

questions.topic: Problem · Min Cost to Connect All Points
questions.q: Why does this version not need a heap?
questions.a: Each round already has to look at every outside point to update its best value, so finding the minimum in the same O(n) scan adds nothing. A heap helps only when there are far fewer edges than n².

questions.q: Why is comparing each node only with its children not enough?
questions.a: A node can be on the correct side of its parent and still break the rule for a grandparent or higher ancestor. In [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] the 3 is a valid left child of 6 but lies in the right subtree of 5.

questions.q: Solve it with an in-order traversal.
questions.a: Traverse left, node, right while remembering the previous value. The tree is valid exactly when each value is strictly greater than the previous one.

questions.q: How would you allow duplicate values on one side?
questions.a: Loosen the comparison on that side only, for example allow node.val equal to the lower bound for the right subtree, and state the convention clearly because definitions differ.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.q: Solve it with quickselect. What are the trade-offs?
questions.a: Partition around a pivot as in quicksort, then continue only in the side that contains position n − k. O(n) on average and O(1) extra space, but O(n²) in the worst case, it reorders the array, and it needs all the data up front.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.q: How do the sift-up and sift-down index formulas work?
questions.a: With the heap stored in an array from index 0, the children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and the parent is at (i − 1) / 2. Sift up swaps with the parent while smaller; sift down swaps with the smaller child while larger.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.q: What changes if the numbers arrive as an endless stream?
questions.a: The heap approach works unchanged, since it only keeps k values. Quickselect and sorting do not apply because the data never ends.

questions.q: Describe the O(n log n) method.
questions.a: Keep an array where entry i is the smallest tail value of any increasing subsequence of length i + 1. For each number, binary-search the first entry that is not smaller and overwrite it, or append if there is none. The array's length is the answer.

questions.q: How do you recover the subsequence itself?
questions.a: Alongside dp, store for each index the previous index that gave its best value. Start at the index with the largest dp and follow the stored links backwards.

questions.q: Count how many longest increasing subsequences there are.
questions.a: Keep a second array of counts. When dp[j] + 1 beats dp[i], copy count[j]; when it ties, add count[j]. Sum the counts of all indices whose dp equals the maximum.

questions.q: Recover the subsequence, not just its length.
questions.a: Walk back from the bottom-right cell. If the characters match, take that character and move diagonally. Otherwise move to whichever neighbour, up or left, holds the larger value. Reverse what you collected.

questions.q: Reduce the space to O(min(m, n)).
questions.a: Each row depends only on the row above, so keep two rows, or one row plus a saved diagonal value. Put the shorter string on the column axis.

questions.q: How does edit distance differ?
questions.a: Edit distance counts the fewest insertions, deletions and replacements to turn one string into the other. Its table takes a minimum over three operations instead of a maximum over two, and its first row and column are 0, 1, 2 and so on rather than zeros.

questions.q: Why must the inner loop run downward?
questions.a: Scanning upward would let reach[s − x] already include x from earlier in the same pass, so x could be used more than once. That is the unbounded knapsack, which is a different problem.

questions.q: Return the actual subset.
questions.a: Keep, for each reachable sum, the number that first made it reachable, or keep the full two-dimensional table. Walk back from target subtracting the recorded number each time.

questions.q: How does this relate to Coin Change?
questions.a: Both are knapsack problems over sums. Coin Change lets each coin be used any number of times, so its inner loop runs upward and it minimises a count. Here each number is used at most once, so the loop runs downward and the table holds true or false.

questions.topic: Problem · Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
questions.q: Why is the copy of the cost array needed?
questions.a: Without it, a price improved earlier in the same round could be used by a later flight in that round, chaining two or more flights and breaking the 'at most r flights after round r' guarantee.

questions.topic: Problem · Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
questions.q: How does full Bellman–Ford detect a negative cycle?
questions.a: Run V − 1 rounds, then one more. If any distance still improves in the extra round, a negative cycle is reachable from the source.

questions.topic: Problem · Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
questions.q: Could you solve this with Dijkstra?
questions.a: Yes, if the state is (city, flights used) rather than the city alone, so that a dearer route with fewer flights is not discarded. The heap then holds (cost, city, flights) entries.

questions.topic: Problem · Insert into a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: Write it recursively.
questions.a: If the node is nil return a new node. Otherwise assign the result of inserting into the left or right child back to that child, and return the node. It uses O(h) call stack.

questions.topic: Problem · Insert into a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: How do self-balancing trees keep the height small?
questions.a: They store extra information per node, such as a height or a colour, and after each insert or delete they perform rotations that restore a balance rule. That keeps the height O(log n).

questions.topic: Problem · Insert into a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: How would you handle duplicate values?
questions.a: Pick one convention and apply it everywhere, for example send equal values to the right subtree, or store a count in the node instead of adding a second node.

questions.topic: Problem · Delete Node in a BST
questions.q: Could you use the predecessor instead of the successor?
questions.a: Yes. The largest value in the left subtree works the same way: copy it into the node and delete it from the left subtree. Alternating between the two can help keep the tree from leaning.

questions.topic: Problem · Delete Node in a BST
questions.q: Why does copying the successor's value keep the tree valid?
questions.a: The successor is the smallest value larger than the deleted key. Everything in the left subtree is smaller than it and everything remaining in the right subtree is larger, so the ordering still holds at that node.

questions.topic: Problem · Delete Node in a BST
questions.q: Write it without recursion.
questions.a: Walk down keeping a reference to the parent and which side you came from. Handle the zero and one child cases by relinking the parent. For two children, find the successor and its parent, copy the value, and unlink the successor.

questions.topic: Problem · Product of Array Except Self
questions.q: Why not divide the total product by each element?
questions.a: Division fails when any element is zero, and the problem usually forbids it. It can also lose precision or overflow differently with other number types.

questions.topic: Problem · Product of Array Except Self
questions.q: How would you handle it if division were allowed but zeros may appear?
questions.a: Count the zeros. With two or more, every answer is 0. With exactly one, only that position is non-zero and equals the product of the others. With none, divide the total by each element.

questions.topic: Problem · Product of Array Except Self
questions.q: Can the same idea give prefix and suffix maximums?
questions.a: Yes. Any operation that combines a left part and a right part works the same way: keep a running maximum from the left and another from the right.

questions.q: Why move the shorter line and not the taller one?
questions.a: The shorter line caps the water level. Keeping it and moving the taller line makes the container narrower without raising that cap, so the area can only shrink.

questions.q: What if both lines have the same height?
questions.a: Either pointer may move. Neither line can form a larger container with a line further in unless that line is taller, and moving one of them will find it.

questions.q: How does Trapping Rain Water differ?
questions.a: Here you choose two lines and ignore the ones between. In Trapping Rain Water every bar holds water above itself, limited by the tallest bars on both sides, and the amounts are summed.

questions.q: How do you avoid sorting each word?
questions.a: Count the 26 letters of each word and use the counts as the key, for example as an array of 26 integers, which is Hashable. That costs O(L) per word.

questions.q: What if the words contain Unicode characters?
questions.a: Sorting Characters still gives a correct key. A fixed 26-slot count no longer works, so use a dictionary of character counts or the sorted string. Decide whether accents and case should be treated as equal.

questions.q: How would you return the groups in a stable order?
questions.a: Remember the order in which keys first appear in a separate array and output the groups in that order, or sort the groups at the end.

questions.q: Use a second stack that stores only the minimums. How does it save space?
questions.a: Push onto the second stack only when the new value is less than or equal to its top, and pop it only when the value removed equals its top. It stores fewer entries when the minimum rarely changes.

questions.q: Can it be done with O(1) extra space?
questions.a: Yes, by storing an encoded value such as 2 × value − min when a new minimum is pushed and decoding on pop. It is fragile because of overflow and is rarely worth it.

questions.q: How would you add getMax as well?
questions.a: Store the maximum so far in each entry as well. Each entry becomes (value, min so far, max so far) and every operation stays O(1).

questions.topic: Problem · Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: What changes if duplicates are allowed?
questions.a: When nums[lo], nums[mid] and nums[hi] are all equal you cannot tell which half is sorted. Shrink the range by one from each end and continue. The worst case becomes O(n).

questions.topic: Problem · Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: Find the minimum element instead.
questions.a: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] is larger the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Stop when lo equals hi.

questions.topic: Problem · Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: Why is the comparison nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] and not <?
questions.a: When lo equals mid, which happens with two elements, the left half is a single element and counts as sorted. Using < would send that case to the wrong branch.

questions.q: Why start from all rotten oranges at once?
questions.a: Each fresh orange rots at the time of its nearest rotten orange. Starting them all at level 0 gives that minimum directly in one pass, instead of running a separate search from each.

questions.q: How would you return the time each orange rots?
questions.a: Keep a grid of times. When an orange is added to the next queue, record the current minute plus one in its cell.

questions.q: What if rot also spread diagonally?
questions.a: Use eight direction pairs instead of four. Nothing else changes.

questions.q: Handle duplicate numbers without duplicate orderings.
questions.a: Sort the input. At each position skip a number when it equals the previous number and that previous one is not currently used, so equal values are placed in one fixed order only.

questions.q: Generate the next permutation in lexicographic order.
questions.a: From the right, find the first element smaller than its right neighbour. Swap it with the smallest larger element to its right, then reverse the part after it. If no such element exists, the sequence is the last permutation.

questions.q: How does this differ from generating subsets?
questions.a: Subsets decide for each element whether to include it, and order does not matter, so the loop moves forward from a start index. Permutations use every element and order matters, so each level scans all unused elements.

questions.q: Find the minimum number of jumps.
questions.a: Track the end of the range reachable with the current number of jumps and the farthest index reachable with one more. When the scan reaches the end of the current range, add a jump and extend the range. O(n).

questions.q: Solve it scanning from the right.
questions.a: Keep the leftmost index known to reach the end, starting at the last index. Moving left, an index becomes the new goal if it can jump at least that far. The answer is whether the goal reaches index 0.

questions.q: Why is DP unnecessary here?
questions.a: The only fact needed about the past is the farthest reachable index, and it can be updated in O(1). Remembering reachability for each index separately adds nothing.

questions.q: Solve it for lowercase letters only with a fixed array.
questions.a: Use an array of 26 integers indexed by the letter's distance from "a", reading the strings as UTF-8 bytes. Increment for s, decrement for t, and require all zeros.

questions.q: Why is the final all-zero check needed?
questions.a: Without it, a t that is shorter than s would pass, because the loop only detects characters that t has too many of. Comparing lengths first is an equivalent fix.

questions.q: How would you find all anagrams of a word inside a long text?
questions.a: Slide a window of the word's length across the text, keeping letter counts for the window, and compare with the word's counts at each position. O(n) overall.

questions.q: Why is the loop not O(n²)?
questions.a: The counting loop starts only at the smallest value of each run. Every value belongs to one run and is stepped over once, so the inner loops total at most n steps.

questions.q: Return the run itself, not just its length.
questions.a: Remember the starting value along with the best length, then produce start, start + 1 and so on.

questions.q: Solve it with Union Find.
questions.a: Union each value with value + 1 when that is also present, tracking component sizes. The largest component is the answer. It works but is heavier than the set method.

questions.q: How do you extend this to four numbers?
questions.a: Add an outer loop that fixes one more value and run the three-number method on the rest, skipping duplicates at each level. That is O(n³).

questions.q: Find the triple whose sum is closest to a target.
questions.a: Use the same sorted two-pointer scan, but instead of testing for zero keep the sum with the smallest distance to the target, and move the pointers by comparing the sum with the target.

questions.q: Why is skipping duplicates on the left pointer alone enough?
questions.a: After a hit both pointers move. Once the left value differs from the previous one, the required right value differs too, so the same triple cannot be formed again.

questions.q: Why must b be popped before a?
questions.a: The right operand was pushed last, so it comes off first. For subtraction and division the order changes the result.

questions.q: How would you convert an infix expression to postfix?
questions.a: Use the shunting-yard method: output numbers directly, keep operators on a stack, and pop operators of higher or equal precedence before pushing a new one. Parentheses are pushed and popped as markers.

questions.q: How would you report a malformed expression?
questions.a: Check that at least two values are on the stack before applying an operator, that a divisor is not zero, and that exactly one value remains at the end. Throw or return nil otherwise.

questions.topic: Problem · Middle of the Linked List
questions.q: Return the first middle node for even lengths.
questions.a: Stop one step earlier: loop while fast.next?.next exists. Slow then rests on the first of the two middle nodes.

questions.topic: Problem · Middle of the Linked List
questions.q: Delete the middle node.
questions.a: Keep a reference to the node before slow, and at the end link it past slow. A list with one node becomes empty.

questions.topic: Problem · Middle of the Linked List
questions.q: Why does the loop test fast.next and not fast?
questions.a: fast is advanced by two, so it may land on the last node or on nil. Testing fast.next covers both: optional chaining makes it nil in either case, and the loop stops.

questions.q: Do it iteratively with a queue.
questions.a: Put the root in a queue. Repeatedly take a node, swap its two children, and add the non-nil children to the queue.

questions.q: Check whether a tree is symmetric.
questions.a: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirror images: the two roots must be equal, and each one's left subtree must mirror the other's right subtree.

questions.q: Does the order (swap first or recurse first) matter?
questions.a: No. Swapping and then recursing into both children gives the same result as recursing first, as long as both subtrees are processed exactly once.

questions.q: What if some cells are blocked?
questions.a: Set a blocked cell's count to 0 instead of adding. The first row and column can no longer be assumed to be 1; a block there cuts off everything after it.

questions.q: Give the combinatorial formula and explain it.
questions.a: Every route is a sequence of m − 1 downs and n − 1 rights. Choosing which positions are downs gives C(m + n − 2, m − 1).

questions.q: Find the path with the smallest sum of cell values.
questions.a: Use the same table but take the minimum of the cell above and the cell to the left, plus the current cell's value.

questions.q: What does Swift provide for this?
questions.a: Every integer type has nonzeroBitCount, along with leadingZeroBitCount and trailingZeroBitCount.

questions.q: Count the bits for every number from 0 to n.
questions.a: Use DP: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1), or bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1. O(n) in total.

questions.q: How do you test whether a number is a power of two?
questions.a: It must be positive and satisfy x & (x − 1) == 0, meaning it has exactly one set bit.

questions.q: Solve it with prefix and suffix maximum arrays.
questions.a: Build leftMax[i], the tallest bar from the start to i, and rightMax[i], the tallest from i to the end. The water over bar i is min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) − height[i]. O(n) time and O(n) space.

questions.q: Solve it with a monotonic stack.
questions.a: Keep a stack of indices with decreasing heights. When a taller bar arrives, pop the top as the floor of a basin; the water added is the distance between the new bar and the new top, times the height difference above the floor.

questions.q: How does it change in two dimensions?
questions.a: Use a min-heap seeded with all border cells. Repeatedly pop the lowest boundary cell and visit its neighbours: a lower neighbour holds water up to the boundary height and is then pushed with that height.

questions.topic: Problem · Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.q: Why is the dummy node needed?
questions.a: When the head itself is removed there is no real node before it. The dummy node gives every node, including the head, a predecessor, so one piece of code handles all cases.

questions.topic: Problem · Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.q: What if n can be larger than the length?
questions.a: Stop while advancing the lead pointer if it reaches nil, and return the list unchanged or report an error, depending on what is agreed.

questions.topic: Problem · Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.q: Do it recursively.
questions.a: Recurse to the end and count on the way back. Each call returns its distance from the end; the call whose next node has distance n unlinks it. It uses O(n) call stack.

questions.topic: Problem · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: Why hi = mid and not mid − 1?
questions.a: mid may itself be the minimum. Setting hi = mid − 1 could discard it. Because the loop runs while lo < hi and mid is always below hi, hi = mid still shrinks the range.

questions.topic: Problem · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: What changes with duplicates?
questions.a: When nums[mid] equals nums[hi] you cannot tell which side holds the minimum, so reduce hi by one. The worst case becomes O(n).

questions.topic: Problem · Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.q: How do you find the rotation count?
questions.a: It is the index of the minimum element, which this search already locates in lo.

questions.q: Return the path itself.
questions.a: Have each call also return the deepest leaf of its subtree, or store parent links. When best improves, record the node and the two leaves, then join the two root-to-leaf paths.

questions.q: What if edges have weights?
questions.a: Return the largest weighted depth instead of a count of levels, adding each edge's weight, and update best with the sum of the two largest weighted depths.

questions.q: Why can the answer not be read from the root alone?
questions.a: The longest path may sit entirely within one subtree, far from the root. Only checking every node as a possible bending point finds it.

questions.q: Each number may be used only once.
questions.a: Sort the candidates, recurse with i + 1 instead of i, and skip a candidate equal to the previous one at the same depth so equal values do not produce repeated combinations.

questions.q: Why pass i instead of i + 1?
questions.a: Passing i lets the same candidate be chosen again at the next level. Passing i + 1 would allow each candidate at most once.

questions.q: Only count the combinations instead of listing them.
questions.a: Use DP as in the coin-change counting problem: ways[0] = 1, and for each candidate add ways[a − candidate] to ways[a] for a from the candidate up to the target.

questions.q: Return one valid segmentation.
questions.a: Store, for each reachable end, the start that made it reachable. Walk back from the end of the string following those starts to read off the words.

questions.q: Return all segmentations.
questions.a: Use backtracking with memoisation: for each start position return every list of words that segments the rest. The number of results can be exponential.

questions.q: How would a trie help?
questions.a: Insert the dictionary into a trie. From each reachable start, walk the trie along the string and mark every position where a word ends. This avoids building and hashing substrings.

questions.q: Why is tracking only the maximum wrong?
questions.a: A large negative product becomes a large positive one when multiplied by another negative. If only the maximum is kept, that information is lost.

questions.q: Return the subarray itself.
questions.a: Track the start index of the runs behind hi and lo along with their values. When best improves, record the start of the hi run and the current index.

questions.q: How do zeros affect the state?
questions.a: After a zero, both hi and lo become 0, and the next element starts a fresh run because the candidate 'x alone' wins or ties. So a zero splits the array into independent parts.

questions.q: Could binary search speed this up?
questions.a: Binary search can find where the overlap begins and ends in O(log n), but building the output array is still O(n). It helps only with a structure that supports cheap splicing.

questions.q: Do it in place.
questions.a: Find the first and last overlapping positions, replace that span with the single merged range using replaceSubrange, and return. Array shifting keeps it O(n).

questions.q: How does this relate to Merge Intervals?
questions.a: Merge Intervals sorts first and then sweeps. Here the input is already sorted and only one new range can cause merging, so a single linear sweep is enough.

questions.q: What if rows and columns are each sorted but rows do not chain?
questions.a: Start at the top-right corner. Move left when the value is too large and down when it is too small. Each step discards a row or a column, giving O(rows + cols).

questions.q: Solve it with two binary searches.
questions.a: First binary-search the rows for the last row whose first value is ≤ target, then binary-search inside that row. The cost is log rows + log cols, the same total.

questions.q: Why use division and remainder by cols, not rows?
questions.a: A row holds cols values, so position p is in row p / cols at column p % cols. Dividing by rows would only be right for a square grid.

questions.q: Why is hi = speed and not speed − 1?
questions.a: The middle speed may itself be the smallest that works, so it must stay in the range. Because the loop runs while lo < hi and speed is below hi, the range still shrinks.

questions.q: How do you round up with integer arithmetic?
questions.a: Compute (pile + speed − 1) / speed. Adding speed − 1 before dividing pushes any remainder up to the next whole number.

questions.q: Name another problem solved by searching the answer.
questions.a: Examples: the smallest ship capacity to deliver packages within d days, splitting an array so the largest part is minimal, and the smallest divisor keeping a sum under a threshold.

questions.q: Why refill only when the outbox is empty?
questions.a: If elements were poured while the outbox still held some, the newer elements would land on top of older ones and leave first, breaking arrival order.

questions.q: Explain the amortised O(1) bound.
questions.a: Charge each element three units when it is pushed: one for the push, one for its single move to the outbox, one for its pop. No element is moved twice, so n operations cost O(n) in total.

questions.q: Implement a stack using queues.
questions.a: Use one queue. After each push, rotate the queue by moving the elements in front of the new one to the back, so the newest is at the front. Push is O(n) and pop is O(1).

questions.q: Why is checking only the root's two heights not enough?
questions.a: The two subtrees can have equal heights while one of them is badly unbalanced inside. The rule must hold at every node.

questions.q: What does the guard with two bindings do when the left result is nil?
questions.a: guard let with two bindings evaluates them in order and stops at the first nil. If the left result is nil, the right subtree is never visited.

questions.q: How do AVL trees use this property?
questions.a: An AVL tree stores a height or balance factor in each node and restores this property after every insert or delete by rotating nodes, keeping operations O(log n).

questions.q: What changes for a directed graph?
questions.a: A directed version has two failure cases: a node with two parents, and a cycle. You record the two candidate edges for the double parent and use Union Find to see which one must go.

questions.q: Solve it with DFS.
questions.a: Before adding each edge, run DFS from one end to see whether the other end is already reachable. If it is, that edge is the answer. This is O(n²) overall.

questions.q: Why is the first edge that fails also the last edge of the cycle?
questions.a: Until the cycle closes, the edges form a forest. The first edge whose ends are already connected completes the cycle, so every other edge of that cycle came earlier in the input.

questions.q: Solve it with a sum.
questions.a: Subtract the sum of the array from n(n + 1) / 2. In languages with fixed-width integers watch for overflow on large n.

questions.q: What if two numbers are missing?
questions.a: XOR alone gives a ^ b. Use the sum and the sum of squares to form two equations, or split the numbers by a set bit of a ^ b and XOR each group separately.

questions.q: Why start acc at n?
questions.a: The loop covers indices 0 to n − 1, but the range of numbers goes up to n. Starting acc at n includes that last number.

questions.q: Why does the loop stop before the last index?
questions.a: Reaching the last index needs no further jump. If the loop included it and it happened to equal end, an extra jump would be counted.

questions.q: Return the path of indices.
questions.a: Remember for each index the index it was best reached from, updating whenever farthest improves, then walk back from the end.

questions.q: What if the end might be unreachable?
questions.a: Check whether i ever exceeds farthest, as in Jump Game, and return −1 or nil in that case.

questions.q: Why sort by end and not by start?
questions.a: Sorting by start can keep a long range that begins early and blocks many short ones. The range that ends earliest always leaves the most room.

questions.q: How many meeting rooms would avoid any removal?
questions.a: Sweep the sorted start and end times and track how many ranges are open at once; the maximum is the number of rooms needed.

questions.q: Return the ranges that are kept.
questions.a: Collect each range at the point where it is kept instead of only updating lastEnd.

questions.q: Check whether one tree is a subtree of another.
questions.a: For every node of the larger tree, run the same-tree check against the smaller tree's root; return true if any succeeds. That is O(n · m) in the worst case.

questions.q: Do it iteratively.
questions.a: Keep a queue or stack of node pairs. Pop a pair, apply the same nil and value checks, and push the two pairs of children.

questions.q: Check whether a tree is a mirror of itself.
questions.a: Compare the left and right subtrees as mirror images: the roots must be equal, and each one's left must mirror the other's right.

questions.q: Use the recurrence based on i & (i − 1).
questions.a: bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1, because i & (i − 1) is i with its lowest set bit removed.

questions.q: Why is this dynamic programming?
questions.a: Each answer is built from the answer to a smaller sub-problem that was stored earlier, which is the definition of bottom-up DP.

questions.q: What is the total number of 1 bits from 0 to n?
questions.a: Sum the list, or count per bit position: for each position, full cycles of 2^(p+1) contribute 2^p ones each, plus the remainder.

questions.q: How does this differ from Number of Islands?
questions.a: Number of Islands only counts how many flood fills start. Here each flood fill also returns how many cells it erased, and the largest is kept.

questions.q: Avoid deep recursion.
questions.a: Use an explicit stack or a queue of cells in place of recursion, marking a cell when it is added.

questions.q: Count the perimeter of an island instead.
questions.a: For each land cell add 4, then subtract 1 for every neighbouring land cell on its four sides.

questions.q: How do you produce the lexicographically smallest order?
questions.a: Replace the queue with a min-heap so the smallest available course number is always taken next.

questions.q: Solve it with DFS.
questions.a: Run a DFS with three states per node. Append a node after all the nodes that depend on it are finished, then reverse the list. Meeting an in-progress node means a cycle.

questions.q: Why is the queue itself the answer?
questions.a: Courses are appended only when all their prerequisites are already in the queue, and nothing is ever removed, so the final contents are in a valid order.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.q: The tree changes often and the query is frequent. How do you speed it up?
questions.a: Store in each node the size of its left subtree. Then go left if k is at most that size, return the node if k is one more, otherwise go right with k reduced. That is O(h) per query.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.q: Do it recursively.
questions.a: Do an in-order recursion with a counter captured from the outer function; record the value when the counter reaches k and stop descending.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.q: Find the kth largest.
questions.a: Do the mirrored traversal: go right first, then the node, then left.

questions.q: Solve it with DP. What does the table mean?
questions.a: dp[i][j] is true when s[i...j] is a palindrome: the end characters match and dp[i + 1][j − 1] is true (or the length is under 3). Fill by increasing length. O(n²) time and space.

questions.q: Count all palindromic substrings.
questions.a: Use the same centre expansion and add 1 for every successful match instead of tracking the longest.

questions.q: What does Manacher's algorithm do differently?
questions.a: It reuses the palindrome radii already computed to the left of the current position, using symmetry inside the widest palindrome found so far, so most expansions start from a known length. Total O(n).

questions.q: Why can the stations between start and i be skipped?
questions.a: Leaving the current start with an empty tank, the car reached each station in between with a tank of 0 or more. Starting at one of those with exactly 0 can only do worse, so it also fails by station i.

questions.q: Why does total ≥ 0 guarantee an answer?
questions.a: Split the circle at the last restart. The part before it has a net deficit and the part from it to the end never goes negative. Since the whole lap is non-negative, the surplus carried from the second part covers the first.

questions.q: Return all valid starting stations.
questions.a: Compute the running balance around the circle once. A station is a valid start exactly when the balance just before it is the minimum of the whole lap, so report every position that attains that minimum.

questions.q: What if the array can be updated?
questions.a: Use a Fenwick tree or a segment tree. Both support point updates and range sums in O(log n).

questions.q: Extend it to a 2D matrix.
questions.a: Build prefix[r + 1][c + 1] as the sum of the rectangle from the origin. A query combines four entries by inclusion and exclusion.

questions.q: Why is the leading 0 useful?
questions.a: It lets a range starting at index 0 use the same formula as any other, with no special case.

questions.q: How would you make it O(n + m)?
questions.a: Serialise both trees with markers for missing children and a separator before each value, then search for one string in the other with a linear-time matcher such as KMP. Alternatively hash every subtree bottom-up and compare hashes.

questions.q: Why is comparing in-order traversals alone wrong?
