questions.a: Different trees can share the same in-order sequence. Without markers for missing children, and without separators between values, the sequence does not determine the shape.

questions.q: How does this differ from checking that one tree's shape is contained in another?
questions.a: Here the match must include every descendant down to the leaves. A containment check would allow the larger tree to continue below the matched part.

questions.topic: Problem · Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: Solve it for a general binary tree.
questions.a: Use post-order recursion: return the node if it is one of the targets, otherwise search both children. If both sides return something, the current node is the answer; otherwise pass up whichever side found one.

questions.topic: Problem · Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: What if a target may be missing?
questions.a: First confirm that both values exist with two ordinary BST searches, or have the search report how many targets were found, and return nil if either is missing.

questions.topic: Problem · Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
questions.q: Write it recursively.
questions.a: If both values are smaller, return the result for the left child; if both are larger, for the right child; otherwise return the node. It uses O(h) call stack.

questions.q: Why are two passes enough?
questions.a: Every valid plan leaves out the first house or the last house. Solving once without each covers all plans, and a plan that leaves out both is included in either pass.

questions.q: Why does a single house need its own case?
questions.a: With one house both slices are empty and would give 0, but the house can be taken. With two or more houses the slices handle everything.

questions.q: What if the houses form a tree?
questions.a: Use DFS returning two values per node: the best total taking the node and the best not taking it.

questions.q: Add a wildcard character that stands for any digit 1–9.
questions.a: Count the choices per position: a wildcard alone has 9 options; as the first of two digits it can be 1 or 2 depending on the second; as the second it has 9 options after 1 and 6 after 2. Multiply the earlier counts by those factors.

questions.q: Return the decodings themselves.
questions.a: Use backtracking: at each position try one digit and, if valid, two digits, appending the letter and recursing. The number of results can be exponential.

questions.q: Why does 0 need special care?
questions.a: 0 has no letter of its own. It is valid only as the second digit of 10 or 20, so a 0 after any other digit, or at the start, makes the count 0.

questions.q: Why does the walk start at index 0?
questions.a: Values are between 1 and n, so nothing points to index 0. That guarantees index 0 is outside the cycle, which the second phase of Floyd's method requires.

questions.q: Solve it with binary search on the value.
questions.a: Pick a middle value and count how many numbers are less than or equal to it. If the count exceeds the middle value, the duplicate is in the lower half; otherwise in the upper half. O(n log n) time, O(1) space.

questions.q: What if the array may be modified?
questions.a: Mark visits by negating the value at the index each number points to; meeting an already negative value reveals the duplicate. Or place each value at its own index by swapping.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in a Stream
questions.q: Why a min-heap and not a max-heap?
questions.a: The value needed is the smallest of the k largest. A min-heap has exactly that at its root, and it is also the one to discard when a larger number arrives.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in a Stream
questions.q: What if k can change between calls?
questions.a: Keep all values in two heaps or a balanced tree so the boundary can move, since a heap of size k has discarded what a larger k would need.

questions.topic: Problem · Kth Largest Element in a Stream
questions.q: How would you track the median instead?
questions.a: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size. The median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops.

questions.q: Why is it safe not to decrease maxCount?
questions.a: The answer only improves when a window has a higher most-common count than any before. A stale value can make the window keep its size instead of shrinking, but it never lets the window grow beyond what a real count justified.

questions.q: Solve it with an exact maximum.
questions.a: After removing the left character, recompute the maximum over the 26 counts. That costs O(26 · n), which is still linear.

questions.q: What if only certain replacements are allowed?
questions.a: Then the cost of fixing a window depends on which letters it contains, so track the cost per target letter separately, for example by running the window once per allowed target.

questions.q: How would you speed it up for many calls?
questions.a: Precompute the reversal of every byte in a 256-entry table, then reverse a 32-bit value by reversing its four bytes and swapping their order.

questions.q: Do it with masks and swaps.
questions.a: Swap the two 16-bit halves, then the 8-bit halves of each, then 4-bit, 2-bit and 1-bit groups, using a mask and two shifts at each stage. Five steps in total.

questions.q: Why loop exactly 32 times instead of until x is 0?
questions.a: Stopping when x reaches 0 would leave the result short by the number of leading zeros, which must appear as trailing zeros in the answer.

questions.q: How can you prune early?
questions.a: Check first that the board contains every letter of the word often enough. Searching from the rarer end of the word also cuts branches.

questions.q: Search for many words at once.
questions.a: Put the words in a trie and run one DFS per cell that walks the trie along with the board, collecting every word reached. That is the approach for Word Search II.

questions.q: Why restore the cell after exploring?
questions.a: The mark means 'used on the current path'. If it stayed after a failed attempt, later paths that legitimately need that cell would be blocked.

questions.q: Why must the list be cut before weaving?
questions.a: Without the cut, the first half still links into the second half, so the weave would create a cycle or lose track of where the first half ends.

questions.q: Do it with a stack.
questions.a: Push every node on a stack, then walk from the head taking n / 2 nodes from the stack and inserting each after the current front node. It uses O(n) extra memory.

questions.q: Which three smaller problems does this combine?
questions.a: Finding the middle of a list, reversing a list, and merging two lists alternately.

questions.q: Why a doubly linked list and not a singly linked one?
questions.a: Removing a node needs its predecessor. With a doubly linked list that is one step; a singly linked list would need a search from the head.

questions.q: Why is prev declared weak?
questions.a: Each node's next reference already owns the following node. If prev were also strong, neighbouring nodes would own each other and ARC could never free them.

questions.q: How would you make it safe to use from several threads?
questions.a: Guard get and put with a lock or run them on a serial queue, or make the cache an actor. Even get must be guarded because it changes the order.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.q: Why floor the child gains at 0?
questions.a: A branch with a negative total would lower the sum, and a path is free to stop at the node instead of going down that side.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.q: Why return max(l, r) rather than l + r?
questions.a: A path through the parent can continue into only one child's side. Using both would make the path fork, which is not a path.

questions.topic: Problem · Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.q: Return the path itself.
questions.a: Have each call also return the nodes of its best branch, and when best improves, store the left branch reversed, the node, and the right branch.

questions.q: What does the extra height 0 at the end do?
questions.a: It is lower than every bar, so it pops everything still on the stack and their rectangles get measured. Without it, increasing bars would never be resolved.

questions.q: Why store indices rather than heights?
questions.a: The width of a rectangle comes from positions. An index gives the position and, through the array, the height.

questions.q: Use this to find the largest rectangle of 1s in a grid.
questions.a: Treat each row as the base of a histogram whose bar heights count consecutive 1s above it, and run this algorithm on every row. O(rows × cols).

questions.q: Why can need go negative?
questions.a: A negative value records a surplus: the window holds more of that character than required. It lets the shrink step know that removing one does not break the window.

questions.q: Return all shortest windows.
questions.a: When a window ties the best length, add its start to a list instead of ignoring it; clear the list when a strictly shorter window is found.

questions.q: What if the characters of t must appear in order?
questions.a: Then it is a subsequence problem. Track for each position the latest start from which t can be matched in order, using DP or a forward and backward scan.

questions.q: Solve it by merging pairs of lists.
questions.a: Merge lists in pairs so the number of lists halves each round. There are log k rounds and each touches all N nodes: O(N log k), with no heap.

questions.q: Why is merging one list at a time into the result slower?
questions.a: The growing result is rescanned for every list, so early nodes are compared again and again: O(N · k) in total.

questions.q: How would this work with files too large for memory?
questions.a: Read one block from each file, keep the current smallest items in a heap, and write output in blocks. This is the merge phase of external sorting.

questions.topic: Problem · Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.q: Use in-order and post-order instead.
questions.a: The last value in post-order is the root. Process post-order from the end and build the right subtree before the left.

questions.topic: Problem · Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.q: Why are pre-order and post-order alone not enough?
questions.a: Both list the root at an end but neither shows where the left subtree stops, so a node with a single child could be on either side.

questions.topic: Problem · Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.q: What breaks with duplicate values?
questions.a: A value's position in the in-order list is no longer unique, so the split point is ambiguous and several trees fit.

questions.topic: Problem · Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.q: Do it level by level instead.
questions.a: Write values in BFS order with a marker for each missing child. To read, keep a queue of parents and give each the next two tokens as its children.

questions.topic: Problem · Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.q: How would you make the string shorter?
questions.a: Drop trailing markers, use a compact binary encoding, or for a BST store pre-order alone, since the ordering rule recovers the shape.

questions.topic: Problem · Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
questions.q: Why are the markers necessary?
questions.a: Without them, different trees give the same sequence of values. The markers record where each subtree ends.

questions.q: Search from both ends at once.
questions.a: Run BFS from the start and from the end alternately, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stop when the two meet. It explores far fewer words.

questions.q: Return the chain itself.
questions.a: Record for each discovered word the word it came from, then walk back from the end word to the start and reverse the list.

questions.q: Why remove a word when it is discovered rather than when it is processed?
questions.a: If removal waited until processing, the same word could be queued several times from different parents within one level, wasting work.

questions.q: Only count the solutions.
questions.a: Keep the same search but increment a counter at row n instead of building the board strings.

questions.q: Why do row − col and row + col identify diagonals?
questions.a: Moving one step down-right adds 1 to both row and column, so row − col stays the same. Moving down-left adds 1 to the row and subtracts 1 from the column, so row + col stays the same.

questions.q: Use bitmasks instead of sets.
questions.a: Represent the attacked columns and diagonals as three integers. The free squares in a row are the zero bits of their combination, and shifting the diagonal masks moves them to the next row.

questions.topic: Problem · Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.q: Why search the shorter array?
questions.a: The split in the other array is half − i. Searching the shorter one keeps that value from going negative or past the end, and makes the cost log of the smaller length.

questions.topic: Problem · Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.q: Find the kth smallest of the two arrays.
questions.a: Use the same partition idea with k in place of half, or repeatedly discard k / 2 elements from whichever array has the smaller value at that offset.

questions.topic: Problem · Median of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.q: What do the Int.min and Int.max stand for?
questions.a: They mean 'nothing on this side of the split'. Int.min never exceeds a right-hand value and Int.max is never below a left-hand value, so the comparisons still work at the ends.

questions.topic: Problem · Find Median from Data Stream
questions.q: Why does every number go through low first?
questions.a: It guarantees the ordering between the halves: the value that crosses to high is the largest of low after the new number joined, so nothing in low exceeds anything in high.

questions.topic: Problem · Find Median from Data Stream
questions.q: What if numbers can also be removed?
questions.a: Use two balanced trees or heaps with lazy deletion: mark removed values and discard them when they reach a top, tracking the real sizes separately.

questions.topic: Problem · Find Median from Data Stream
questions.q: What if all numbers are between 0 and 100?
questions.a: Keep 101 counters. Adding is O(1), and the median is found by walking the counters to the middle position, which is a constant amount of work.

questions.q: Remove finished words from the trie to speed things up.
questions.a: When a word is reported and its node has no children left, delete the node from its parent. Dead branches then stop attracting the search.

questions.q: Why store the whole word at the node?
questions.a: The DFS then knows the word as soon as it reaches the node, without rebuilding it from the path, and clearing it marks the word as already reported.

questions.q: How does this differ from Word Search?
questions.a: Word Search looks for one word, guided by its letters. Here many words are searched in a single pass, guided by the trie, so shared prefixes are walked once.

questions.q: Do it with O(1) extra space.
questions.a: Use bottom-up merge sort: merge runs of length 1, then 2, then 4, relinking nodes with a loop instead of recursion. No call stack is needed.

questions.q: Why start fast one node ahead of slow?
questions.a: With fast one ahead, slow stops at the last node of the first half, which is the node whose next must be cut. For two nodes this splits them one and one instead of looping forever.

questions.q: Why is merge sort preferred for linked lists?
questions.a: Merging relinks nodes without extra arrays, and splitting needs no random access. Quicksort and heapsort both rely on indexing.

questions.q: Do it with BFS.
questions.a: Put the start node in a queue and its copy in the dictionary. For each node taken from the queue, look at its neighbours: create and queue copies for unseen ones, and append each neighbour's copy to the current copy.

questions.q: Why must the copy be registered before the loop?
questions.a: A cycle leads back to a node whose neighbours are still being copied. If its copy were not yet registered, the recursion would create another copy and never finish.

questions.q: How would you copy a linked list that has random pointers?
questions.a: Use a dictionary from original node to copy in two passes: first create all the copies, then set each copy's next and random through the dictionary.

questions.q: Why search from the oceans instead of from each cell?
questions.a: A search from each cell repeats work for neighbouring cells. Two searches from the edges visit every cell at most twice in total.

questions.q: Do it with BFS.
questions.a: Put all of one ocean's edge cells in a queue and expand to unmarked neighbours that are at least as high; repeat for the other ocean.

questions.q: What changes if water also flows diagonally?
questions.a: Use eight directions in the climb. Nothing else changes.

questions.topic: Problem · Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.q: How would you speed up patterns with many dots?
questions.a: Group stored words by length so a pattern only meets words of its own length, or keep counts of what lies below each node so impossible branches can be skipped.

questions.topic: Problem · Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.q: Support * matching any number of letters.
questions.a: At a star, try matching zero letters (stay on this node and advance the pattern) or one letter (move to each child and keep the star). Memoise on node and pattern position.

questions.topic: Problem · Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.q: Why not use a hash set?
questions.a: A hash set answers exact lookups only. A pattern with dots would have to be compared with every stored word.

questions.q: How many rooms are needed if they do overlap?
questions.a: That is Meeting Rooms II: the answer is the largest number of meetings running at the same time.

questions.q: Return the conflicting pair.
questions.a: Return the two neighbours at the point where the check fails; after sorting they are a genuine overlapping pair.

questions.q: What if meetings arrive one at a time?
questions.a: Keep the meetings in a structure ordered by start time. On insertion, compare only with the neighbour before and the neighbour after.

questions.q: Solve it with a min-heap of end times.
questions.a: Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use. For each meeting, pop the earliest end if it is not later than the start, then push this meeting's end. The largest heap size is the answer.

questions.q: Why may starts and ends be sorted independently?
questions.a: Only the number of meetings in progress matters, not which start pairs with which end. Sorted separately, the two lists still give the correct count at every moment.

questions.q: Assign an actual room number to each meeting.
questions.a: Keep a heap of (end time, room) pairs and a pool of free room numbers; when a room's end time passes, return its number to the pool.

questions.topic: Problem · Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
questions.q: Solve it with DFS.
questions.a: Build an adjacency list, then run DFS from every unvisited node, counting how many times a search starts.

questions.topic: Problem · Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
questions.q: Edges arrive over time: report the count after each.
questions.a: Union Find handles this directly: process each edge as it arrives and report the current count.

questions.topic: Problem · Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
questions.q: How do you tell whether the graph is a tree?
questions.a: It must have exactly n − 1 edges and a single component. Equivalently, no edge may join two nodes that are already connected, and the final count must be 1.
